lessons.title: what is djing?

song.why: a clap on two and four, the beat a dj counts to

lessons.learn: What a DJ actually does, why the beat never stops, and how DJs count so they know when to bring the next track in.
youCan: say what a dj's job is on a night
hear two tracks playing in time as one
count beats, bars and phrases like a dj
play the backbeat into your song

say.mentor:
This is the kind of groove a DJ plays all night. Kick on every beat, a clap on two and four, hats in between.
A DJ's job is simple to say and hard to do: keep people moving. One track ends, the next is already playing, and the floor never notices the join. Everything you learn in this world is about making those joins feel like one long piece of music.
say.straight:
A typical dance groove: kick on every beat, clap on two and four, hats between.
A DJ keeps the music going without gaps, moving from one track to the next so the room keeps dancing. This world teaches how to make those changes smooth.
say.eli5:
Hear that? That is the kind of beat that makes people dance.
A DJ plays songs one after another without ever stopping, so the dancing never stops either. The trick is to slide from one song into the next so nobody notices the change.

say.mentor:
Tap track a, then track b, then both. That last one is what DJing sounds like.
Two different tracks at the same speed, lined up so their kicks hit at exactly the same moment. When they line up, they sound like one bigger groove. When they don't, the kicks flam against each other and it sounds like a train wreck. Getting them to line up is called beatmatching, and it is the first real skill you will learn here.
say.straight:
Play a, b, then both. Two tracks, same tempo, kicks aligned: that is a mix.
If the kicks line up, the two tracks become one groove. If they drift, you hear double kicks and it falls apart. Lining them up is beatmatching, the core DJ skill.
say.eli5:
Tap track a, then track b, then both together.
When both play together and their booms happen at the same time, they sound like one big song. If the booms don't line up, it sounds messy, like two people clapping out of time. Making them line up is called beatmatching.

deeper.title: where it came from
deeper.say: In the 1970s disco DJs in New York started blending records instead of stopping between them, using two turntables and a mixer. Hip hop DJs in the Bronx looped the drum breaks of records the same way. Every DJ setup since, CDJs, controllers, laptops, does the same job.

say.mentor:
DJs are always counting, even when it looks like they are just nodding along. Count with the groove: one, two, three, four. That is one bar. The clap lands on two and four.
Bars come in groups, usually eight bars, called a phrase. Dance tracks change at the start of a phrase: a new sound comes in, the bass drops out, a big moment arrives. So a DJ brings the next track in at the start of a phrase, and the change lands where the dancers expect something to happen.
say.straight:
Count one to four with the groove: that is a bar, with the clap on two and four.
Eight bars make a phrase. Tracks change on phrase boundaries, so DJs start their transitions on the first beat of a phrase. That way the mix lines up with the music's structure.
say.eli5:
Count along: one, two, three, four. That is one bar. Hear the clap on two and four?
Songs change every eight bars or so, like chapters in a story. DJs count those so they can bring the next song in right when a new chapter starts.

deeper.title: why two and four
deeper.say: The clap or snare on two and four is called the backbeat. It gives the steady kick a push and pull, and it is what most people clap along to without thinking.

say.mentor:
To mix you need to feel where two and four are, so play them. This clap goes into your song, on top of whatever is already there.
Press rec, let the four clicks go by, then tap the clap pad on beat two and beat four. Count out loud if it helps: one, CLAP, three, CLAP. Any clap that comes in early or late shows up red, so you can play it again.
say.straight: Record a clap on two and four. Press rec, wait out the count-in, then tap clap on beats two and four. Off-beat hits show red.
say.eli5: Your turn! Press rec and wait for four clicks. Then count one, two, three, four, and tap the clap pad on two and on four. If a clap is too early or late it turns red, so you can try again.

steps.q: What is a DJ's main job on a night?
options: keep people dancing by moving from track to track without gaps
play one song at a time with breaks between
steps.why: The music never stops. A DJ chains tracks together so the floor keeps moving.

whyWrong.1: Gaps are exactly what a DJ avoids.
whyWrong.2: Volume matters, but it is not the job.
whyWrong.3: Some DJs talk, but the job is the music.

steps.q: Two tracks play together and you hear double kicks. What is wrong?
options: their beats are not lined up
steps.why: Double kicks mean the beats are not hitting at the same moment. Lining them up is beatmatching.

whyWrong.1: Quiet or loud, the kicks would still clash if they are not lined up.
whyWrong.2: Keys affect the notes. Double kicks are a timing problem.
whyWrong.3: A good mix sounds like one groove, not two.

steps.q: Where does the clap usually land in a dance groove?
steps.why: The clap or snare on two and four is the backbeat.

whyWrong.1: That is where the kick goes in four on the floor.
whyWrong.2: One is where the bar starts. The clap comes on two and four.
whyWrong.3: Between the beats is where hats usually sit.

steps.q: When does a DJ usually bring the next track in?
options: at the start of a phrase
in the middle of a bar
steps.why: Tracks change on phrases, usually every eight bars, so starting there makes the mix feel natural.

whyWrong.1: Mid-bar changes sound like a mistake.
whyWrong.2: Feel matters, but timing it to a phrase is what makes it smooth.
whyWrong.3: Waiting for the end leaves no time to blend.

steps.q: How many bars are usually in a phrase?
steps.why: Eight bars is the usual phrase in dance music, often grouped into bigger sections of 16 or 32.

whyWrong.1: Two bars is short. Most changes come every eight.
whyWrong.2: Dance music almost always counts in fours and eights.
whyWrong.3: Sixty-four bars is a whole section, made of several phrases.

steps.next: Next: the gear. Decks, a mixer and headphones, and what each one is for.

lessons.title: the gear

song.why: you'll mix your own song against other tracks, so first you learn the desk

lessons.learn: Two decks and a mixer: what the channel faders, the low eq and the crossfader do, with your song on one deck and a track from the bank on the other.
youCan: say what each part of a dj setup does
move between two tracks with the crossfader
turn a track's low end down with its eq

say.mentor: A dj plays two tracks at once and moves between them so the music never stops. That's all the gear is for: two decks to play the tracks, and a mixer in the middle to blend them. Tap through track a, track b and both in time to hear what a blend sounds like.
say.straight: Two decks play two tracks; the mixer blends them. Tap through to hear each, then both together.
say.eli5: A dj has two music players and a mixer in the middle. They play two songs and slide from one to the other so the dancing never stops.

say.mentor:
This is your desk. Deck a is your own song. Deck b is a track from the bank; pick a different one below if you like. Each deck has a channel fader, how loud it is, and a low knob, which turns its bass up or down.
The wide slider in the middle is the crossfader. All the way left you only hear deck a, all the way right only deck b, in the middle both. Slide it all the way to b, then all the way back to a.
say.straight: Deck a: your song. Deck b: a bank track. Channel faders set each deck's level, low knobs its bass. The crossfader blends between them: slide it fully to b, then back to a.
say.eli5: Your song is on deck a. Another song is on deck b. The big sideways slider picks which one you hear. Slide it all the way to b, then all the way back to a.

say.mentor: One piece of gear you can't see here: headphones. On a real mixer each deck has a cue button that sends it to your headphones only, so you can hear and line up the next track before the crowd does. It's the most important habit in djing, and you'll use it once you play on real gear.
say.straight: Real mixers have a cue button per deck that sends it to your headphones only, so you prepare the next track without the crowd hearing.
say.eli5: Djs wear headphones so they can listen to the next song secretly before everyone else hears it.

steps.q: What does the crossfader do?
options: blends between deck a and deck b
steps.why: Left is deck a, right is deck b, the middle is both.

whyWrong.1: That's the tempo fader.
whyWrong.3: Recording is separate.

steps.q: What is a channel fader for?
options: which deck you hear in headphones
steps.why: Each deck has its own volume fader.

whyWrong.1: That's tempo.
whyWrong.3: Key is a property of the track.

steps.q: Why do djs use headphones?
options: to hear the next track before the crowd does
because the speakers are too quiet
steps.why: Cue lets you line up the next track in private.

whyWrong.1: They want to hear the room too.
whyWrong.3: Recording is done from the mixer.

steps.next: Next: tempo and bpm. Two tracks at different speeds, and matching them by ear.

lessons.title: tempo and bpm

song.why: tracks only blend when they run at the same tempo

lessons.learn: Why two tracks fall apart when their tempos differ, and matching them by ear with the tempo fader.
youCan: hear when two tracks are drifting apart
match a track's tempo to yours with the tempo fader
check the match with the numbers

say.mentor: Two tracks only blend when they run at exactly the same speed. Even one bpm apart, the kicks start together and slowly slide apart, first a flam, then a gallop, then a mess. A dj's first skill is hearing that and fixing it.
say.straight: Tracks at different tempos drift apart: flam, then gallop, then chaos. Matching tempos fixes it.
say.eli5: If two songs go at different speeds, their booms stop lining up. It sounds like a horse galloping. Djs make them the same speed.

say.mentor:
Deck b is playing at its own tempo, a little off yours. Listen to the kicks: they drift. Watch the two rows of lights too: when the tempos match, they flash together.
Move deck b's tempo fader until the drifting stops. Use your ears first, then check the numbers. That's beatmatching.
say.straight: Deck b is off your tempo. Move its tempo fader until the kicks stop drifting and the lights flash together. Ears first, numbers second.
say.eli5: The other song is going a bit too fast or slow. Slide its tempo slider until both booms happen at the same time and the lights blink together.

steps.hint: If the kicks gallop faster and faster, you're moving the wrong way.

say.mentor: Modern decks have a sync button that matches tempos for you. Most working djs use it, and that's fine. But learning to do it by ear means you'll hear when something's off, fix it when sync gets it wrong, and play on any gear, including vinyl.
say.straight: Sync matches tempo automatically and most djs use it. Matching by ear still matters for fixing mistakes and playing any gear.
say.eli5: Some players have a button that does this for you. Learning to do it yourself means you'll always know when it sounds right.

steps.q: Two tracks are 2 bpm apart. What do you hear?
steps.why: Even small differences add up beat after beat.

whyWrong.1: Two bpm drifts audibly within a few bars.
whyWrong.3: The key stays the same on modern decks.

steps.q: Matching tempos by ear is called?
steps.why: Beatmatching, lining up the beats of two tracks.

whyWrong.1: Crossfading moves between decks.
whyWrong.3: Eq mixing is for the bass swap.

steps.next: Next: your first blend. Bring a track in, swap the bass, and let your song go.

lessons.title: your first blend

song.why: this is the moment you mix your own song like a dj

lessons.learn: A full blend: bring a track in under yours, swap the bass, and hand over to it, all on your own song.
youCan: bring a second track in under yours
swap the bass with the low eq
finish a blend with the crossfader or fader

say.mentor: This is the move at the heart of djing. Two tracks, matched, playing together, and you slowly hand the room from one to the other. The trick is the bass: two bass lines at once turn to mud, so you swap them.
say.straight: A blend hands over from one track to the next. Only one bass at a time, so you swap them with the eq.
say.eli5: Now the big one: start with your song, sneak the other song in, swap their basses, and let your song fade away.

say.mentor:
Your song is on deck a, playing out loud. Deck b is matched and waiting with its fader down.
One: bring deck b's fader up. Hear both tracks? Two: turn deck a's low knob down, so only deck b's bass is left. That's the bass swap. Three: crossfade over to b, or pull deck a's fader down. You've just mixed out of your own song.
say.straight: Bring deck b's fader up, cut deck a's low, then crossfade to b or pull a down.
say.eli5: Push deck b's slider up. Turn deck a's low knob down. Then slide over to b.

steps.hint: Do it slowly. A blend usually takes 16 or 32 bars.

steps.q: Why do djs swap the bass instead of playing both?
options: two bass lines together turn to mud
only one deck can have bass
steps.why: Two low ends stack up into a muddy blur.

whyWrong.1: It's about clashing, not level.
whyWrong.2: Both decks can, it just sounds bad together.
whyWrong.3: Eq doesn't touch tempo.

steps.q: What's the first move of a blend?
options: bring the new track's fader up
steps.why: First you get the new track in, quietly, under the old one.

whyWrong.1: You'd lose all the low end.
whyWrong.2: Then it's a cut, not a blend.
whyWrong.3: Key is chosen when you pick the track.

steps.next: Next: phrasing. When to bring the next track in so it lands on the one.

lessons.title: phrasing, count in eights

song.why: a track that comes in on the one of a phrase sounds planned; one that comes in anywhere sounds like a mistake

lessons.learn: Dance music moves in phrases of eight bars. Bring the next track in on bar one of a phrase and the blend sounds like part of the music.
youCan: count bars in phrases of eight
bring a track in on the one of a phrase

say.mentor: Count the bars: one, two, three, all the way to eight, then back to one. Dance tracks change every 8, 16 or 32 bars: a new hat, the bass dropping out, a riser. Those blocks are phrases, and djs count them without thinking.
say.straight: Dance tracks change every 8, 16 or 32 bars. Those blocks are phrases.
say.eli5: Count the bars up to eight, then start again. Songs change at the start of each group of eight.

say.mentor: Watch the phrase counter on the screen: bar 1 of 8 up to 8 of 8. Deck b is matched and waiting with its fader down. Bring it up exactly as the counter goes back to bar one. If you bring it in mid phrase, pull it down and try again on the next one.
say.straight: Bring deck b's fader up right as the phrase counter returns to bar 1.
say.eli5: Watch the counter. When it says bar 1, push deck b's slider up.

steps.hint: Count down the last bar, four, three, two, one, go.

steps.q: How long is a typical phrase in dance music?
steps.why: Eight bars, often grouped into 16 and 32.

whyWrong.1: A beat is much shorter.
whyWrong.2: Dance music groups in fours and eights.
whyWrong.3: A song has many phrases.

steps.q: Why bring a track in on bar one of a phrase?
options: the change lines up with the music, so it sounds planned
steps.why: Changes in the music happen on phrase starts, so your blend lands with them.

whyWrong.1: Volume isn't the reason.
whyWrong.3: Nothing to do with power.

steps.next: Next: eq mixing, the bass swap on its own.

lessons.title: eq mixing

song.why: only one bass at a time keeps a blend clean

lessons.learn: The low, mid and high knobs on a mixer, and the bass swap: the move that keeps two tracks from turning to mud.
youCan: use the low eq to swap basses
hear mud when two basses overlap

say.mentor: Tap both, in time. Two kicks and two bass lines stacked up: the low end gets thick and muddy. The fix every dj uses is the eq on the mixer, three knobs per channel for low, mid and high.
say.straight: Two tracks together: the lows pile up. The mixer eq fixes that.
say.eli5: Both songs together get a bit muddy down low. The mixer knobs fix it.

say.mentor: Deck b is matched. Bring its fader up and listen to the low end get muddy. Now turn deck a's low knob down and keep deck b's low up. Suddenly it's clean: one kick, one bass, and the rest of both tracks still playing. That's the bass swap.
say.straight: Fader b up, low a down, low b up. One bass at a time.
say.eli5: Push deck b up, then turn deck a's low knob down. Now only one bass plays.

steps.q: What does the low knob on a mixer channel do?
options: turns that track's bass up or down
steps.why: It's an eq for the low end of that channel.

whyWrong.1: Key stays the same.
whyWrong.3: The play button starts it.

steps.q: In a bass swap, what happens?
options: one track's low goes down as the other's comes up
steps.why: Only one bass at a time.

whyWrong.1: That's the mud you're avoiding.
whyWrong.3: The crossfader can stay put.

steps.next: Next: cue and headphones, getting the next track ready in private.

lessons.title: cue and headphones

song.why: you always line up the next track before the room hears it

lessons.learn: What the cue button does, how djs listen to two things at once, and getting deck b ready before it goes out.
youCan: say what cue does
prepare a track before bringing it in

say.mentor: On a real mixer, every channel has a cue button. Press it and that deck goes to your headphones only, so you can hear it, match it and find the right spot while the room still hears the other track. Most djs keep one ear on the headphones and one on the room.
say.straight: Cue sends a deck to your headphones only, so you prepare it in private.
say.eli5: The cue button lets you hear the next song in your headphones before anyone else.

say.mentor: Imagine deck b is only in your headphones. Match it to your song by ear, the way you would in the booth, before the room hears it. When the lights flash together, it's ready to go out.
say.straight: Match deck b as if it were only in your headphones.
say.eli5: Make deck b the same speed as your song, like you're getting it ready in secret.

steps.q: What does the cue button do?
options: sends a deck to your headphones only
plays the track to the room
steps.why: Cue is your private listening.

whyWrong.1: That's the channel fader.
whyWrong.3: Key stays the same.

steps.next: Next: the cut and the long blend.

lessons.title: the cut and the long blend

song.why: knowing when to blend for a minute and when to cut on the one is half of djing

lessons.learn: Two ways to change tracks: the long blend over 16 or 32 bars, and the cut, a hard switch on the one.
youCan: cut from one track to another on the one
choose between a cut and a blend

say.mentor: Some changes take a minute: both tracks playing, basses swapped, the old one fading out. Others are instant: a hard switch on the one, like a jump cut in a film. Both are tools. Long blends suit deep, hypnotic sets; cuts suit high energy and hip hop.
say.straight: Long blend: both tracks for 16 or 32 bars. Cut: a hard switch on the one.
say.eli5: You can change songs slowly, or super fast in one move.

say.mentor: Both decks are matched. Deck a is playing. Slam the crossfader from a to b in one quick move, right on the one of a bar. It should sound like the music meant to change there.
say.straight: Slam the crossfader from a to b in one quick move on the one.
say.eli5: Swipe the big slider from a to b really fast, right on the boom.

steps.q: When does a cut usually land?
options: on the one of a bar or phrase
at the end of the song
steps.why: On the one, so it sounds planned.

whyWrong.1: Mid beat sounds like a mistake.
whyWrong.3: You'd lose the whole track.

steps.next: Next: picking tracks that work together.

lessons.title: picking tracks

song.why: a set is only as good as the tracks you choose to put next to each other

lessons.learn: What makes two tracks work together: tempo, key and energy, and picking from the bank.
youCan: pick tracks with nearby tempos
pick tracks whose keys fit

say.mentor: Djs spend more time choosing tracks than mixing them. Three things make two tracks sit together: a tempo close enough to match, keys that fit, and an energy that makes sense next to each other.
say.straight: Tempo, key and energy decide whether two tracks work together.
say.eli5: Good djs pick songs that go well together: similar speed, matching notes, same energy.

say.mentor: Your song's key is on deck a. Go through the bank on deck b and find a track whose key fits yours: the same Camelot number, or one step either side with the same letter. The screen tells you when it fits. Listen to how the melodies sit together.
say.straight: Pick a bank track whose key fits yours: same number, or one either side with the same letter.
say.eli5: Find a song for deck b that the screen says fits. Listen to how nice they sound together.

steps.q: Which three things make two tracks work together?
steps.why: Tempo to match, key to fit, energy to flow.

whyWrong.1: None of these change how they mix.
whyWrong.2: Those don't decide if they blend.
whyWrong.3: Those are mixing controls.

steps.next: Next: key and harmonic mixing, up close.

lessons.title: key and harmonic mixing

song.why: tracks in keys that fit blend without a sour clash

lessons.learn: The Camelot wheel, the code djs use for keys, and finding tracks that fit your own song's key.
youCan: read a Camelot code
say which keys fit together

say.mentor: When two tracks in clashing keys play together, the melodies rub and it sounds sour even if the beats are perfect. Djs use the Camelot wheel: every key gets a number and a letter, and keys that fit sit next to each other on the wheel.
say.straight: Clashing keys sound sour. The Camelot wheel numbers keys so fitting ones sit side by side.
say.eli5: Some songs sound bad together because their notes clash. Djs use number codes to find songs that fit.

say.mentor: Twelve numbers round a wheel, A for minor and B for major. A key fits the same code, one step either side with the same letter (8A fits 7A and 9A), or the same number with the other letter (8A fits 8B). Your song's code is shown on deck a.
say.straight: Same code, one either side with the same letter, or the same number across.
say.eli5: Look for the same number, or one bigger or smaller with the same letter.

say.mentor: Find a bank track that fits your song's key. Try one that clashes first and listen for the sourness, then one that fits.
say.straight: Find a bank track that fits your key. Try a clashing one first to hear the difference.
say.eli5: Find a song that fits yours. Try one that doesn't first, and listen.

steps.q: Your song is 8A. Which key fits?
steps.why: One step on the wheel with the same letter.

whyWrong.1: Too far round the wheel.
whyWrong.3: Different letter and number.

steps.next: Next: cue points and loops.

lessons.title: cue points and loops

song.why: a cue on the one lets you start the next track exactly where you want

lessons.learn: Cue points mark where a track should start. Loops hold a section so you can stretch a blend.
youCan: say what a cue point is
start a track on the one of a phrase

say.mentor: A cue point is a marker you set on a track, usually on the first kick of a phrase. Press play from it and the track starts exactly there, on the one. Loops do the opposite job: hold four bars round and round, so you have time to finish a blend.
say.straight: Cue: a marker where the track starts. Loop: repeat a section to buy time.
say.eli5: A cue point is a bookmark in a song. A loop plays the same bit over and over.

say.mentor: Deck b is cued to its first kick. Bring it in on bar one of your song's phrase so the two ones land together.
say.straight: Bring deck b in on bar one of the phrase.
say.eli5: Push deck b up when the counter says bar 1.

steps.q: Where do djs usually set a cue point?
options: on the first kick of a phrase
in the middle of a breakdown
steps.why: On the one, so the track starts on time.

whyWrong.1: A breakdown is a hard place to start.
whyWrong.2: The end won't help you start.
whyWrong.3: It has to line up.

steps.next: Next: reading waveforms.

lessons.title: reading waveforms

song.why: seeing the drop coming lets you plan the blend

lessons.learn: What a waveform shows, how to spot a breakdown and a drop, and planning a blend around them.
youCan: spot a breakdown and a drop in a waveform
plan a blend from what you see

say.mentor: Every dj screen shows a waveform: the track drawn as its loudness over time. Thin parts are quiet, fat parts loud. A breakdown is a thin stretch, the drop is where it fattens again. Seeing that lets you plan: bring the next track in during the outro, never across someone else's drop.
say.straight: A waveform is loudness over time. Thin is a breakdown, the fat part after is the drop.
say.eli5: The wiggly line shows loud and quiet parts. A thin bit is a breakdown, then it gets fat at the drop.

say.mentor: Play around: bring deck b in, swap the bass, crossfade. Think about where you'd do it in a full track: over the intro and outro, not across a drop.
say.straight: Free play. Think about where in a track you'd blend.
say.eli5: Play with the mixer however you like.

steps.q: What does a thin stretch of waveform usually mean?
options: a quiet part, like a breakdown
steps.why: Quiet parts draw thin.

whyWrong.1: Loud parts draw fat.
whyWrong.2: It's how the track is made.
whyWrong.3: The bass usually makes it fatter.

steps.next: Next: the energy arc of a set.

lessons.title: the energy arc

song.why: a set that goes somewhere keeps a room for hours

lessons.learn: How djs shape a set: warm up, build, peak, and come down, and ordering tracks by tempo and energy.
youCan: order tracks into a warm up, build and peak
say why the first hour is lower energy

say.mentor: A set isn't a playlist of your favourite bangers. It's a journey: a warm up that lets people arrive, a build, a peak, and sometimes a come down. Djs often creep the tempo up a few bpm across a night and save the biggest tracks for the peak.
say.straight: A set goes warm up, build, peak. Tempo and energy rise across the night.
say.eli5: A dj set starts gentle, gets bigger and bigger, then has a huge moment.

say.mentor: Look at the bank's tempos: 126 up to 135. In your head, put them in order for a set that builds. Then blend from your song into the one you'd play next.
say.straight: Order the bank by tempo for a set that builds, then blend into your next pick.
say.eli5: Put the bank songs from slowest to fastest in your head, then mix into the next one.

steps.q: Why is a warm up set usually lower energy?
options: people are still arriving and settling in
steps.why: You build the room before you peak.

whyWrong.1: Speakers don't need warming.
whyWrong.2: It's a choice for the crowd.
whyWrong.3: It's craft, not a rule.

steps.next: Next: effects in performance.

lessons.title: effects in performance

song.why: an echo out turns an ending into a moment

lessons.learn: Echo and filter on the mixer, and the echo out: letting the last beat of a track ring away.
youCan: do an echo out
use effects with restraint

say.mentor: Mixers have effects: echo, filter, reverb. The classic move is the echo out: turn the echo up on the outgoing track and cut its fader, so the last hit repeats and fades while the new track carries on. Used once in a while it's a moment. Used every mix it's noise.
say.straight: Echo out: echo up on the old track, fader down, let it ring.
say.eli5: Turn on the echo, then pull the song down. The last sound echoes away.

say.mentor: Both decks are playing and matched. Turn deck a's echo up, then pull deck a's fader down (or crossfade to b). Listen to your song echo away under the new track.
say.straight: Echo a up, then fader a down.
say.eli5: Turn up echo on deck a, then slide deck a down.

steps.q: What is an echo out?
options: echo on the old track as its fader comes down
steps.why: The last beat repeats and fades as the new track takes over.

whyWrong.1: The music keeps going.
whyWrong.3: Key isn't involved.

steps.next: Next: preparing a set.

lessons.title: preparing a set

song.why: preparation is what lets you relax and read the room

lessons.learn: Crates, rough orders, backups: how working djs prepare, and practising a transition before the gig.
youCan: build a crate for a set
practise a transition before the gig

say.mentor: Working djs bring more tracks than they need, sorted into crates by mood or energy. They plan a rough order, not a script, so they can react to the room. And they bring backups: a second USB, a second set of headphones. The best way to prepare is to practise the hard transitions until they're easy.
say.straight: Bring more tracks than you need, sorted by mood. Rough order, not a script. Backups. Practise the hard blends.
say.eli5: Pack lots of songs in folders. Have a plan but be ready to change it. Bring spare stuff.

say.mentor: Practise one transition now: your song into a bank track, the full blend.
say.straight: Practise one full blend.
say.eli5: Practise one mix from start to finish.

steps.q: Why do djs bring more tracks than they'll play?
options: so they can react to the room
steps.why: A rough plan with options lets you follow the crowd.

whyWrong.1: It's about choices.
whyWrong.3: It's about music, not space.

steps.next: Next: recording your set.

lessons.title: recording your set

song.why: a recording is how promoters and friends hear what you do

lessons.learn: Recording a mix, what to listen for when you play it back, and sending it to a promoter.
youCan: record a short mix
listen back and fix one thing

say.mentor: Every working dj records their sets, even at home. Listening back is the fastest way to improve: you'll hear a drift you missed, a blend that went on too long. A short, clean recording of your best blends is also how promoters decide who to book, CCD included.
say.straight: Record your sets, listen back, fix one thing. A short clean mix is how promoters book you.
say.eli5: Record your mixes and listen back. You'll hear what to fix.

say.mentor: Do your cleanest blend now, as if it's being recorded: match, bring b in on the phrase, swap the bass, crossfade.
say.straight: Do your cleanest blend.
say.eli5: Do your best mix.

steps.q: Why record practice sets?
options: listening back shows what to fix
steps.why: You hear mistakes you missed while playing.

whyWrong.1: Recording doesn't change volume.
whyWrong.2: It's a habit, not a rule.
whyWrong.3: Key is untouched.

steps.next: Next: from dj to artist, playing your own track in your set.

lessons.title: from dj to artist

song.why: the djs people remember play music nobody else has

lessons.learn: Playing your own track in a set, and what it takes to get booked at a CCD night.
youCan: play your own song in a set
say what makes a dj an artist

say.mentor: The djs people travel for play music nobody else has: their own tracks, edits and remixes. You made a song in this app. Now you can play it out, blended with other tracks, like at a CCD night. The best learner tracks and mixes get played at our nights.
say.straight: The djs people remember play their own tracks. Yours is ready to play out.
say.eli5: The best djs play songs they made themselves. You made one!

say.mentor: Your song is on deck a. Play the bank track into it, or out of it, your choice: the full blend, your song in a set.
say.straight: Blend your song with a bank track.
say.eli5: Mix your song with another one.

steps.q: What makes djs stand out?
steps.why: Your own tracks and edits are your signature.

whyWrong.1: Gear helps, but sound matters more.
whyWrong.3: Length isn't either.

steps.next: That's the dj world. Send your song and your mix to CCD.

lessons.title: bonus, reading the room

song.why: great djs play the room, not the playlist

lessons.learn: What a dancefloor tells you, and what to do when it dips.
youCan: read a dancefloor
choose the next track for the room

say.mentor: Look at feet, not faces. A full floor moving together is working. People drifting to the bar or checking phones means it's dipped. The fix is rarely a bigger track. Often it's something more familiar, or a groove change, or a slightly lower energy track that resets ears.
say.straight: Watch feet. When it dips, try familiar, a groove change, or a reset.
say.eli5: Watch people's feet. If they stop dancing, try a different kind of song.

steps.q: The floor is emptying. What's often better than your biggest track?
options: something familiar or a groove change
steps.why: A reset often brings people back better than more intensity.

whyWrong.1: More of the same rarely fixes it.
whyWrong.3: Louder doesn't help.

steps.next: Back to the set: effects in performance.

lessons.title: bonus, handling mistakes

song.why: everyone trainwrecks; the pros fix it before the room notices

lessons.learn: What to do when two tracks drift apart mid blend, and staying calm.
youCan: fix a drifting blend fast

say.mentor: A trainwreck is when two tracks drift apart and the kicks gallop. It happens to everyone. The fix: pull the new track down fast, fix the tempo in your headphones, bring it back in on the next phrase. The crowd forgives a quick fix. They notice a long mess.
say.straight: Trainwreck: kicks gallop. Pull the new track out, fix it, bring it back on the next phrase.
say.eli5: When songs go out of time, take one away fast, fix it, try again.

say.mentor: Deck b is off. Fix it fast: match the tempo until the lights flash together.
say.straight: Match deck b fast.
say.eli5: Fix the speed of deck b.

steps.q: Two tracks start galloping mid blend. First move?
steps.why: Get the clash out of the room, then fix it.

whyWrong.1: Louder makes it worse.
whyWrong.3: It only gets messier.

steps.next: Back to the set: recording your set.

lessons.title: dj culture and history

song.why: the first trick in dj history was keeping a groove going across two decks, and you'll do it with your song

lessons.learn: Where djing came from, from radio to the Bronx, Chicago and Detroit, and the move that started it, played on your own song.
youCan: name the scenes modern djing grew out of
say what Kool Herc did with two copies of one record
keep a groove going across two decks

say.mentor:
Two grooves, one beat. In the Bronx in the 1970s, a dj called Kool Herc noticed the crowd went wildest in the break, the short part of a funk record where everything drops out except the drums.
So he bought two copies of the same record. He played the break on one, then the break on the other, back and forth, so it never ended. That back and forth between two decks is the root of everything you'll do in this world.
say.straight: In the 1970s Kool Herc played the drum break of a record on one deck, then the same break on a second copy, back and forth, so it never ended. Hip-hop djing started there.
say.eli5: A long time ago a dj called Kool Herc saw people loved the drum part of a song most. He used two copies of the record and switched between them so the drum part kept going.

say.mentor:
The name came first, from radio. In the 1940s and 50s, radio presenters playing records got called disc jockeys, and records started replacing live bands.
Then came the scenes. In the Bronx, Herc's breaks gave birth to hip-hop djing, and Grandmaster Flash took turntable technique further, using the records themselves as a rhythm instrument. In Chicago, Frankie Knuckles played at a club called the Warehouse, and the music there became house. In Detroit, Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, known as the Belleville Three, made techno.
None of these were big business. They were underground scenes built by their communities, and house grew out of Black and gay club culture. Knowing that is part of carrying it on.
say.straight: Radio gave us the name disc jockey in the 1940s and 50s. Then the Bronx gave us hip-hop djing (Kool Herc, Grandmaster Flash), Chicago gave us house (Frankie Knuckles at the Warehouse), and Detroit gave us techno (the Belleville Three). All underground, all built by their communities.
say.eli5: First, people on the radio played records and got called disc jockeys. Then new kinds of dance music grew in different cities: hip-hop in New York, house in Chicago, techno in Detroit.

deeper.title: detroit and techno
deeper.say: The Belleville Three were Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson. They made techno in Detroit in the 1980s: futuristic music from an industrial city.

deeper.title: turntablism
deeper.say: Turntablism treats the record player as an instrument. Scratching, cutting and juggling breaks are played the way you'd play a drum. You'll meet it again in the lessons on the crossfader and on digital vinyl.

say.mentor:
Now do Herc's move on your song. Deck a is your song, deck b a track from the bank. Slide the crossfader all the way to b, then all the way back to a.
Listen to the groove carry on across the switch. Herc did this with two copies of one record. You're doing it with two different tracks, which is exactly where djing went next.
say.straight: Deck a is your song, deck b a bank track. Slide the crossfader fully to b, then fully back to a, and keep the groove going.
say.eli5: Your song is on one side, another song on the other. Slide the big sideways slider all the way over, then all the way back. The music never stops.

steps.q: What did Kool Herc do with two copies of the same record?
options: played the break on one, then the other, to make it last
played both at once to make it louder
scratched one while the other played
steps.why: Switching between two copies made the drum break go on as long as the crowd wanted.

whyWrong.1: It was about making the break longer, not louder.
whyWrong.2: Scratching came after, with Grandmaster Flash and the turntablists.
whyWrong.3: Both copies were in play.

steps.q: Which city is house music linked to?
steps.why: Chicago, and a club called the Warehouse where Frankie Knuckles played.

whyWrong.1: Detroit gave us techno.
whyWrong.2: The Bronx gave us hip-hop djing.
whyWrong.3: London wasn't one of the scenes in this lesson.

steps.q: Where did the name disc jockey come from?
steps.why: Radio presenters playing records were the first disc jockeys.

whyWrong.1: Chicago clubs came decades later.
whyWrong.3: Cdjs are much newer than the name.

steps.next: Back to the song path: the gear. Two decks, a mixer, and your song on deck a.

lessons.title: the booth

song.why: your song only reaches a crowd if both decks come through the speakers at the same level

lessons.learn: The path your music takes from deck to speaker, setting levels so neither deck jumps out, and the soundcheck before the night starts.
youCan: follow the signal from deck to speakers
set two decks to the same loudness
soundcheck both decks before you play

say.mentor: Track a, track b, then both. Before a single blend, a dj has to get both of those out of the speakers at the right level. Walking into a booth and getting everything working is a skill of its own, and it's what stands between you and dead air, the silence when nothing is playing.
say.straight: Before you mix, both decks have to reach the speakers at the right level. Setting up the booth is a skill that prevents dead air.
say.eli5: Before a dj plays, they check that both music players come out of the speakers. Otherwise there might be no music at all.

say.mentor:
Sound travels in a line. The deck (a cdj or a laptop) feeds a channel on the mixer, the mixer's master output feeds an amplifier, and the amplifier feeds the speakers. Break any link and nothing comes out. That line is the signal chain.
Each channel also has a gain knob, which sets how strong the signal is as it comes in. Set it so the loud parts sit high on the meter without hitting the red, which is called clipping and sounds harsh. That's gain staging, and it's how two tracks end up at the same loudness before you touch a fader.
say.straight: Deck, mixer channel, master output, amplifier, speakers: the signal chain. Set each channel's gain so peaks sit high on the meter without clipping. That's gain staging.
say.eli5: The music goes from the player, into the mixer, out to a big amplifier, then to the speakers. A knob on each channel sets how strong it comes in: strong, but not so strong it crackles.

deeper.title: line and phono
deeper.say: Mixer channels expect one of two kinds of signal. Line is for cdjs and controllers. Phono is for the much quieter signal from a turntable. The wrong setting gives you a channel that's very quiet or distorted, so check the input switch on every channel you use.

deeper.title: the booth monitor
deeper.say: The booth monitor is a speaker in the dj booth just for you, with its own level, separate from the speakers the crowd hears. It's how you hear your mix clearly while the room's sound bounces around.

deeper.title: arrive early
deeper.say: Do the soundcheck before the crowd arrives: play a track on each deck and confirm sound reaches the speakers. A problem found during setup takes minutes to fix. Found at midnight, it's dead air.

say.mentor:
Here's your booth. Deck a is your song. Pick a track for deck b from the bank below.
Now soundcheck. Slide the crossfader all the way to a and listen, then all the way to b. Both should come through.
Then set the two channel faders so the decks sound about as loud as each other. When you crossfade, nothing should jump out. When it sounds even both ways, you're set up.
say.straight: Pick a bank track for deck b. Crossfade fully to a, then fully to b, to check both come through. Then set the channel faders so both decks sound equally loud.
say.eli5: Pick a song for deck b. Slide the big slider all the way one way, then the other, and check you hear each song. Then make both songs equally loud.

steps.q: Where does the sound go after the mixer's master output?
options: into an amplifier, then the speakers
steps.why: Master output, amplifier, speakers. That's the end of the signal chain.

whyWrong.1: The deck is where the sound starts.
whyWrong.2: Headphones get a separate cue feed.
whyWrong.3: The gain knob is at the start of each channel.

steps.q: What is gain staging?
options: setting each channel's input so it's strong but not clipping
turning everything up as far as it goes
putting the crossfader in the middle
steps.why: Strong enough to be clean, not so strong it clips.

whyWrong.1: Too loud clips and sounds harsh.
whyWrong.2: The crossfader is a different control.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is the pitch fader's job.

steps.q: A turntable is plugged into a channel set to line. What happens?
options: the channel is very quiet or sounds wrong
steps.why: Turntables need the phono setting. On line, the signal is far too weak.

whyWrong.1: Line expects a much stronger signal.
whyWrong.3: Input settings don't touch key.

steps.next: Back to the song path: tempo and bpm. Matching two tracks by ear.

lessons.title: rekordbox

song.why: before a track goes in a set a dj reads its bpm and key, and your song has both

lessons.learn: What rekordbox is, what its analysis finds in every track, and reading your own song's bpm and key the way a dj would.
youCan: say what rekordbox is for
read a track's bpm and key
use the key to pick a track that fits your song

say.mentor:
Every track has a speed and a key. The speed is its bpm, beats per minute. The key is the set of notes it's built on. Before a dj plays anything they want both numbers, and software works them out for you.
The one you'll meet in most clubs is rekordbox, made by Pioneer DJ, the company behind the cdjs, the club players you'll find in most booths.
say.straight: Every track has a bpm and a key. Djs want both before they play it. rekordbox, from Pioneer DJ, the maker of club cdjs, works them out for you.
say.eli5: Every song has a speed and a set of notes. Djs use a program called rekordbox that finds both for them.

say.mentor:
When you add a track, rekordbox analyses it. It finds the bpm, the key, the waveform (the picture of the sound over time) and the beat grid, a marker on every beat so the software knows where each one lands.
All your tracks live in one library called the collection. From there you build playlists and get your music ready to play out.
say.straight: Add a track and rekordbox analyses it: bpm, key, waveform and beat grid. Everything lives in your collection, where you build playlists.
say.eli5: When you add a song, rekordbox listens to it and works out its speed, its notes, and where every beat is. All your songs live in one big list.

deeper.title: two modes
deeper.say: rekordbox has two main ways of working. Export mode gets a usb drive ready with your analysed tracks and playlists, to plug into club cdjs. Performance mode turns rekordbox itself into the decks, played with a controller.

deeper.title: pro dj link
deeper.say: Pro dj link is the network connection between rekordbox and cdj hardware, so the software and the players can work together.

say.mentor:
Look at deck a. Next to your song's name you'll see its bpm and its key, written as a code like 8A. Those are the two things an analysis gives you.
Every bank track shows the same two numbers on its chip. Use them. Find a deck b track whose key fits your song: the screen tells you when it fits. You'll learn how the codes work properly in the key lesson.
say.straight: Deck a shows your song's bpm and key code. Each bank track shows its own. Pick a deck b track whose key fits yours.
say.eli5: Your song's speed and note code are on deck a. Each other song has its own code. Find one the screen says fits.

steps.q: What does rekordbox find when it analyses a track?
options: bpm, key, waveform and beat grid
steps.why: The four things a dj needs before playing a track.

whyWrong.1: It reads the music itself, not just the name.
whyWrong.2: That comes from the track's tags, not analysis.
whyWrong.3: Analysis doesn't know about popularity.

steps.q: What is the collection in rekordbox?
steps.why: Every track you've added, analysed and ready to organise.

whyWrong.1: Playlists are built from the collection.
whyWrong.3: The usb is what you export to.

steps.q: What is export mode for?
options: getting a usb ready for club cdjs
steps.why: It prepares your tracks and playlists on a usb you plug into the club players.

whyWrong.1: Recording is a separate job.
whyWrong.2: Effects are for playing, not preparing.
whyWrong.3: It's about files on a usb.

steps.next: Back to the song path: tempo and bpm. Matching two tracks by ear.

lessons.title: pulse and tempo

song.why: every song starts with a pulse, and yours starts with a kick you play in yourself, at a speed you choose

lessons.learn: The steady beat under every dance track, how fast it goes, and the first sound in your own song: a kick you play in and set to your own tempo.
youCan: feel the pulse of a track and count along with it
play a kick in on the beat
say what bpm means and roughly what speed house and techno sit at
set your song's tempo by ear

say.mentor:
Hear that thump? That's a kick drum, and it's playing the pulse: a steady beat that never speeds up or slows down. Every dance track you've ever moved to has one underneath it. It's the thing your foot taps to without asking.
Your song is going to start right here, with a pulse of your own.
say.straight: This is a kick drum playing the pulse: one hit on every beat, perfectly even. Every dance track is built on a pulse like this. Your song starts with one.
say.eli5:
Boom, boom, boom, boom. That's a kick drum. It's like a heartbeat for music: it goes at the same speed the whole time. When you tap your foot to a song, you're tapping to this.
Your song is going to start with a boom like this.

say.mentor:
Count with it, out loud if you can: one, two, three, four, then start again at one. Each kick is a beat. The pulse is just beats in a row.
Musicians count in fours almost all the time, because it's easy to feel and easy to dance to. You'll hear why that matters in the next lesson.
say.straight: Each kick is one beat. Count one to four and start again. Dance music almost always counts in fours.
say.eli5: Let's count the booms: one, two, three, four, and again, one, two, three, four. Every boom is called a beat. Musicians love counting to four.

say.mentor:
Now play the pulse yourself. This bar becomes the first thing in your song.
Press rec. You'll hear four clicks to count you in, so just listen. Then tap the kick pad once on each of the next four clicks. Any kick that lands early or late turns red, and you can play it again. Tap undo to take one back, hold it to start over.
say.straight: Record the pulse. Press rec, wait out four clicks, then tap the kick on each of the next four. Red means off the beat; undo takes one back, hold clears.
say.eli5: Your turn! Press the red rec button. Let four ticks go by, then tap the kick pad on every tick, four times. If a tap is too early or too late it goes red, so you can try that one again.

say.mentor:
That's your kick, looping. Now turn the knob and listen to what happens.
How fast the pulse goes is called the tempo, and it's counted in bpm: beats per minute. At 120 bpm there are two beats every second. Turn it down and everything feels heavier and lazier. Turn it up and it gets urgent. House usually lives around 120 to 128, techno a bit faster, garage and dubstep around 140.
Try the four speeds on the right, then pick the one that feels like your song. You can change it any time later.
say.straight: This is your kick at different speeds. Tempo is measured in bpm, beats per minute: 120 bpm is two beats a second. House sits around 120 to 128, techno a little higher, garage and dubstep near 140. Pick a tempo for your song.
say.eli5:
Turn the big knob and listen: your kick goes faster or slower. How fast the booms come is called the tempo. We count it in bpm, which means booms per minute. 120 bpm is two booms every second.
Slow feels sleepy and heavy. Fast feels exciting. Pick the speed you like best for your song.

steps.hint: The number is how many kicks you'd hear in one minute.

say.mentor:
So your song now has a pulse: a kick on every beat, at a tempo you chose. Everything you add from here lines up with it. The hats, the bass, the melody, all of it counts along with this kick.
Producers set the tempo first because changing it later changes how everything feels. A tune that's cheeky at 128 can sound sad at 100.
say.straight: Your song has a pulse and a tempo. Everything you add later is timed against it, which is why the tempo usually gets set first.
say.eli5: Now your song has a heartbeat, and you picked how fast it goes. Every sound you add later will dance along to it.

deeper.title: why 120 to 128 for house
deeper.say: It's close to a brisk walking pace, which is about as fast as people can dance to for hours without getting tired. Early Chicago house sat around 120. Techno from Detroit and Berlin pushed faster.

deeper.title: half time
deeper.say: Dubstep is 140 bpm, but it often feels like 70, because the big drums only hit on every other beat. The pulse is still 140 underneath. You'll hear the same trick in a lot of trap and drum and bass.

steps.q: What does bpm stand for?
steps.why: Beats per minute. 120 bpm means 120 beats, 120 kicks here, in one minute.

whyWrong.1: A bar is a group of beats. Tempo counts the beats themselves.
whyWrong.2: Close, but it's per minute. That's what makes it a speed.
whyWrong.3: It's beats, the steady pulse you counted along with.

steps.q: At 120 bpm, how many beats happen every second?
steps.why: 120 beats in 60 seconds is two every second.

whyWrong.1: One a second would be 60 bpm, half your song's speed.
whyWrong.2: Four a second would be 240 bpm, far faster than any house track.
whyWrong.3: Twelve a second would be a buzz, not a beat.

steps.q: You turn the tempo from 120 up to 140. What happens to your kick?
options: the kick gets higher in pitch
you get more kicks in each bar
steps.why: Same pattern, played faster. Each beat is shorter, so the kicks arrive sooner.

whyWrong.1: Tempo changes speed, not volume.
whyWrong.2: The kick sounds the same, it just comes round more often.
whyWrong.3: Still one kick per beat. There are just more beats in each minute.

steps.q: Roughly what tempo does house music usually sit at?
steps.why: House usually sits between 120 and 128. Techno goes a little faster.

whyWrong.1: That's ballad speed, slower than most dance music.
whyWrong.3: That's faster than almost any dance floor.

steps.q: Why does the click play while you record?
options: so you have something to play along to
it becomes part of your song
to count how many kicks you played
steps.why: The click is a guide to keep you on the beat. It never goes into your song.

whyWrong.1: The click stays out of your song. Only your kicks go in.
whyWrong.2: It doesn't touch the kick at all.
whyWrong.3: It just ticks on every beat.

steps.q: At 60 bpm, how long is one beat?
steps.why: 60 beats in 60 seconds, so one beat every second.

whyWrong.1: Half a second is a beat at 120 bpm.
whyWrong.2: Two seconds a beat would be 30 bpm.
whyWrong.3: That would be 600 bpm.

steps.q: Why do producers usually set the tempo first?
options: changing it later changes how everything feels
the kick only works at one tempo
bpm sets how loud the song is
steps.why: Every part is played against the pulse. Change the speed and the whole mood shifts with it.

whyWrong.1: You can change it any time. It just changes the feel of everything already there.
whyWrong.2: A kick works at any tempo.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is speed, not loudness.

steps.q: Dubstep is 140 bpm but often feels like 70. Why?
options: the big drums hit on every other beat
the bass is out of time
steps.why: Half time. The pulse is still 140, but the heavy drums skip every other beat, so it feels half as fast.

whyWrong.1: Clubs play it at 140.
whyWrong.2: The bass is right on the grid, it just leaves space.
whyWrong.3: There's always a pulse underneath.

steps.next: Next: bars and counting. A clap on two and four turns your pulse into a groove, and your loop grows to four bars.

lessons.title: bars and counting

song.why: a clap on two and four turns a pulse into a groove you can dance to

lessons.learn: How musicians count, what a bar is, and the clap on two and four that turns your kick into a groove.
youCan: count bars of four along with a track
hear the backbeat, the clap on two and four
play a clap in on two and four over your kick
read 4/4 and know what it means

say.mentor:
Same steady kick as before, with one thing added: a clap on every other beat. Listen to how much that changes. The kick on its own just marches. With the clap it starts to swing back and forth, and your head wants to nod.
That clap is called the backbeat, and it's in almost every song you know.
say.straight: A kick on every beat, plus a clap on every other beat. That clap is the backbeat. It's what turns a pulse into a groove.
say.eli5: Boom, clap, boom, clap. Hear how the clap makes it bouncier? The boom is the kick you already know. The clap comes in between, on every other beat. It makes you want to nod your head.

say.mentor:
Count along again: one, two, three, four. Notice where the clap lands: on two and on four, never on one or three. One and three are the kick on its own. Two and four get the clap.
Those four beats together are called a bar. Musicians count music in bars, the way you'd count a walk in steps: "the bass comes in after eight bars". Dance music is almost always four beats to a bar, written 4/4 and said "four four".
say.straight: Four beats make a bar. The clap lands on beats two and four of every bar. Dance music is nearly always in 4/4: four beats per bar.
say.eli5:
Count with it: one, two, three, four. The clap comes on two and on four. One and three are just the boom.
Four beats in a row make a bar, like four steps make a little walk. Most dance music counts to four and starts again.

deeper.title: what 4/4 means
deeper.say: The top four is how many beats are in a bar. The bottom four says each beat is a quarter note, the usual size of a beat. You'll see it at the start of sheet music and in your Live set's tempo box.

deeper.title: other counts
deeper.say: A waltz counts in three, 3/4: one two three, one two three. Some music counts in five or seven. You'll find them in jazz, prog and film scores. Clubs stick to four because four is easiest to dance to for a long time.

say.mentor:
Now add the clap to your song, over the kick you played last time.
Press rec, let the four clicks count you in, then tap the clap pad on two and on four: skip one, clap on two, skip three, clap on four. A clap on the wrong beat turns red so you can play it again. Undo takes one back, hold it to start over.
say.straight: Record the backbeat over your kick. Rec, wait out the count-in, then clap on two and four. Red means off the beat.
say.eli5: Your turn! Press rec and wait for four ticks. Then count one, two, three, four, and tap the clap pad only on two and four. Skip one, clap, skip three, clap.

steps.hint: One and three are the kick on its own. Clap in between them.

say.mentor:
That's your first groove: kick on every beat, clap on two and four. The clap on two and four is the backbeat, and it's one of the oldest tricks in pop music.
It works because it pulls against the kick. The kick says "down", the clap says "up", and your body sits in between, nodding. Next time you hear a song, find two and four. You'll hear a clap or a snare there almost every time.
say.straight: Kick on every beat, clap on two and four: that's the backbeat. The kick gives the down, the clap the up, and that back and forth is the groove.
say.eli5: Now your song goes boom, clap, boom, clap. That clap on two and four has a name: the backbeat. Almost every song has one. See if you can spot it in the next song you hear.

deeper.title: where the backbeat comes from
deeper.say: Rhythm and blues and early rock and roll drummers hit the snare hard on two and four in the 1940s and 50s, and pop never let it go. Disco kept it, house swapped the snare for a drum machine clap, and here we are.

deeper.title: clap or snare
deeper.say: House and techno often use a clap, hip hop and rock a snare, and plenty of tracks use both at once. You'll compare them properly in the producer world.

steps.q: How many beats are in one bar of dance music?
steps.why: Dance music is almost always 4/4, four beats to a bar.

whyWrong.1: Two beats is half a bar. Count along again and listen for the clap on two and four.
whyWrong.3: Three to a bar is a waltz, not a club track.

steps.q: Which beats does the backbeat clap land on?
steps.why: Two and four. One and three are the kick on its own.

whyWrong.1: One and three are where the kick sits alone. The clap answers it on two and four.
whyWrong.2: Every beat is the kick's job. The clap is on every other one.
whyWrong.3: One is the start of the bar, where the kick lands.

steps.q: What does 4/4 mean?
steps.why: The top four is the number of beats in a bar.

whyWrong.1: Songs have far more than four bars. It's about the beats inside one bar.
whyWrong.2: It's about counting time, not how many sounds play.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is written in bpm. 4/4 is how the beats are grouped.

steps.q: A producer says "the bass comes in after eight bars". At 120 bpm, roughly how long is that?
steps.why: At 120 bpm a bar of four beats lasts two seconds, so eight bars is sixteen seconds.

whyWrong.1: That would be one second a bar, too fast at 120.
whyWrong.3: A minute at 120 is thirty bars.

steps.q: Why does adding a clap on two and four make the beat feel groovier?
options: it pulls against the kick, so the beat goes down and up
steps.why: The kick says down, the clap says up. That back and forth is what makes you nod.

whyWrong.1: The tempo stays the same. Only the pattern changes.
whyWrong.3: A clap has no tune to it.

steps.q: A waltz counts one two three, one two three. How is that written?
steps.why: Three beats to a bar, each one a quarter note.

whyWrong.1: 4/4 is four beats to a bar, like dance music.
whyWrong.2: The bottom number is the size of a beat, usually four.
whyWrong.3: That would mean one beat to a bar.

steps.next: Next: subdivision. Hats on the eighths and sixteenths fill the space between your kicks, and snap shows up to help you place them.

lessons.title: subdivision

song.why: hats fill the space between your kicks, and how finely you split the beat sets how busy the groove feels

lessons.learn: Splitting the beat into halves and quarters, eighths and sixteenths, and a hat pattern in your song that uses them. This is also where snap comes in.
youCan: hear the difference between quarters, eighths and sixteenths
play hats on the eighths or sixteenths with snap on
say what snap does and when to turn it off

say.mentor:
Tap through the three. Same kick each time, but the hats split each beat differently.
Quarters: one hat per beat, right on the kick. Eighths: two per beat, one on the kick and one exactly halfway to the next. Sixteenths: four per beat, a fast tick-tick-tick-tick. Listen to how the groove gets busier and faster-feeling while the tempo stays exactly the same.
say.straight: Three ways to split the beat with a hi hat: quarters (one per beat), eighths (two), sixteenths (four). The tempo never changes, only how finely the beat is cut.
say.eli5: Tap a, b and c. The boom stays the same. The tiny tss sound changes. One tss per boom, then two, then four really quick ones. More tss makes it feel busier, but the song isn't going any faster.

steps.title: halves and quarters of a beat

say.mentor:
Musicians call these note values. A quarter note is one beat. An eighth note is half a beat. A sixteenth is a quarter of a beat. The names come from how many fit in a bar: four quarters, eight eighths, sixteen sixteenths.
People count eighths as "one and two and three and four and", and sixteenths as "one e and a, two e and a". Say it out loud over the sixteenths and you'll hear it lock in.
say.straight: Quarter note: one beat. Eighth: half a beat. Sixteenth: a quarter of a beat. Count eighths as "one and two and", sixteenths as "one e and a".
say.eli5: Grown-up musicians give these names. One tss per boom is a quarter note. Two per boom is an eighth note. Four per boom is a sixteenth note. You can count the fast ones as "one e and a, two e and a".

deeper.title: why the names are fractions
deeper.say: A bar of 4/4 holds one whole note. Cut it in four and you get quarter notes, in eight and you get eighths, in sixteen and you get sixteenths. Sheet music draws each one differently, but in a producer's grid they're just the lines getting closer together.

say.mentor:
Now put hats in your song. Hats on the eighths between your kicks are the classic house sound.
This time you get help: snap. Snap moves every hit to the nearest line on the grid, so a hat that's a hair early still lands exactly on the eighth. It's set to eighths. Tap the snap key to change it to sixteenths or turn it off and hear the difference.
Press rec, wait out the count-in, and tap the hat between the kicks: on every "and".
say.straight: Record hats over your beat. Snap is on, set to eighths, so every hit lands on the nearest eighth. Tap the snap key to try sixteenths or off. Rec, count-in, then tap the hat on every "and".
say.eli5: Your turn to add the tss. A helper called snap is switched on: it nudges every tap onto the nearest line, so it always sounds neat. Press rec, wait for four ticks, then tap the hat in between the booms.

steps.hint: Say "one and two and" and tap on every "and".

say.mentor:
That's snap, also called quantise. Almost every music program has it. It's brilliant for drums that need to be tight, like hats and kicks in a club track.
But it's not always what you want. A little looseness is what makes a groove feel human. Producers often play something in, snap it, then nudge a few hits back off the grid on purpose. You'll do that in the swing lesson next.
say.straight: Snap (quantise) moves hits to the nearest grid line. Use it for tight drums; turn it off or loosen it when you want a human feel.
say.eli5: Snap is like a magnet that pulls your taps onto the lines. Great for neat drums. Sometimes you want a bit of wobble so it feels more alive, and then you switch the magnet off.

steps.q: How many sixteenth notes fit in one beat?
steps.why: A sixteenth is a quarter of a beat, so four fit in one beat and sixteen in a bar.

whyWrong.1: Two per beat is eighths.
whyWrong.2: Sixteen fit in a whole bar of four beats.
whyWrong.3: Eight per beat would be thirty-second notes.

steps.q: You switch your hats from eighths to sixteenths. What happens to the tempo?
steps.why: The pulse doesn't change. The beat is just cut into smaller pieces, so it feels busier.

whyWrong.1: The kick keeps the same speed. Only the hats get busier.
whyWrong.2: Nothing slows down. There are just more hats in each beat.
whyWrong.3: Tempo only changes when you turn the tempo knob.

steps.q: What does snap do to a hit that's slightly early?
options: moves it to the nearest grid line
moves it to the start of the bar
steps.why: Snap pulls each hit onto the nearest line of the grid it's set to.

whyWrong.1: Snap never removes notes.
whyWrong.2: It moves notes in time, it doesn't touch their volume.
whyWrong.3: Only to the nearest line, not all the way back to one.

steps.q: How do musicians count eighth notes?
options: one and two and three and four and
steps.why: Each beat plus an "and" halfway through.

whyWrong.1: One e and a is sixteenths, four per beat.
whyWrong.3: That's counting in twos, not eighths.

steps.q: Why might a producer turn snap off?
options: to keep a looser, more human feel
because snap only works on kicks
steps.why: Perfectly gridded drums can sound stiff. A few hits off the grid feel played by a person.

whyWrong.1: Snap has nothing to do with tempo.
whyWrong.3: Snap moves timing, not volume.

steps.next: Next: groove and swing. Push every other sixteenth a little late and your hats start to bounce.

lessons.title: groove and swing

song.why: swing pushes every other sixteenth a little late, and your beat starts to bounce instead of march

lessons.learn: What swing is, why it makes people move, and a swing setting for your whole song.
youCan: hear the difference between straight and swung
say which notes swing moves and which it leaves alone
set the swing on your song by ear

say.mentor: Tap straight, then swung. Same kick, same clap, same hats. In the swung one, every other hat is pushed a little late, and suddenly it bounces. That's swing, and it's the difference between a beat that marches and a beat that grooves.
say.straight: Straight vs swung. The swung version delays every other sixteenth a little. That small delay is what gives it a bounce.
say.eli5: Tap a, then b. In b, every second tss is a tiny bit late, like a skip in your step. Hear how it bounces now? That's called swing.

say.mentor:
Here's your own song with a swing knob on it. Turn it up and listen to your hats.
Swing only moves the off sixteenths: the "e" and the "a" in "one e and a". The beats and the "ands" stay exactly where they are, so your kick and clap don't move. At about 50 percent the off notes land a third of the way along, a triplet feel. House producers often sit somewhere between 10 and 30 percent. Push it to the top for a heavy shuffle.
Pick the amount that makes you want to move.
say.straight: Swing delays only the off sixteenths. Kick, clap and eighths stay put. Around 50 percent is a triplet feel, house usually sits lower. Set the amount for your song.
say.eli5: Turn the swing knob and listen to your song. More swing makes the in-between tss sounds later and bouncier. Your boom and clap stay right where they are. Stop when it makes you want to dance.

steps.hint: If your hats are only on the eighths, swing won't move them. It needs sixteenths to bite.

say.mentor:
People don't play exactly on a grid. A drummer leans on some notes and lags others, and our ears hear that as feel. Swing is a simple way to get some of that back into programmed music.
Swing in drum machines goes back to Roger Linn's machines and the Akai MPC, the tool behind a lot of hip hop and house. Producers still talk about "MPC swing" as a sound of its own.
say.straight: Real players never sit exactly on the grid. Swing puts a little of that feel back. The MPC made it famous in hip hop and house.
say.eli5: When people play drums, they're never perfectly exact, and that wobble feels good. Swing adds a little wobble on purpose.

deeper.title: swing in tracks you know
deeper.say: Listen to almost any J Dilla beat for heavy, loose swing, or to UK garage, where swung hats and shuffled snares are the whole sound. A lot of deep house has gentle swing you only notice when it's gone.

steps.q: Which notes does swing move?
options: the off sixteenths, the e and the a
the first beat of every bar
steps.why: Swing pushes the off sixteenths late. The beats and the ands stay put.

whyWrong.1: If every note moved the same amount, nothing would sound different.
whyWrong.2: The kick on the beat doesn't move.
whyWrong.3: Beat one stays exactly where it is.

steps.q: Your hats are only on the eighths. You turn swing up. What happens?
steps.why: Eighths are on the beat or the and, which swing leaves alone. Add sixteenths to hear it.

whyWrong.1: Swing changes timing, not volume.
whyWrong.2: Swing only ever pushes notes late.
whyWrong.3: Tempo stays the same.

steps.q: About how much swing gives a triplet feel?
steps.why: At around 50 percent the off notes land a third of the way along, like a triplet.

whyWrong.1: Zero is straight, no swing at all.
whyWrong.2: 5 percent is a hint you can barely hear.
whyWrong.3: The knob tops out before that.

steps.q: Why does swing make a beat feel more human?
options: real players don't sit exactly on the grid
steps.why: People lean on and lag notes. Swing puts back some of that feel.

whyWrong.1: Swing changes timing only.
whyWrong.2: Nothing new is added, only moved.
whyWrong.3: The tempo is the same.

steps.next: Next: what sound actually is, and the first notes of your melody, played over your beat.

lessons.title: what is sound?

song.why: your first sound in your song, a few notes you play yourself

lessons.learn: What sound actually is, the three things every sound has, and the first few notes of your own song.
youCan: explain sound as air being pushed and pulled
tell pitch from loudness
hear how the shape of a wave changes its colour
play your first notes into your song

say.mentor:
Everything you will ever hear, a kick, a voice, a whole song, is the same thing underneath: air being pushed and pulled.
Watch the picture while the note plays. The speaker cone moves out and in, fast. Moving out, it shoves the air in front of it together. Moving in, it leaves the air spread thin. Those bunched and thin patches roll through the room to your ear, and your ear turns them into sound.
say.straight:
All sound works the same way: something moves back and forth and pushes the air around it.
In the picture, the speaker moves out and in. Out squeezes the air, in lets it spread. Those squeezed and spread patches travel to your ear, which hears them as sound.
say.eli5:
Hear that hum? Watch the speaker on the left. It wiggles out and in, really fast.
Each wiggle pushes the air, like ripples when you drop a stone in water. The ripples travel across the room into your ear, and that is what you hear. Sound is just wiggling air.

deeper.title: how fast sound travels
deeper.say: Those pressure patches move at about 343 metres every second in air. That is why you see lightning before you hear thunder: light is far faster.

say.mentor:
Every sound has three things. The first is pitch. Tap low, then high.
One full push and pull of the air is called a cycle. Pitch is how many cycles happen every second. The low note pushes the air about 110 times a second, the high one about 440. Look at the wave: more cycles packed in means a higher note. We count cycles per second in hertz, written Hz.
say.straight:
Thing one: pitch. Low, then high.
Pitch is how many push and pull cycles happen per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Here the low note is about 110 Hz and the high one about 440 Hz. More cycles in the picture, higher note.
say.eli5:
Every sound has three things. Number one is pitch. Tap low, then tap high.
A low note wiggles the air slowly. A high note wiggles it fast. In the picture the high one has lots of wiggles packed close together. More wiggles every second, higher note.

deeper.title: what people can hear
deeper.say: From about 20 cycles a second, a rumble you feel more than hear, up to about 20,000, a faint hiss. A kick drum sits around 50. The A a band tunes to is 440.

say.mentor:
The second thing is loudness. Tap quiet, then loud.
Same note, same pitch. What changes is how hard the air is pushed. The picture shows it as how tall the wave is: a small push makes a short wave and a quiet sound, a big push makes a tall wave and a loud one. Pitch is how often, loudness is how hard.
say.straight:
Thing two: loudness. Quiet, then loud.
The pitch stays the same. The size of the push changes, which shows as the height of the wave. How often is pitch, how hard is loudness.
say.eli5:
Number two is loudness. Tap quiet, then tap loud.
It is the same note. The loud one just pushes the air harder, so the wave in the picture is taller. Gentle push, quiet. Big push, loud.

say.mentor:
The third thing is the shape of the wave, and this is what makes a piano sound different from a guitar playing the same note. Tap soft, saw and square.
All three have the same pitch and loudness. Only the shape changes. The round wave sounds pure and gentle. The saw, a slope then a sudden drop, sounds bright and buzzy. The square sounds hollow, a bit like an old video game. People call this the colour, or timbre, of a sound.
say.straight:
Thing three: the shape of the wave, also called timbre or tone colour. Switch between soft, saw and square.
Same pitch, same loudness, different shape: pure, bright and buzzy, hollow. That is why two instruments playing the same note still sound different.
say.eli5:
Number three is the shape of the wiggle. Tap soft, saw and square.
Same note, same loudness, but they sound different. The soft one hums. The saw buzzes like a bee. The square sounds like an old video game. That shape is why a piano and a guitar never sound the same.

deeper.title: why the shape changes the sound
deeper.say: A smooth wave is just the one pitch. Sharp corners and sudden jumps add lots of extra, higher pitches on top, quietly. Your ear hears that mix as brightness or buzz.

say.mentor:
Now make some sound of your own. These are the first notes of your song, and every lesson after this adds something to it.
Press rec, let the four clicks go by, then play any four or more keys. Every key here fits with the others, so nothing you press can sound wrong. Listen to the pitch go up as you move right.
say.straight: Your first notes, recorded into your song. Press rec, wait out the count-in, then play at least four keys. They are all from one scale, so they all work together.
say.eli5:
Your turn to make sound! Whatever you play goes into your song.
Press rec, wait for four clicks, then press some keys. Any keys. They all sound nice together. Keys on the right are higher, keys on the left are lower.

steps.q: What is sound?
steps.why: Something moves back and forth and pushes the air. Those pressure changes reach your ear as sound.

whyWrong.1: Electricity drives the speaker, but what you hear is the air the speaker moves.
whyWrong.2: Light is a different thing. Sound travels through air.
whyWrong.3: Sound is movement of air, not heat.

steps.q: The high note had more wiggles packed into the picture. What does that mean?
options: the air moves back and forth faster
steps.why: More cycles every second means faster vibration, and that is a higher pitch.

whyWrong.1: Loudness is how hard the air is pushed, not how often.
whyWrong.2: Both notes were the same soft shape. Only the speed changed.
whyWrong.3: Both lasted the same time.

steps.q: What changed between the quiet note and the loud note?
options: how hard the air was pushed
how fast the air moved back and forth
steps.why: Same pitch, bigger push. A taller wave is a louder sound.

whyWrong.1: That would change the pitch. Both notes were the same pitch.
whyWrong.2: Both were the same soft shape.
whyWrong.3: Tap them again. The loud one pushes the air much harder.

steps.q: A piano and a guitar play the same note. Why do they still sound different?
options: the shape of their waves is different
steps.why: Same pitch, different wave shape. That shape is the sound's colour, or timbre.

whyWrong.1: Play them at the same loudness and they still sound different.
whyWrong.2: The question says same note, so the pitch is the same.
whyWrong.3: You heard soft, saw and square sound different on the same note.

steps.q: Which three things does every sound have?
steps.why: How often the air moves (pitch), how hard (loudness) and the shape of each cycle (timbre).

whyWrong.1: Close in spirit, but the three are pitch, loudness and wave shape.
whyWrong.2: Those are parts of the pitch range.
whyWrong.3: Those are about rhythm and music, not about a single sound.

steps.next: Next: frequency and pitch, up close. How notes are named and why some sound good together.

lessons.title: frequency and pitch

song.why: a tune for your song, played on keys that now have names

lessons.learn: Why a high note is high, what a note's name means, and the one rule that makes an octave: twice the speed, same name. Then a short tune of your own.
youCan: say what frequency is and what hertz counts
name the notes a to g and find the same note an octave up
explain why an octave sounds like the same note, higher
play a tune using low and high versions of the same note

say.mentor:
Tap a, then tap the one above it. The second note sounds like the same note, just higher. That is not an accident. It is the one rule that pitch is built on.
A note is the air wiggling back and forth. How fast it wiggles is its frequency, counted in hertz: wiggles per second. The first a wiggles 220 times a second. The second one wiggles 440 times a second, exactly twice as fast. Look at the picture: twice as many waves fit in the same window. Double the speed and you get the same note again, one octave up.
say.straight:
Tap both. The second is the first one, an octave up.
Pitch is frequency: how many times a second the air moves back and forth, measured in hertz. This a is 220 hz. The a above it is 440 hz, double. Doubling the frequency gives you the same note name one octave higher, which is why the picture shows twice as many waves.
say.eli5:
Tap the first button, then the second. Hear how the second one is the same but higher? Like a grown up and a kid singing the same thing.
Sound is air wiggling. Fast wiggles make high notes, slow wiggles make low notes. The first note wiggles 220 times every second. The second one wiggles 440 times, that is two times faster. Two times faster always gives you the same note, just higher up.

deeper.title: what hertz means
