deeper.say: One hertz is one wiggle per second. It is named after Heinrich Hertz, who studied waves in the 1880s. People can hear from about 20 hz, a deep rumble, up to about 20,000 hz, a thin whistle. Most of music sits between 30 hz and 5,000 hz.

deeper.title: the kick and the bass are low frequencies
deeper.say: Your kick's body hums at around 50 hz. A bass line lives between about 40 hz and 200 hz. That is why they are the sounds you feel in your chest: slow, big pushes of air.

say.mentor:
Musicians do not say "440 hertz". They say a. Every pitch has a letter name: a, b, c, d, e, f, g. After g the names start again at a, one octave up. So the a at 440 hz and the a at 220 hz share a name because one is exactly double the other.
The keys you are about to play are labelled with these names. The first key and the last key are both a, an octave apart. The ones between are the notes that fit nicely with a, which is why anything you play on them sounds like it belongs together.
say.straight:
Pitches get letter names, a to g, then the letters repeat an octave higher. Two notes with the same name are a doubling apart: 110, 220, 440, 880 are all a.
The keys in this lesson are labelled. First and last are both a, one octave apart, and the six in between are from a scale that fits with a. More on scales in a later lesson.
say.eli5:
Notes have names, like people. The names are letters: a, b, c, d, e, f, g. After g you get a again, just higher. So a low a and a high a are a bit like a big cat and a kitten with the same name.
The keys you are going to press have their names written on them. The first key is a. The last key is also a, but higher.

deeper.title: why 440
deeper.say: Orchestras tune to the a at 440 hz. That has been the agreed standard since the 1950s, so a piano in Bengaluru and one in Berlin play the same a. Before that, a drifted between about 415 and 460 hz depending on the city.

deeper.title: the notes in between
deeper.say: Between one a and the next there are actually twelve steps, not seven. The five extra ones are the black keys on a piano: a sharp, c sharp, d sharp, f sharp, g sharp. You will meet them when scales come up. For now the seven letters are enough.

deeper.title: bpm and hz are not the same
deeper.say: Your song runs at 120 bpm, beats per minute: two beats a second. The low a is 220 hz, wiggles per second. Different things, both measured as how often something happens.

say.mentor:
Now use the octave in your song. This tune replaces the notes you played in the last lesson.
Press rec and let the four clicks go by. Play the first key, a. Then the last key, the a an octave up. Then two more keys you like. Listen for the jump between the two a's: same note, higher.
say.straight:
Record a short tune for your song. It replaces last lesson's notes.
Rec, wait out the count-in, play the low a (first key), the high a (last key), then any two more. At least four notes.
say.eli5:
Your turn. This tune goes into your song.
Press rec, wait for four clicks. Press the first key. Press the last key. Those are both a, low and high. Then press two more keys you like.

steps.q: A higher note means the air is wiggling
steps.why: Pitch is frequency. More wiggles a second, higher note. The a above went from 220 to 440 a second.

whyWrong.1: Slower wiggles make lower notes. The high a wiggled twice as fast as the low one.
whyWrong.2: How hard the air is pushed is loudness, not pitch. That was the last lesson.
whyWrong.3: How long a note lasts does not change its pitch. The a was high from the first instant.

steps.q: What does hertz count?
steps.why: Hertz is wiggles per second. The low a wiggles 220 times a second, so it is 220 hz.

whyWrong.1: Beats per minute is bpm, the speed of the beat. Hertz is the speed of the wiggle.
whyWrong.2: Bars are groups of four beats. Nothing to do with how fast the air moves.
whyWrong.3: A scale is a set of notes. Hertz measures one note's frequency.

steps.q: An octave up means the frequency
steps.why: Double the frequency, same note name, one octave up. 220 becomes 440.

whyWrong.1: It is not a fixed amount. 220 goes to 440, 440 goes to 880. Each octave doubles.
whyWrong.2: Halving the frequency takes you an octave down.
whyWrong.3: If nothing changed you would hear the same pitch.

steps.q: The low a was 220 hz. What is the a above it?
steps.why: Double 220 and you get 440. That is the a orchestras tune to.

whyWrong.1: 330 is one and a half times, which gives you a different note, not an a.
whyWrong.2: 240 is only a little higher, close enough to sound like an out of tune a.
whyWrong.3: 880 is two octaves up. Doubling twice.

steps.q: How many letter names do notes have before they repeat?
steps.why: Seven letters, a to g, then a again one octave higher.

whyWrong.1: Eight is the number of keys in this lesson, because the last one is a again.
whyWrong.2: There are twelve steps in an octave, counting the in between notes, but only seven letters.
whyWrong.3: Four is the beats in a bar. Notes use seven letters.

steps.q: Two notes an octave apart sound
options: like the same note, one higher
steps.why: Because one is exactly double the other, your ear hears them as the same note at two heights.

whyWrong.1: They share a name for a reason. The high a is the low a going twice as fast.
whyWrong.2: An octave is the most in tune two different notes can be.
whyWrong.3: Loudness is a separate thing. You can play an octave soft or hard.

steps.q: Which of these is a low frequency sound?
steps.why: The kick's body hums at around 50 hz, slow big pushes of air you feel in your chest.

whyWrong.1: Hi hats are mostly high frequencies, thousands of hertz, which is why they sound bright.
whyWrong.2: A whistle is a few thousand hertz, fast wiggles.
whyWrong.3: Birds sing high, usually well above 2,000 hz.

steps.q: Why do the keys in this lesson all sound good together?
options: they are from one scale that fits with a
they are all the same note
steps.why: The keys are picked from a scale built around a. Scales get their own lesson later.

whyWrong.1: They are different notes. Only the first and last share a name.
whyWrong.2: Only the first and last keys are an octave apart.
whyWrong.3: Volume has nothing to do with whether notes fit.

steps.next: Next: amplitude and volume. The same tune played soft, then hard, and why a song needs both.

lessons.title: amplitude and volume

song.why: how loud your melody sits against your beat decides whether it leads or hides

lessons.learn: What makes a sound loud, how loudness is measured, and setting how loud your melody sits in your song.
youCan: say what amplitude is and how it differs from pitch
say roughly what decibels measure
set your melody's level against your beat by ear

say.mentor:
Tap quiet, then loud. Same note, same pitch. The only difference is how hard the air is being pushed. Look at the picture: the wave is the same width, just taller.
That height is called amplitude. Bigger pushes of air reach your ear as a louder sound.
say.straight: Quiet vs loud. Same pitch, different amplitude: how far the air moves with each push. More amplitude, louder sound. The wave gets taller, not faster.
say.eli5: Tap a, then b. Same note, but b is louder. A loud sound pushes the air harder, so the wiggle in the picture gets taller. It doesn't get faster, just bigger.

say.mentor:
Loudness is measured in decibels, written dB. The scale is odd but useful: every 6 dB or so roughly doubles the size of the wave, and about 10 dB sounds roughly twice as loud to most people.
In a music program you'll see a fader marked in dB, with 0 dB near the top. Pulling a part down by a few dB is how producers make room for something else without muting it.
say.straight: Loudness is measured in decibels (dB). About 6 dB doubles the wave's size, about 10 dB sounds twice as loud. Faders are marked in dB, with 0 near the top.
say.eli5: Grown-ups measure loudness with a number called decibels, or dB. Bigger number, louder sound. The sliders that make tracks louder or quieter are marked in dB.

deeper.title: how loud is loud
deeper.say: A quiet room is around 30 dB, a conversation around 60, a club near the speakers can pass 100. Long hours above about 85 dB can damage hearing, which is why DJs and producers wear earplugs at gigs and keep headphones at sensible levels.

deeper.title: velocity
deeper.say: On a keyboard or drum pad, how hard you hit is called velocity. It sets the amplitude of each note. Soft hits and hard hits in the same line are a big part of what makes playing sound human.

say.mentor:
Here's your song, with a level knob on your melody. Turn it down until the melody tucks in behind the beat, then up until it sits on top.
There's no right answer. A melody that's the star of the track sits loud. One that's more of a background colour sits lower. Leave it where your song sounds best to you.
say.straight: Your melody's level in your song. Down tucks it behind the beat, up puts it in front. Set it where it sounds right.
say.eli5: This knob makes your tune louder or quieter in your song. Turn it down and the boom takes over. Turn it up and your tune is the star. Stop where you like it.

say.mentor:
Songs don't stay at one level. A breakdown drops the drums so everything feels softer, then the drop hits harder because of it. Producers call this dynamics: the difference between the quiet and loud moments.
You'll build a breakdown and a drop in your song later. For now, notice it in the next track you hear: where does it get quieter, and how does it feel when it comes back?
say.straight: Dynamics is the contrast between quiet and loud moments. A drop feels big because the part before it was smaller. You'll build one later.
say.eli5: Songs get quiet sometimes and then loud again, and the loud bit feels extra exciting because of the quiet bit before it. That's called dynamics.

steps.q: Two notes have the same pitch but one is louder. What's different?
options: amplitude, how hard the air is pushed
steps.why: Loudness is amplitude. Pitch stays the same because the speed of the wiggle hasn't changed.

whyWrong.1: Frequency is pitch. Same pitch means same frequency.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is the speed of the beat.

steps.q: What unit is loudness measured in?
steps.why: Decibels, dB. Hertz is for pitch, bpm for tempo.

whyWrong.1: Hertz measures frequency, the pitch.
whyWrong.3: Bars are for counting time.

steps.q: In the picture, what happened to the wave when the note got louder?
steps.why: More amplitude, a taller wave. The speed stays the same, so the pitch does too.

whyWrong.1: Faster would be a higher note.
whyWrong.2: Shape is tone colour, the next lesson.
whyWrong.3: It's the height that changes.

steps.q: Why does a drop feel bigger after a breakdown?
options: the quiet part before makes the loud part stand out
a drop is always 10 dB louder
steps.why: That contrast is dynamics. Loud only feels loud next to quiet.

whyWrong.1: The tempo usually stays the same.
whyWrong.2: There's no fixed number. It's the contrast you feel.
whyWrong.3: Key changes are a different trick.

steps.q: On a keyboard, what is velocity?
options: how hard you play each note
how long you hold a note
steps.why: Velocity is how hard you hit, and it sets each note's loudness.

whyWrong.1: That's tempo.
whyWrong.3: That's the note's length.

steps.next: Next: timbre. Why a saw sounds buzzy and a soft wave sounds round, and a filter to change your melody's colour.

lessons.title: timbre and tone colour

song.why: the same melody can sound soft and round or bright and buzzy, and the filter is how you choose

lessons.learn: Why a piano and a synth playing the same note sound different, what harmonics are, and a filter on your melody to change its colour.
youCan: say what timbre is
explain a bright sound as one with lots of harmonics
use a low pass filter to make your melody darker or brighter

say.mentor:
Tap through soft, saw and square. Same note, same loudness, three completely different characters. That character is called timbre, said "tam-ber", or tone colour. It's how you can tell a piano from a guitar even when they play the same note.
Look at the shapes. The smooth wave sounds round and pure. The sharp corners of the saw and the square are what make them bright and buzzy.
say.straight: Same pitch, same loudness, three timbres. Timbre (tone colour) is what makes instruments sound different on the same note. Sharp corners in the wave mean a brighter, buzzier sound.
say.eli5: Tap a, b and c. Same note each time, but they sound totally different: one is smooth like a flute, one is buzzy like a bee, one sounds like an old video game. That difference is called timbre.

say.mentor:
Here's the cool part. A buzzy sound isn't one pitch. It's the note you hear plus a stack of quieter, higher pitches riding on top of it, at two times, three times, four times the frequency and up. Those are called harmonics.
A pure, round wave has almost none. A saw has loads. Your ear blends them into one sound, and the mix of harmonics is the timbre. Sharp corners in the picture are what all those extra harmonics look like.
say.straight: A bright sound is the main note plus harmonics: quieter pitches at 2, 3, 4 times the frequency and up. A round wave has few, a saw has many. The mix of harmonics is the timbre.
say.eli5: Secret: a buzzy sound is really lots of sounds at once. There's the main note, plus a bunch of quiet higher notes hiding on top. They're called harmonics. Smooth sounds have hardly any. Buzzy ones have tons.

deeper.title: why octaves and fifths sound good
deeper.say: The first harmonics are twice and three times the note. Twice is the octave. Three times, brought down an octave, is the fifth. That's part of why those two intervals sound so at home together: they are already hiding inside a single note.

say.mentor:
Now change your own melody's colour. The cutoff knob is a filter: it lets the low part of the sound through and cuts the high harmonics. Turn it down and your melody gets darker and rounder, like hearing music through a wall. Turn it up and all the brightness comes back.
The wave knob picks the starting shape. Try a buzzy wave with the cutoff halfway: that's a classic synth sound.
say.straight: Cutoff is a low pass filter: down removes high harmonics (darker), up lets them back (brighter). Wave picks the starting shape. Set your melody's colour.
say.eli5: The cutoff knob is like a blanket over the speaker. Turn it down and the sound gets muffled and soft. Turn it up and it gets bright and clear again. The wave knob changes the shape. Play until you like how your tune sounds.

steps.q: A piano and a synth play the same note at the same volume. Why do they sound different?
options: different timbre, a different mix of harmonics
steps.why: Same note and loudness, different harmonics. That's timbre.

whyWrong.1: Same note means same pitch.
whyWrong.2: Tempo is the speed of the beat, not one note.
whyWrong.3: Same volume means the same amplitude.

steps.q: What are harmonics?
options: quieter, higher pitches on top of the main note
steps.why: Pitches at two, three, four times the frequency and up, blended into one sound.

whyWrong.1: Chords are separate notes you play. Harmonics hide inside a single note.
whyWrong.2: An echo is a delayed copy. Harmonics happen at the same moment.
whyWrong.3: Beats are about rhythm.

steps.q: You turn the cutoff down on your melody. What happens?
options: it gets darker, the high harmonics are cut
steps.why: A low pass filter keeps the lows and cuts the highs, so the sound gets rounder and darker.

whyWrong.1: The note stays the same. Only its colour changes.
whyWrong.3: Turning it up brings brightness back.

steps.q: Which wave has the most harmonics?
steps.why: The saw's sharp drop is made of loads of harmonics, which is why it sounds the buzziest.

whyWrong.1: The round wave is nearly pure, with very few harmonics.
whyWrong.2: That's why they sound so different.
whyWrong.3: Everything except a pure sine has some.

steps.q: Why is it called a low pass filter?
options: it lets the low part pass and cuts the highs
it makes the sound low in volume
it passes the sound to a lower octave
steps.why: Lows pass through, highs above the cutoff are cut.

whyWrong.1: It changes colour, not overall volume.
whyWrong.3: The pitch stays the same.

steps.next: Next: waveforms. Sine, triangle, saw and square side by side, and the one that suits your melody.

lessons.title: waveforms

song.why: the wave you start from sets the whole character of your melody

lessons.learn: The four classic waves every synth starts from, what each is used for, and the one you pick for your melody.
youCan: name the sine, triangle, saw and square waves
say what each one is good for
pick a wave for your melody by ear

say.mentor:
Every synth sound starts life as a simple repeating shape. There are four classics, and you've heard three of them already. Tap through them again and really listen to the character.
The round one is close to a sine: pure, soft, almost no harmonics. The saw ramps up and drops: bright, buzzy, full of harmonics. The square jumps between two levels: hollow and reedy, the sound of old video games.
say.straight: The classic synth waves: sine (pure, soft), saw (bright, buzzy), square (hollow, reedy). The round one here is close to a sine.
say.eli5: Synths start from simple shapes. A smooth round one sounds soft and gentle. A pointy saw sounds buzzy. A blocky square sounds like an old video game. Tap them and listen.

say.mentor:
Sine: sub bass and soft tones. It's so pure that it's mostly felt, which is why 808 basses are close to sines. Triangle: a slightly brighter sine, sweet and flute-like. Saw: the workhorse of dance music, for leads, basses and big chords, because there's so much to filter. Square: hollow, woody tones and chiptune. Squash it into a thin pulse and it gets nasal and buzzy.
Producers pick the wave first and then shape it, the way a painter picks a colour before the brush.
say.straight: Sine: sub bass, soft tones. Triangle: sweet, flute-like. Saw: leads, basses, chords, the most used. Square: hollow, chiptune. Pick the wave, then shape it.
say.eli5: Smooth waves are good for deep, soft bass. Buzzy saws are great for big exciting leads. Square waves sound like game music. Pick the one that sounds like what you want.

deeper.title: the triangle
deeper.say: A triangle ramps up and down in straight lines. It has a few harmonics, much fewer than a saw, so it sits between a sine and a square. Your synth here morphs from saw to square; the soft setting is a saw with the filter closed right down, which gets close to a sine.

say.mentor: Pick the wave for your melody. Turn wave from saw to square and listen to your own tune change character, then use cutoff to round it off. For something soft and sine-like, close the cutoff right down. For a bright lead, open it up.
say.straight: Choose your melody's wave: saw to square, then round it off with cutoff. Low cutoff gets you close to a sine.
say.eli5: Turn the wave knob to change the shape of your tune's sound. Then turn cutoff to make it softer or brighter. Keep the one you like.

steps.q: Which wave is best for a deep, soft sub bass?
steps.why: A sine is pure, with almost no harmonics, so it's mostly felt as a deep rumble.

whyWrong.1: A saw is bright and buzzy, more for leads and mid basses.
whyWrong.2: A square is hollow and reedy.
whyWrong.3: Noise has no pitch at all.

steps.q: Why is the saw so popular in dance music?
options: it's full of harmonics, so there's lots to filter
steps.why: All those harmonics give you plenty to shape with a filter.

whyWrong.1: Waves can be any volume.
whyWrong.3: Any wave can play any note.

steps.q: What does a square wave sound like?
options: hollow and reedy, like old video games
steps.why: Hollow and reedy, the chiptune sound.

whyWrong.1: That's a sine.
whyWrong.2: A kick is a drum, not a wave shape.
whyWrong.3: That's noise more than a wave.

steps.q: How can you get close to a sine on this synth?
options: a saw with the cutoff closed right down
steps.why: Closing the filter removes the harmonics, leaving something close to the pure note.

whyWrong.1: That's the brightest, buzziest setting.
whyWrong.3: Pitch doesn't change the wave's shape.

steps.next: Next: harmonics up close, and a second note a fifth above your melody.

lessons.title: harmonics up close

song.why: notes that share harmonics fit together, and the fifth is the first one hiding inside every note

lessons.learn: The harmonic series, why some pairs of notes fit together, and a fifth played into your melody.
youCan: say what the harmonic series is
explain why octaves and fifths sound smooth
play a fifth on the keys

say.mentor:
Remember the octave: same note, twice as fast. That's the first harmonic above any note. The next one is three times as fast, and if you bring that down an octave you get a note called the fifth. Tap through these two and keep the octave in your ear.
Every note you've played already has its octave and its fifth quietly ringing inside it. That's why those two always sound at home next to it.
say.straight: Harmonics come at 2, 3, 4 and more times a note's frequency. Twice is the octave. Three times, an octave down, is the fifth. That's why both sound smooth with the note.
say.eli5: Every note has quiet helper notes hiding inside it. The first helper is the same note higher up, the octave. The next one is called the fifth. Notes sound good together when they share helpers.

say.mentor:
Line up the harmonics of a low a: a, then a an octave up, then e, then a again, then c sharp, then e, and on and on, getting closer together as they go. That's the harmonic series, and a lot of music theory comes out of it.
Notes near the start of the series, the octave and the fifth, sound smooth and stable together. Notes further up sound more colourful and tense. You'll use both later.
say.straight: The harmonic series of a: a, a, e, a, c sharp, e and up. Early ones (octave, fifth) sound stable together; later ones sound more colourful.
say.eli5: The helper notes come in a line, each one higher and closer to the last. The first few, the octave and the fifth, make the smoothest friends for your note.

say.mentor: Now play a fifth into your melody. On these keys, the fifth above the first key is five keys along, counting the first one as one. Press rec, wait out the count-in, and play the first key then the fifth, then anything else you like. Listen to how settled those two sound together.
say.straight: Record a phrase with a fifth: first key, then five keys along (counting the first as one), then anything you like.
say.eli5: Press rec, wait for four ticks. Press the first key. Then count five keys along, one, two, three, four, five, and press that one. They're best friends. Then play whatever you like.

steps.q: What is the first harmonic above a note?
steps.why: Twice the frequency, the same note an octave up.

whyWrong.1: The fifth comes from the next one, three times the frequency.
whyWrong.2: Harmonics are always above the note.
whyWrong.3: They follow a fixed pattern, whole number multiples.

steps.q: Why does a fifth sound smooth with its root note?
options: it's already a harmonic inside the note
it's always in tune with everything
steps.why: The fifth rings quietly inside every note, so the two share a lot.

whyWrong.1: It's a different pitch, just a very friendly one.
whyWrong.2: Loudness has nothing to do with it.
whyWrong.3: It fits its own root note, not every note.

steps.q: On a keyboard scale, how far is the fifth from the note you start on?
options: five keys along, counting the first
steps.why: Count the start as one, then two, three, four, five.

whyWrong.1: Two along is a third, a different interval.
whyWrong.3: The next key is a step.

steps.next: Next: noise. Hats and claps have no pitch at all, and that's exactly why they work.

lessons.title: noise, the odd friend

song.why: your hats are noise, and shaping the noise changes how your whole groove feels

lessons.learn: What noise is, why every hat, clap and cymbal is made of it, and shaping your hats.
youCan: say what noise is and how it differs from a note
hear that hats and claps are short bursts of noise
shape your hats with decay and tune

say.mentor: Listen to the hats between the kicks. Try to hum their note. You can't, because there isn't one. Hats are noise: every frequency at once, all jumbled, with no repeating shape. That's the hiss you hear from an untuned radio, and it's the raw material of hats, claps, cymbals and snares.
say.straight: Hats have no note. They're noise: all frequencies at once with no repeating pattern. Hats, claps, snares and cymbals are all shaped noise.
say.eli5: Try to sing along with the tss sound. You can't, because it has no note. It's noise, like the shhh of a waterfall. Hats and claps are made of noise.

say.mentor:
A hat is a tiny burst of noise with the low end filtered away, so only the bright sizzle is left. A short burst is a closed hat. Let it ring and it's an open hat. A clap is several bursts very close together, like a few people clapping at once.
So when you shape a hat, you're shaping noise: how long it lasts and how bright it is.
say.straight: Closed hat: a short burst of bright noise. Open hat: a longer one. Clap: a few bursts in a row. Shaping them means changing length and brightness.
say.eli5: A short shhh is a closed hat. A long shhhhh is an open hat. A clap is a few quick shh-shh-shh at once.

deeper.title: noise in synths
deeper.say: Synths have a noise source too. Mixed in a little, it adds breath to a pad. Swept up with a filter, it becomes the riser you hear before a drop. You'll build one in the producer world.

say.mentor: Here's your groove with your hats on two knobs. Decay sets how long each burst rings: short is tight and crisp, long starts to sound like an open hat. Tune moves the noise brighter or darker. Find hats that sit nicely between your kicks.
say.straight: Decay: how long each hat rings. Tune: brighter or darker. Shape your hats.
say.eli5: Decay makes your tss short or long. Tune makes it brighter or darker. Play until it sounds good.

steps.q: Why can't you hum the note of a hi hat?
options: it's noise, it has no single pitch
steps.why: Noise has every frequency at once and no repeating shape, so there's no note to hum.

whyWrong.1: You can't hum it even when it's loud.
whyWrong.2: Speed isn't the reason. A single hat has no pitch.
whyWrong.3: To be out of tune it would need a note in the first place.

steps.q: What makes an open hat different from a closed one?
steps.why: Same bright noise, left to ring longer.

whyWrong.1: Both are noise, neither has a note.
whyWrong.2: It's a separate sound from the kick.
whyWrong.3: The tempo is the song's, not the hat's.

steps.q: What is a clap made of?
options: a few quick bursts of noise
steps.why: A few bursts very close together, like a handful of people clapping.

whyWrong.1: A sine is a pure tone, the opposite of noise.
whyWrong.3: You'd hear nothing.

steps.next: Next: samples and loops, and a real recorded sound in your song.

lessons.title: scales, major and minor

song.why: the scale is the set of notes your whole song draws from, and it sets the mood before anything else

lessons.learn: What a scale is, how major and minor feel different, and the scale your song will use from now on.
youCan: say what a scale is
hear the difference between major and minor
set your song's scale

say.mentor:
The keys you've been playing aren't all twelve notes. They're seven of them, picked so they fit together. That set of notes is called a scale, and it's why nothing you played sounded wrong.
Your song has been in a minor scale. Next you'll hear what happens when you switch it.
say.straight: The keys you've used are a scale: seven of the twelve notes, chosen to fit together. Your song has been in minor.
say.eli5: Here's a secret: the keys you've played aren't all the notes there are. They're a team of seven that always sound nice together. That team is called a scale.

say.mentor:
Here's your own song. Tap major, then minor, and listen to your melody. The notes move to their place in the new scale, so the tune keeps its shape, but the mood flips.
Minor tends to sound darker, moodier, a bit serious. Major sounds brighter and happier. Most house and techno lives in minor, but plenty of feel-good disco and pop house is major. Pick the one that feels like your song.
say.straight: Switch your song between minor and major. Same shape of melody, different mood: minor is darker, major brighter. Pick one.
say.eli5: Tap major, then minor. Your tune keeps its shape but changes feeling. Minor sounds a bit moody. Major sounds happy and sunny. Pick the one you like.

say.mentor:
The difference is in the gaps. A scale climbs in steps: some are whole steps, two keys apart, some are half steps, the very next key. Major goes whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. Minor moves two of those half steps to different places, and that one change is the whole mood.
Look at the keys in the picture: the lit ones are your scale.
say.straight: Scales are patterns of whole steps (two keys) and half steps (one key). Major: whole whole half whole whole whole half. Minor puts the half steps elsewhere.
say.eli5: A scale is like stairs with big steps and little steps. Major and minor put the little steps in different places, and that's what makes one happy and one moody.

deeper.title: relative major and minor
deeper.say: A minor and C major use exactly the same seven notes. They just start from a different home note. That's why switching a song from a minor to C major can feel subtle: the home changes, not the notes.

steps.q: What is a scale?
options: a set of notes chosen to fit together
steps.why: A scale is the set of notes a song draws from, usually seven of the twelve.

whyWrong.1: Loudness is amplitude.
whyWrong.3: Drums are rhythm, not notes.

steps.q: How does minor usually sound compared with major?
steps.why: Minor tends to sound darker; major brighter.

whyWrong.1: Scale doesn't change tempo.
whyWrong.3: Both can be played at any height.

steps.q: How many notes are in a major or minor scale?
steps.why: Seven, then it starts again an octave up.

whyWrong.1: Twelve is every note, the whole keyboard pattern.
whyWrong.2: Five is a pentatonic scale, coming up soon.
whyWrong.3: The eighth note is the first one again, an octave up.

steps.q: What is a half step?
steps.why: The smallest step on a keyboard, the very next key.

whyWrong.1: Two keys apart is a whole step.
whyWrong.2: Half a beat is an eighth note, that's rhythm.
whyWrong.3: That's loudness.

steps.next: Next: intervals, the distance between two notes, and a two-note phrase in your melody.

lessons.title: intervals

song.why: every melody is a chain of jumps between notes, and the size of the jump is what you feel

lessons.learn: The distance between two notes, how close jumps feel smooth and wide ones dramatic, and a phrase built on a jump you choose.
youCan: say what an interval is
hear the difference between a step, a third, a fifth and an octave
play a phrase with a jump you picked

say.mentor:
Two notes, a jump between them. The distance of that jump is called an interval. This one's an octave, the biggest jump that still sounds like the same note.
Small intervals sound like walking. Big ones sound like leaping. Every melody you love is just a string of these.
say.straight: An interval is the distance between two notes. This is an octave. Small intervals feel smooth, big ones dramatic.
say.eli5: When a tune goes from one note to another, the jump has a size. That's an interval. Little jumps feel like walking, big jumps feel like leaping.

say.mentor:
A step: the next key in your scale. Smooth, like talking. A third: skip one key. Sweet, it's the heart of major and minor. A fifth: skip three keys. Strong and open, the sound of power chords and big leads. An octave: eight keys up, counting both. Same note, higher.
Count by keys in your scale, starting from one: a third is the third key, a fifth the fifth, an octave the eighth.
say.straight: Step (next key), third (skip one), fifth (count to five), octave (count to eight). Count keys in the scale from one.
say.eli5: A step is the very next key. A third skips one. A fifth is five keys along. An octave is eight along, and sounds like the same note but higher.

say.mentor: Build a phrase on a jump. Press rec, then play the first key, jump to the third or the fifth, and come back down by steps. Try it a couple of times with different jumps and keep the one you like.
say.straight: Record a phrase: first key, jump to the third or fifth, step back down. At least three different notes.
say.eli5: Press rec. Play the first key. Jump up to the third or the fifth. Then walk back down one key at a time.

steps.q: What is an interval?
steps.why: The distance between two notes, counted in steps.

whyWrong.1: That's a different kind of gap.
whyWrong.2: Scales are made of intervals, but they're not the same thing.
whyWrong.3: Loudness is amplitude.

steps.q: Counting from one, which key is the fifth?
steps.why: Count the start as one; the fifth is five keys along.

whyWrong.1: The second key is a step.
whyWrong.2: The eighth key is the octave.
whyWrong.3: Twelve half steps is an octave.

steps.q: How do small intervals usually feel in a melody?
steps.why: Steps feel smooth. Big jumps feel dramatic.

whyWrong.1: That's big intervals.
whyWrong.3: Interval is pitch, not speed.

steps.next: Next: writing a melody. A motif, repeat it, change one note.

lessons.title: writing a melody

song.why: a good melody repeats enough to remember and changes enough to stay interesting

lessons.learn: The simplest way to write a melody that sticks: a short motif, played again, with one note changed.
youCan: say what a motif is
write a melody by repeating and changing a motif
hear question and answer phrases

say.mentor: Low, then high. Two notes is already the start of a tune. The trick most hooks use is simple: a short idea, called a motif, then the same idea again with one small change. Your ear loves hearing something come back, and loves a little surprise when it does.
say.straight: Most hooks are a short motif, repeated, with one change. Repetition makes it stick; the change keeps it interesting.
say.eli5: Here's the secret of catchy tunes: play a little tune, then play it again but change one note. Your brain loves hearing it come back, with a tiny surprise.

say.mentor: Think of a melody as a conversation. The first half asks a question: it ends somewhere that feels unfinished, maybe up high. The second half answers: same shape, but it lands back home on the first key of your scale. Say it out loud: da da da daa? da da da dum.
say.straight: Phrase one ends unfinished (a question), phrase two repeats it and lands on the home note (an answer).
say.eli5: A tune can ask a question and then answer it. The first part ends up in the air. The second part is nearly the same, but it comes home to the first key.

say.mentor: Write it. Press rec and play a motif of three or four notes in the first half of the bar. In the second half, play it again, but change the last note so it lands on the first key. Record it as many times as you like until it sounds like a tune you'd hum.
say.straight: Record a motif in the first half of the bar, then repeat it in the second half ending on the first key.
say.eli5: Press rec. Play three or four notes. Then play the same notes again, but make the last one the very first key. That's your melody!

steps.q: What is a motif?
options: a short musical idea that repeats
steps.why: A short idea, often three or four notes, that a melody is built from.

whyWrong.1: A motif is much smaller than a song.
whyWrong.2: Drums can have motifs too, but here it's a few notes of melody.
whyWrong.3: A scale is the set of notes; a motif is what you play with them.

steps.q: What makes an answer phrase feel finished?
options: it lands on the home note, the first key
steps.why: Landing on the first note of the scale feels like coming home.

whyWrong.1: Volume doesn't finish a phrase.
whyWrong.3: It's where it lands, not how many notes.

steps.q: Why repeat the motif with one change instead of something totally new?
options: repetition sticks, the change keeps it interesting
steps.why: Your ear remembers what comes back and enjoys the small surprise.

whyWrong.1: It's about how it sounds, not effort.
whyWrong.2: You can play anything you like.
whyWrong.3: Length isn't the reason.

steps.next: Next: the pentatonic hook. Five notes, no wrong ones.

lessons.title: the pentatonic hook

song.why: five notes with no clashes make it easy to play a hook that always fits

lessons.learn: The five-note scale behind countless hooks and solos, and a hook of your own played on it.
youCan: say what a pentatonic scale is
find the five notes on your keys
play a hook using only those five

say.mentor: Some of the catchiest melodies ever use only five notes. Take a minor scale, drop the two notes most likely to clash, and you get the minor pentatonic. It's in blues, rock solos, African and Asian folk music, and a lot of dance hooks, because nothing in it can sound wrong over the chords.
say.straight: The minor pentatonic: a minor scale minus the two notes most likely to clash. Five notes, no wrong ones, used everywhere.
say.eli5: Take your seven notes and leave out two. The five that are left all get along perfectly. That's called a pentatonic scale.

say.mentor: On your keys, the minor pentatonic is keys one, three, four, five and seven, counting from the first. Skip two and six. In a minor that's a, c, d, e and g. Try it: run up those five and down again, and hear how open and singable it is.
say.straight: Keys 1, 3, 4, 5, 7 of your minor scale. Skip 2 and 6.
say.eli5: Use keys one, three, four, five and seven. Skip key two and key six.

say.mentor: Make a hook on those five. Press rec and play a short phrase using only keys one, three, four, five and seven. Keep it simple: hooks are short, rhythmic and repeat. Record it until you'd want to hear it again.
say.straight: Record a short hook using only keys 1, 3, 4, 5 and 7.
say.eli5: Press rec and play a little tune using only keys one, three, four, five and seven.

steps.hint: Short and repeated beats long and complicated.

steps.q: How many notes are in a pentatonic scale?
steps.why: Penta means five.

whyWrong.1: Seven is a full major or minor scale.
whyWrong.3: Three notes is a chord.

steps.q: Why is the pentatonic so easy to play hooks on?
options: the notes that clash most are left out
steps.why: Dropping the two clashiest notes leaves five that always fit.

whyWrong.1: It's about which notes, not volume.
whyWrong.3: Scales don't set the tempo.

steps.q: Which keys of your minor scale make the minor pentatonic?
steps.why: Leave out two and six.

whyWrong.1: Close, but it skips two and includes seven.
whyWrong.2: Those are some of the ones you leave out.
whyWrong.3: That's the full scale.

steps.next: Next: chords. Three notes at once, and the harmony under your melody.

lessons.title: what are chords?

song.why: chords are the harmony under your melody, the colour of the whole song

lessons.learn: What a chord is, how three notes make one, major and minor chords by ear, and chords in your song.
youCan: say what a chord and a triad are
hear a major chord from a minor one
play chords into your song

say.mentor:
One note on its own is a line. Play three notes from your scale at once, skipping a key between each, and you get a chord: a little cloud of harmony that colours everything played over it.
That stack of three, the first, third and fifth, is called a triad. It's the building block of almost every song.
say.straight: A chord is several notes at once. The basic one is a triad: a note, the third above it and the fifth.
say.eli5: Play three notes at the same time and you get a chord. It's like three friends singing together. The main kind uses notes one, three and five.

say.mentor:
Like scales, chords come in major and minor, and you can hear it straight away: major chords sound bright, minor ones darker. The only difference is the middle note, the third, moved by one key.
The chord pads in the next step are labelled the way musicians write them: big letters for major, small for minor. Roman numerals say which note of the scale the chord starts on.
say.straight: Major chords sound bright, minor darker. The difference is the third, one key apart. Pads use roman numerals: capitals major, lower case minor.
say.eli5: Some chords sound happy (major), some sound a bit sad (minor). The pads have little names on them: big letters for happy chords, small letters for sad ones.

deeper.title: why skip a key
deeper.say: Notes right next to each other rub and buzz. Skipping one each time gives notes that share harmonics, so they blend. That's the harmonic series from the harmonics lesson again.

say.mentor: Put chords in your song. Press rec, wait out the count-in, and play two chords: one at the start of the bar, one halfway. Start on i, the home chord, and try any other for the second. Hold each one down for a while so it rings.
say.straight: Record two chords into your song: i at the start of the bar, any other halfway.
say.eli5: Press rec, wait for four ticks. Press the first chord pad and hold it. Halfway through, press a different one.

steps.q: What is a triad?
options: three notes: a root, its third and its fifth
steps.why: Root, third and fifth, the basic chord.

whyWrong.1: That's time, not harmony.
whyWrong.3: Drums have no pitch to make chords.

steps.q: What makes a chord major or minor?
steps.why: Move the third by one key and the chord flips between major and minor.

whyWrong.1: Volume doesn't change the chord.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is the song's speed.

steps.q: On the chord pads, what does a capital roman numeral mean?
steps.why: Capitals for major, lower case for minor.

whyWrong.1: Minor is lower case.
whyWrong.3: Numerals say which note it starts on.

steps.next: Next: chord progressions. Four chords in a row and how they pull you along.

lessons.title: chord progressions

song.why: chords that move in a good order carry the listener through the song

lessons.learn: How chords move from one to the next, the progressions behind countless songs, and four chords in your song.
youCan: say what a chord progression is
play a four chord progression
hear which chord feels like home

say.mentor: A chord progression is just chords in an order. Some orders feel like a journey: away from home and back again. Four chords, round and round, is the backbone of a huge amount of pop and dance music.
say.straight: A progression is a sequence of chords. Four chords looping is the backbone of most pop and dance tracks.
say.eli5: Chords in a row make a progression, like a little journey. Most songs use four chords going round and round.

say.mentor:
Your i chord is home. Every other chord pulls a little away from it, and the progression feels satisfying when it comes back. In minor, a classic is i, VI, III, VII: home, then three steps that each feel like they're heading somewhere, then home again on the loop.
You've heard it in countless tracks. Once you know it, you'll hear it everywhere.
say.straight: i is home. Others pull away. In minor, i VI III VII is a classic four chord loop.
say.eli5: The first chord is home. The others go on an adventure. Then the loop brings you home again. Try i, VI, III, VII.

deeper.title: four chords everywhere
deeper.say: The same four chords, in major or minor order, sit under an enormous number of hits. Producers don't worry about that: the sound, rhythm and melody on top are what make a track yours.

say.mentor: Play a four chord progression into your song, one chord on each beat. Start on i, then try VI, III and VII, or any order you like. Listen for which one makes you want to go back to i.
say.straight: Record four chords, one per beat, starting on i. Try i VI III VII or your own order.
say.eli5: Press rec. Play four chord pads, one on each tick. Start with i, then try VI, III and VII.

steps.q: What is a chord progression?
steps.why: A sequence of chords, often looped.

whyWrong.1: A scale is single notes.
whyWrong.3: Fills are drums.

steps.q: In your scale, which chord feels like home?
steps.why: The chord built on the first note of the scale is home.

whyWrong.1: VII pulls back toward i.
whyWrong.3: It's about the note it's built on.

steps.q: How many chords are in a lot of pop and dance loops?
steps.why: Four chords, round and round, is the most common loop.

whyWrong.1: One chord can work, but it's not a progression.
whyWrong.3: That's a lot for a loop.

steps.next: Next: bass follows the chords. Root notes under your progression.

lessons.title: bass follows the chords

song.why: a bass on the root of each chord glues the harmony to the beat

lessons.learn: What a root note is, why the bass usually plays it, and a bass line under your chords.
youCan: say what a root note is
play a bass line that follows your chords
hear how the bass holds the harmony together

say.mentor:
Listen to the low one. Low notes carry a lot of weight: they tell your ear which chord it's hearing. That's why the simplest bass line is just the bottom note of each chord, played low.
That bottom note is called the root, the note the chord is named after.
say.straight: Low notes define the chord. The simplest bass line plays the root, the note each chord is built on.
say.eli5: Low notes are like the floor a chord stands on. The easiest bass line just plays the lowest note of each chord. That note is called the root.

say.mentor: Play the root of each of your chords on the bass. The bass keys are low versions of your scale, so key one is the root of i, key six the root of VI, key three of III, key seven of VII. Press rec and play the roots in the same order as your chords, one per chord.
say.straight: Record the roots of your chords on the bass keys, in order. Key number matches the numeral: i is one, VI is six, III three, VII seven.
say.eli5: Press rec. Play the bass key with the same number as each chord: one for i, six for VI, three for III, seven for VII.

say.mentor: Hear how the song suddenly sits down? The bass locks the chords to the kick. Producers spend ages on this relationship, because the bass and the kick both live down low and can fight. In the producer world you'll learn to make room for both.
say.straight: The bass ties the chords to the beat. Bass and kick share the low end, so they need room; you'll fix that in the producer world.
say.eli5: Now your song has a floor under it! The bass and the boom both live down low, so later you'll learn how to make them share.

steps.q: What is a root note?
options: the note a chord is named after and built on
steps.why: The root is the bottom note the chord is built up from.

whyWrong.1: Usually it's the lowest, not highest, in a basic chord.
whyWrong.3: It's a note, not a song.

steps.q: Why does the bass often play the root?
options: low notes tell the ear which chord it is
the root is the loudest note
the bass can't play other notes
steps.why: Low notes carry the most weight, so the root defines the chord.

whyWrong.1: It's about sound, not effort.
whyWrong.3: A bass can play anything.

steps.q: Your chord is VI. Which bass key plays its root?
steps.why: The numeral tells you the scale note it starts on.

whyWrong.1: Key one is the root of i.
whyWrong.3: Key seven is VII.

steps.next: Next: tension, release and structure. Your loop becomes a song with an intro and a drop.

lessons.title: samples and loops

song.why: recorded sounds bring a real room and real hits into your song

lessons.learn: What a sample is, how loops are built from them, and real recorded drums playing your own beat.
youCan: say what a sample and a loop are
hear the difference between a synth and a recorded drum
put recorded drums in your song

say.mentor: A sample is a recording you play back as an instrument: a single drum hit, a vocal, a chord from an old record. A loop is a sample that repeats, usually a bar or two long. Hip hop was built on loops cut from funk and soul records, and house producers sample constantly.
say.straight: A sample is a recording used as an instrument. A loop is a sample that repeats.
say.eli5: A sample is a recorded sound you can play like an instrument. A loop is a sample that goes round and round.

deeper.title: sampling and permission
deeper.say: Using a few seconds of someone else's record still needs permission if you release it. Lots of producers record their own sounds or use sample packs that come cleared. The drums here were recorded for CCD School and are free to use.

say.mentor: Here's your beat. The drums so far have been made by the engine. Switch to recorded and the same pattern plays on real recorded hits: a kick, a clap, a hat and a snare. Listen to the texture.
say.straight: Your beat on synth drums or recorded samples. Pick one.
say.eli5: Same beat, made by the computer or played on real recorded drums. Which sounds better to you?

steps.q: What is a sample?
options: a recording used as an instrument
steps.why: Any recording you play back as an instrument.

whyWrong.1: A melody can be sampled, but a sample is any recording.
whyWrong.3: A drum machine may play samples, but it isn't one.

steps.q: What is a loop?
steps.why: A bar or two of audio that plays round and round.

whyWrong.1: A single hit is a one-shot.
whyWrong.3: Reverb is space.

steps.next: Next: tension, release and structure. Your loop becomes a song.

lessons.title: tension, release and structure

song.why: a song is a loop that changes over time

lessons.learn: How songs build and release tension, the sections of a dance track, and your loop arranged into a song.
youCan: say what tension and release mean in music
name an intro, build, drop and break
arrange your loop into sections

say.mentor: Music works by building tension and releasing it. A chord that wants to go home, a drum roll before a change, the drums dropping out so their return feels huge. Dance music does this with arrangement: the same loop, with parts taken away and brought back.
say.straight: Tension builds, release pays it off. Dance tracks do it by taking parts away and bringing them back.
say.eli5: Songs make you wait for something, then give it to you. That waiting feeling is tension. Getting it is release.

say.mentor: Here's your loop laid out as a song: intro, build, drop, break, drop. Each row is one of your parts. Tap a square to switch a part off or on in that section, and tap fill for a drum roll at the end. Play it through. You've just made a song.
say.straight: Your loop as sections. Tap squares to switch parts off or on; tap fill for a roll.
say.eli5: Tap squares to turn sounds on and off in each part. Press play and hear your whole song.

steps.q: What is a breakdown?
options: a section with the drums taken out
steps.why: Drums out, so their return is a big release.

whyWrong.1: That's the drop.
whyWrong.3: That's the start of the intro.

steps.q: In music, what is release?
steps.why: Tension builds, release resolves it.

whyWrong.1: Loudness is separate.
whyWrong.3: That's a synth's release knob, a different idea.

steps.next: Next: the producer world. Make every part of your song sound its best.

lessons.title: bonus, higher or lower

song.why: nothing changes in your song here; this round trains the ears you use on every part of it

lessons.learn: A quick ear round: two notes, which one is higher? It gets harder as you get them right.
youCan: hear which of two notes is higher, even when they're close

say.mentor: A quick one, just for your ears. Tap low, then high. Easy when they're far apart. In the round coming up they start far apart and get closer together as you get them right, until it's a real test. Producers do this all day: is the bass a little too high, is that note a touch flat.
say.straight: Ear round: which of two notes is higher. They get closer as you get them right.
say.eli5: A listening game! You'll hear two notes. Say which one is higher. They start far apart and get closer and closer.

steps.say: Two notes. Which one was higher? Replay as often as you like.

steps.q: Two notes, one at 220 hz and one at 233 hz. Which is higher?
options: you can't tell from the numbers
steps.why: More wiggles a second, higher note. 233 is higher, though only a little.

whyWrong.1: 220 is the lower of the two.
whyWrong.2: They're 13 hz apart, about one key on a piano.
whyWrong.3: The bigger number is always the higher pitch.

steps.next: Back to your song: waveforms, and picking the shape for your melody.

lessons.title: bonus, your ear

song.why: nothing changes in your song here; this round trains the ears you use on every part of it

lessons.learn: A quick ear round on intervals and pitch: hear the jump, name the direction.
youCan: hear small and large pitch changes

say.mentor: An ear round. You know the octave by now. The round coming up asks which of two notes is higher, and the gap shrinks as you get them right. It's the same skill you use to hear a bass that's out of key or a lead that's a touch flat.
say.straight: Ear round: which of two notes is higher. The gap shrinks as you go.
say.eli5: A listening game. Two notes, which is higher? It gets trickier as you go.

steps.say: Which one was higher? Replay as often as you like.

steps.next: Back to your song: chords, and the harmony under your melody.

lessons.title: bonus, listen like a producer

song.why: nothing changes in your song here; you're learning to hear it like a producer

lessons.learn: How producers listen: one part at a time, then the whole, then the journey.
youCan: listen to one part of a track at a time
describe a track's structure by ear

say.mentor:
Producers listen in layers. First pick one part and follow only it for the whole track: just the hats, say. Then listen to the whole, and ask what's loudest, what's in front, what's far away. Then listen to the journey: when do things come in and go out, where's the drop, how long is the break.
Try it on your own song in the studio, then on a track you love.
say.straight: Listen to one part, then the balance, then the structure. Your song first, then a track you love.
say.eli5: Pick one sound and only listen to that. Then listen to everything. Then listen for when things change.

steps.q: What's a good first way to listen like a producer?
options: follow one part through the whole track
turn it up as loud as possible
steps.why: Following one part teaches you what each part is doing.

whyWrong.1: You'd miss the build that makes it work.
whyWrong.3: The intro tells you a lot.

steps.next: The producer world is next: make every part of your song sound its best.

lessons.title: what is rhythm?

song.why: moving one kick off the beat shows you what the pulse is doing for your song

lessons.learn: The difference between the pulse and the rhythm on top of it, and what happens to your beat when one kick leaves the pulse.
youCan: say the difference between pulse and rhythm
hear when a kick has moved off the beat
keep a kick off the beat, or put it back

say.mentor:
Tap your foot to this. Your foot finds the kick straight away, because it never changes: one, two, three, four. That steady tick is the pulse.
The clap doesn't land on every tick. It lands on two of them. Where the sounds land, and where they don't, is the rhythm. The pulse stays put and the rhythm is everything you choose to put on top of it.
say.straight: The pulse is the steady tick your foot finds. Rhythm is the pattern of sounds placed over it, some on the ticks, some between them. The pulse stays, the rhythm varies.
say.eli5: Tap your foot. Your foot follows the boom, boom, boom, like a clock. That's the pulse. The clap only joins in sometimes. Where the sounds land is called rhythm.

say.mentor:
A single hit on its own has no rhythm. Play a second one a moment later and suddenly there's a gap between them, and your brain starts measuring it. Repeat it and you've got a pattern in time. That's all rhythm is: when things happen, and when they don't.
Here's the cool part. Most dance music is recognised by its rhythm long before its melody. A four on the floor kick tells you it's house before a single note plays.
say.straight: One hit has no rhythm. Two hits at different times start one. Rhythm is when sounds happen and when they don't. Dance styles are recognised by their rhythm first.
say.eli5: One boom on its own isn't a rhythm. Two booms with a gap between them start one. Rhythm is about when sounds happen.

deeper.title: pulse, metre and accent
deeper.say: The pulse is the steady beat. Metre is how those beats group into bars that repeat, like four beats in a bar of 4/4 or three in a waltz. Accents are the beats that get extra weight, and they are a big part of what gives a groove its feel.

deeper.title: in live
deeper.say: The tempo box sits in the Control Bar at the top of Live. Turn on the Metronome to hear the pulse while you work. Tap Tempo, next to the tempo box, lets you tap a beat to set the bpm.

say.mentor:
Now break your own beat on purpose. Press rec, wait out the count-in, and tap the kick four times: three right on the beat, and one on an "and", exactly halfway between two beats. Snap is on, so that one lands dead in the middle.
While you record, your old kick keeps time underneath. At the end you'll hear your song with the moved kick and without it. Listen for the stumble: your body expected the pulse and got something else. Some people love that push, some want it back on the beat. Keep whichever feels like your song.
say.straight: Record four kicks: three on the beat, one on an "and" between beats. Snap is on. At the end, compare your song with the moved kick and without it, and keep one.
say.eli5: Press rec, wait for four ticks, then tap the kick four times. Put three on the ticks and one in between two ticks. Listen to how it trips. Then you can keep it or put it back.

steps.hint: Say "one, two and three, four" and tap the kick on the "and".

steps.q: What is the pulse?
options: the steady beat your foot taps to
the loudest sound in the song
steps.why: The pulse is the steady beat underneath, the one you tap along to.

whyWrong.1: Loud or quiet, the pulse is about steady timing.
whyWrong.2: The melody sits on top of the pulse.
whyWrong.3: That's the tempo, the speed of the pulse. The pulse is the beat itself.

steps.q: Rhythm is mostly about
options: which key the song is in
steps.why: Rhythm is the pattern of when sounds happen and when they don't.

whyWrong.1: Which notes is melody and harmony.
whyWrong.3: Keys are about notes, not time.

steps.q: You move one kick onto an "and". What stays the same?
steps.why: The pulse keeps ticking at the same speed. Only the pattern on top changed.

whyWrong.1: The rhythm is exactly what you changed.
whyWrong.3: The pulse and the tempo stay put.

steps.q: What is metre?
options: how beats group into repeating bars
steps.why: Metre is how the beats group, four to a bar in 4/4, three in 3/4.

whyWrong.1: Speed is tempo.
whyWrong.2: Pitch is about notes, not time.
whyWrong.3: Length is counted in bars, but metre is how each bar is grouped.

steps.next: Back to the pulse path. Next: bars and counting, and a clap on two and four.

lessons.title: syncopation

song.why: an accent on the offbeat pulls against your kick, and that pull is what makes a beat move

lessons.learn: What syncopation is, why a hit between the beats makes people move, and an open hat accent on the offbeat in your own song.
youCan: say what syncopation means
hear an accent pulling against the beat
put an offbeat accent in your hats

say.mentor:
Listen to the open hats. They don't hit with the kick, they hit in the gaps between kicks, on the "and". Hear how the whole loop lifts and bounces?
That's syncopation: putting the accent, the hit that stands out, on a beat that's normally weak. The pulse doesn't change at all. The rhythm just leans against it.
say.straight: The open hats land between the kicks, on the "and". Accenting the weak spots between beats is called syncopation. The pulse stays the same; the rhythm pulls against it.
say.eli5: Hear the tss in between the booms? It doesn't land with the boom, it lands in the gap. That makes the beat bounce. Hitting in the gaps is called syncopation.

say.mentor:
A hit on the offbeat creates a little tension. Your body knows where the strong beat is, and the accent arrives somewhere else. Then the next downbeat lands and the tension lets go. That tiny push and pull, over and over, is a big part of why people dance.
A pattern with no syncopation feels square, like a march. Add even one offbeat accent and the loop comes alive. Funk, reggae and most dance music live on it.
say.straight: An offbeat accent builds a little tension that lets go on the next downbeat. No syncopation sounds like a march. One offbeat hit makes it groove.
say.eli5: A hit in the gap makes your body wait a tiny bit for the next boom. When the boom comes, it feels good. That's why it makes you want to move.

deeper.title: the backbeat and the anticipation
deeper.say: The clap on two and four is already a kind of syncopation, called the backbeat: the accent sits on the weaker beats instead of one and three. An anticipation is a hit just before a strong beat, arriving early so the music feels like it's rushing forward. Funk bass lines use it all the time.

deeper.title: three, three, two
deeper.say: Split the eight eighths of a bar into groups of three, three and two and accent the first of each group. It feels off and inevitable at the same time. It's the shape of a lot of Latin rhythm and plenty of dance music.

deeper.title: where it comes from
deeper.say: Syncopation in popular music traces back to West African rhythm. Through blues, jazz, funk and soul it reached house and techno.

say.mentor:
Put an accent in your own hats. Your closed hats keep going; you're adding the open hat on top.
Press rec, wait out the count-in, and tap the open hat on two of the "ands", the gaps halfway between kicks. Snap is on and set to eighths, so each hit lands right in the gap. Try the "and" after two and the "and" after four, or put them wherever the loop lifts most.
say.straight: Add open hats on top of your closed hats. Rec, count-in, then tap the open hat on two of the "ands". Snap puts them exactly between the kicks.
say.eli5: Press rec and wait for four ticks. Then tap the open hat pad in the gaps between the booms, two times. Listen to it bounce.

steps.hint: Count "one and two and" and tap the open hat on an "and".

steps.q: Syncopation means
options: accenting the offbeats and weak beats
playing only on the main beats
steps.why: Syncopation puts the accent where the beat is normally weak, between or off the strong beats.

whyWrong.1: That's the opposite. Only main beats sounds square.
whyWrong.2: The bar stays the same. The accents move.
whyWrong.3: The tempo doesn't change.

steps.q: In 4/4, the backbeat lands on
steps.why: Two and four, where the clap or snare usually sits.

whyWrong.1: One and three are the strong beats, usually the kick's.
whyWrong.2: Every beat is the pulse, not the backbeat.
whyWrong.3: The ands are offbeats. The backbeat is on two and four.

steps.q: Why does an offbeat accent make people move?
options: it builds tension that lets go on the next beat
steps.why: The accent arrives where you don't expect it, and the next downbeat resolves it.

whyWrong.1: It can be quiet and still work.
whyWrong.3: Rhythm doesn't touch the key.

steps.q: What happens if everything is syncopated and nothing marks the one?
steps.why: Syncopation needs a steady pulse to pull against. Without one, people lose their place.

whyWrong.1: It gets looser and harder to follow.
whyWrong.3: Losing the one changes everything.

steps.next: Back to the beat path. Next: groove and swing, and a swing setting for your whole song.

lessons.title: polyrhythm

song.why: a shaker counting in threes over a kick counting in fours gives your beat a rolling, hypnotic motion

lessons.learn: What a polyrhythm is, why two rhythms at once feel hypnotic, and a shaker in threes over your kick in fours.
youCan: say what a polyrhythm is
count threes against fours
add a shaker in threes to your beat

say.mentor:
Listen to the last part, the fast sixteenth hats. Count them in fours along with the kick: one e and a, two e and a. Easy.
Now count the same hats in threes instead: one two three, one two three. The hats haven't changed, but your counting has drifted away from the kick. Two ways of counting at once. That's the feeling you're about to put into your song.
say.straight: Count the sixteenths in fours with the kick, then in threes. Same hats, two groupings at once. That's the start of a polyrhythm.
say.eli5: Listen to the fast tss tss tss. Count them one two three four, with the boom. Now count them one two three, one two three. Your counting stops matching the boom. Fun, right?

say.mentor:
A polyrhythm is two rhythms playing at the same time, each with its own pulse. The classic is three against two: one part plays three even hits while another plays two in the same space. They line up at the start, pull against each other in the middle, and meet again at the end.
Your ear keeps flipping between hearing the three and hearing the two, and that's why polyrhythms feel hypnotic. Minimal techno and Afrobeats use a pattern in threes over a straight four on the floor kick all the time.
say.straight: A polyrhythm is two rhythms at once, each with its own pulse, like three against two. They line up at the start and pull apart in between. Common in techno and Afrobeats.
say.eli5: Two people clap different patterns at the same time. They start together, drift apart, then meet again. That's a polyrhythm.

deeper.title: polyrhythm or polymeter
deeper.say: In a polyrhythm both parts fill the same span, three hits against two. In a polymeter the steps are the same size but the loops are different lengths, say a three beat loop against a four beat loop, so their starts drift apart and only line up again after twelve beats. In Live, clips of different lengths in Session View loop on their own, which is an easy way to make one.

deeper.title: keep them apart
deeper.say: Two rhythms only sound like two rhythms if your ear can tell them apart. Give them different sounds, different pitches or different places in the stereo, and keep them quieter than the kick so the one still wins. Start slower than about 100 bpm when you're learning a new one.

deeper.title: where it comes from
deeper.say: West African drumming is built on polyrhythm, many interlocking parts layered at once. Ewe, Yoruba and Akan drumming are the usual examples.

say.mentor:
Now put it in your song. Your closed hats keep going; you're adding a shaker on top.
Tap the snap key until it says sixteenths. Press rec, wait out the count-in, then count the sixteenths in threes, one two three, one two three, and tap the shaker on every "one". Start counting again at each new bar.
Here's what you'll hear: the shaker and the kick land together on beat one, pull apart, and meet again three beats later. Sixteen doesn't split evenly into threes, so the last count of each bar gets cut short and two shakes land close together as the bar starts over. That rolling, never quite settling feel is three against four.
say.straight: Set snap to sixteenths. Rec, then count sixteenths in threes and tap the shaker on every "one", restarting each bar. Shaker and kick meet on beat one and again three beats later.
say.eli5: Press rec and wait for four ticks. Count really fast, one two three, one two three, and tap the shaker every time you say one. It starts with the boom, wanders off, and comes back.

steps.hint: Sixteenths 1, 4, 7, 10, 13 and 16 of the bar, counting from 1. Six shakes a bar.

steps.q: A polyrhythm is
options: two rhythms at once, each with its own pulse
steps.why: Two or more rhythms with their own pulses, played together.

whyWrong.1: Fast isn't the point. It's two pulses at once.
whyWrong.3: A waltz has one pulse, counted in threes.

steps.q: In three against two, where do the two parts line up?
options: at the start of each cycle
only at the end of the song
steps.why: They share the first beat, pull apart, and meet again when the cycle starts over.

whyWrong.1: Then they'd be one rhythm.
whyWrong.2: They always meet at the start of the cycle.
whyWrong.3: They meet every cycle, not once.

steps.q: What helps you hear two rhythms instead of one mess?
options: a different sound, pitch or place for each part
steps.why: Your ear needs a way to tell the parts apart. Different sounds or positions do that.

whyWrong.1: Same sound, same place, and they blur into one.
whyWrong.2: More layers make it busier, not clearer.
whyWrong.3: The downbeat is the anchor where they meet.

steps.q: How is polymeter different?
steps.why: Same size steps, different loop lengths, so the starts drift apart.

whyWrong.1: Triplets are three notes in the space of two, a different idea.
whyWrong.3: The kick can stay.

steps.next: Back to the beat path. Next: groove and swing, and a swing setting for your whole song.

lessons.title: rhythm in production

song.why: hats played in by hand, a hair behind the grid, make a programmed beat feel like someone is playing it

lessons.learn: The grid as a tool, when to stay on it and when to leave it, and hats in your song played by hand with snap off.
youCan: say what the grid and quantise do
hear the difference between tight and laid back
play hats in by hand without snap

say.mentor:
Tap straight, then swung. In the first one every hat sits exactly on the grid, the lines that split each beat. In the second some hats are moved off those lines. Same notes, different feel.
A music program will put every hit on the grid for you. Whether you let it is one of the most important choices in a track.
say.straight: Straight: every hat on the grid. Swung: some moved off it. On the grid is tight, off it feels played.
say.eli5: Tap a, then b. In a, every tss is exactly in line like soldiers. In b, some wobble a bit. The wobbly one feels more like dancing.

say.mentor:
Snapping notes to the grid is called quantising. It gives you tight, machine timing, which is great for a club kick that has to hit exactly. Moving notes off the grid gives a played, human feel.
Off the grid has two directions. A hit slightly after the beat feels laid back, relaxed and deep, the classic hip hop and soul pocket. A hit slightly before feels pushing, urgent, leaning forward. Most producers lock the kick and bass first, then loosen the parts on top.
say.straight: Quantise snaps notes to the grid for tight timing. Off the grid feels human. Slightly late is laid back, slightly early is pushing. Lock kick and bass first, loosen the rest.
say.eli5: A helper can line every tap up perfectly. That sounds neat but a bit robot. Taps a tiny bit late sound relaxed. Taps a tiny bit early sound excited.

deeper.title: in live
deeper.say: Quantize snaps selected notes to the grid, and quantize strength lets you go part of the way: at 80 percent every note moves 80 percent of the way to the line, tighter but still human. The Groove Pool takes the timing, velocity and length from one clip and applies it to another, so you can borrow the feel of a real drum break.

deeper.title: record slow, then speed up
deeper.say: If a part is hard to play in time, drop the tempo, record it, then bring the tempo back up. Notes you recorded as midi follow the tempo, so the part plays back at full speed with your timing intact.

say.mentor:
Now play your hats in by hand. Snap is off this time, so every hit lands exactly where you tap.
Press rec, wait out the count-in, and tap the hat on each "and", between the kicks. Don't rush. Let a couple of them land a hair late, just behind where you'd expect. Then listen to the loop: that slight drag is the laid back feel producers spend hours chasing. If it sounds sloppy rather than relaxed, play it again a little tighter.
say.straight: Snap is off. Rec, count-in, then tap the hat on every "and", letting a couple land a touch late. Keep it if it feels relaxed, replay if it feels sloppy.
say.eli5: No helper this time. Press rec, wait for four ticks, and tap the hat in between the booms. It's fine if some are a tiny bit late. That makes it feel relaxed.

steps.hint: Count "one and two and" and tap on the "and", lazily.

steps.q: What does quantising do?
steps.why: Quantise snaps each note to the nearest grid line for tight timing.

whyWrong.1: Quantise takes the human wobble out. Leaving notes off the grid keeps it.
whyWrong.3: Timing, not pitch.

steps.q: A hat played slightly after the beat feels
steps.why: Slightly late feels relaxed and deep.

whyWrong.1: Pushing is slightly before the beat.
whyWrong.3: Drums aren't in a key here, and timing doesn't change pitch.

steps.q: Which parts do producers usually lock down first?
steps.why: If kick and bass groove, the rest falls into place on top.

whyWrong.1: Melody usually comes after the rhythm sits.
whyWrong.3: Hats sit on top of the kick and bass.

steps.q: Quantising at 80 percent strength
options: moves notes 80 percent of the way to the grid
steps.why: Every note moves most of the way, so it tightens up but keeps some feel.

whyWrong.1: All the notes move, each only part of the way.
whyWrong.3: It still snaps, just not all the way.

steps.next: Your beat is done for now. Next path: sound, and a melody over your beat.

lessons.title: sound in space

song.why: reverb and level together decide whether your lead sits right in your ear or across the room

lessons.learn: Why every room sounds different, what reverb is, and how near or far your lead sits in your song.
youCan: say what reverb is
name decay, pre-delay and dry and wet
place your lead near or far with reverb and level

say.mentor:
Picture this note played in a small tiled bathroom, then in a huge cathedral. Same note, but you can already hear how different they'd be: one splashy and short, one ringing for seconds.
That difference is the room. When sound leaves a speaker, some of it reaches your ears directly. The rest bounces off walls, floor and ceiling and arrives a moment later, a little softer.
say.straight: A sound reaches you directly, then again as reflections off every surface, slightly later and softer. Small tiled rooms sound splashy, big halls ring for seconds.
say.eli5: Imagine singing this note in a bathroom, then in a giant church. In the church it rings and rings. That's because the sound bounces off the walls and comes back to you.

say.mentor:
Hundreds of those reflections blur together into one smooth tail. That tail is called reverb. Your brain uses it to work out how big a room is and how far away the sound is, which is why a sound with no reverb at all can feel flat, like it's inside your head.
Three words you'll see on every reverb. Decay is how long the tail lasts. Pre-delay is the short gap before the tail starts. Dry and wet is the balance between the original sound and the reverb.
say.straight: Reverb is many reflections blurred into a tail. Decay is how long it lasts, pre-delay the gap before it starts, dry and wet the balance of original and effect.
say.eli5: All those bounces mix into one long ring called reverb. It tells your ears how big the room is.

deeper.title: decay and rt60
deeper.say: Rooms are measured by RT60, the time it takes the reverb to fall by 60 dB. A bedroom is around 0.3 seconds, a concert hall 1.5 to 2.5, a cathedral 4 or more.

deeper.title: pre-delay
deeper.say: Twenty to forty milliseconds of pre-delay lets the dry sound land first and the room follow behind it, so a vocal or lead stays upfront while still sounding like it's in a space.

deeper.title: in live
deeper.say: A send carries a copy of a track to a return track, a shared effect lane. Put one reverb on a return and send several tracks to it: it uses less of the computer, and everything sounds like it's in the same room.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with two knobs on your lead. Send is how much of your lead goes to the reverb. Level is how loud the lead is.
Close sounds are louder, with more direct sound and less reverb. Far sounds are quieter and mostly tail. So move them together: send up and level down pushes your lead to the back of the room. Send down and level up brings it right into your ear. Somewhere in between is usually where a lead lives. Leave it where it sounds right in your song.
say.straight: Send: how much lead goes to the reverb. Level: how loud it is. Near is louder and dry, far is quieter and wet. Move both together and set the distance.
say.eli5: Turn send up and level down: your tune walks far away across the room. Turn send down and level up: it comes right up close. Stop where you like it.

steps.q: What is reverb?
options: reflections off surfaces, blurred into a tail
steps.why: Reverb is the blur of many reflections arriving just after the direct sound.

whyWrong.1: Reflections don't change the speed.
whyWrong.3: Distortion changes the shape of the wave. Reverb adds reflections.

steps.q: How do you push your lead further back?
options: more reverb and a lower level
more reverb and a higher level
steps.why: Far sounds are quieter and mostly tail, so turn both knobs that way.

whyWrong.1: Louder pulls it forward again.
whyWrong.3: Tempo doesn't change distance.

steps.q: Pre-delay is
options: the gap before the reverb tail starts
steps.why: It's the short wait before the tail, which keeps the dry sound clear.

whyWrong.1: That's the dry and wet balance.
whyWrong.3: Width is a separate setting.

steps.q: RT60 measures
options: how long a reverb takes to fall by 60 dB
the highest note a room can hold
steps.why: It's the standard way to say how live or dead a room is.

whyWrong.1: Nothing to do with heat.
whyWrong.3: It measures time, not notes.

steps.next: Back to the sound path. Next: frequency and pitch, and a jump of an octave in your melody.

lessons.title: how we hear

song.why: a kick and a bass in the same low range hide each other, and ducking lets your ears hear both

lessons.learn: How your ears hear, why they aren't fair to every sound, and masking: your bass and your kick hiding each other, with and without a duck.
youCan: say what masking is
say why mixes sound different at different volumes
duck your bass so your kick comes through

say.mentor:
Sound reaches your eardrum, which pushes three tiny bones, which push fluid inside a spiral called the cochlea. Different spots along that spiral react to different pitches, and your brain turns the pattern into what you hear.
The surprise is that your ears aren't fair. They hear the middle, roughly 2 to 5 khz where speech sits, best of all. Deep bass and very high sounds need more energy to seem just as loud.
say.straight: Your ear sorts sound by pitch in the cochlea. It hears best around 2 to 5 khz, where speech is. Deep bass and very high sounds need more energy to seem as loud.
say.eli5: Inside your ear is a tiny curly snail shape called the cochlea. Different parts of it hear different notes. Your ears hear talking voices best, and very deep booms not as well.

say.mentor:
Here's the one that matters most in a mix. A loud sound makes quieter sounds near the same pitch hard or impossible to hear. That's called masking.
Your kick and your bass both live down low. When they hit at the same moment, the louder one masks the other, and the two smear into one thick boom. You don't hear a kick and a bass, you hear mud.
