steps.q: Why does a drop feel big?
options: the drums were missing just before
steps.why: Contrast. After the break, the drums return with full force.

whyWrong.1: It's usually the same level; it just feels bigger.
whyWrong.3: It's the same song.

steps.next: Next: finish and export. Name it, take it to Live, send it to CCD.

lessons.title: finish and export

song.why: a song is finished when it leaves the app

lessons.learn: Naming your song, exporting it as midi for Ableton Live, and what happens next.
youCan: export your song as midi
open it in Live and keep working
say what stems are

say.mentor:
Lots of producers have hundreds of loops and no finished songs. Finishing is a skill, and you've just done it: a beat, a bass, a lead, chords, a mix and an arrangement, all yours.
From here you can take it into Ableton Live to keep going: more sounds, vocals, a proper master. You export it as midi, the notes of every part, and Live plays them on its own instruments.
say.straight: Finishing matters. Export your song as midi and open it in Live to keep going.
say.eli5: You made a whole song! Now you can take it into a big music program called Ableton Live.

deeper.title: stems
deeper.say: Stems are each part exported as its own audio file: drums, bass, lead and so on. Engineers and djs use them to remix and master. They're coming to CCD School soon.

say.mentor: Here's your finished song. Give it a name, play it through once more, and download the midi. Drop the file into Live and every part lands on its own track. And if you're proud of it, send it to CCD: the best learner tracks get played at our nights.
say.straight: Name it, play it, download the midi, open it in Live. Send it to CCD if you're proud of it.
say.eli5: Type a name for your song. Then tap download and open it in Live.

steps.q: What does a midi file hold?
steps.why: Midi is notes, timing and velocity. Live plays them on its instruments.

whyWrong.1: That's an audio export.
whyWrong.3: It's music data only.

steps.q: Where would you go next in Live to try this?
options: the deeper lessons in this path

whyWrong.1: Live can do all of it.

The deeper lessons in this path walk through each.

steps.q: Where would you go next in Live to try this?
options: the deeper lessons in this path
steps.why: Each deeper lesson here walks through one part of it, on your own song.

whyWrong.1: Live can do all of it.

lessons.title: what is live?

song.why: your song is already a set of tracks, each with its own level and place, which is exactly how Live sees it

lessons.learn: What a DAW is, how Live sees your song as tracks and clips, and its two views: the clip grid and the timeline.
youCan: say what a DAW is
name Live's two views and what each is for
set one track's level and pan in your song

say.mentor:
Listen to this loop: a kick, a clap and some hats. It sounds like one thing, but it's three parts stacked up, each playing its own pattern. Your song works the same way. Your kick, your clap, your hats and your lead each live in their own lane.
In a music program those lanes are called tracks. Ableton Live, the program pros use for this kind of music, would show your song as one track per part.
say.straight: A loop is parts stacked up: kick, clap, hats. Your song is the same, one lane per part. In a music program those lanes are tracks.
say.eli5: This sounds like one beat, but it's three sounds playing together. Your song is the same: every sound gets its own lane, called a track.

steps.title: a daw, and its two views

say.mentor:
Live is a DAW, short for digital audio workstation: a program you make, record and mix music in. Most DAWs give you one timeline that runs left to right, like reading a page.
Live gives you that timeline, called arrangement view, and also a grid of clips you can start in any order, called session view. A clip is a short piece of music on one track, like your hat pattern. Same song, two windows onto it.
The cool part: nothing you do to a sound in Live changes the original file. Stretch it, chop it, reverse it, and the recording on your computer stays exactly as it was.
say.straight: A DAW (digital audio workstation) is a program for making music. Live has two views: arrangement, a timeline left to right, and session, a grid of clips you launch in any order. Edits never change the original file.
say.eli5: Live is a music-making program. It can show your song as a long line from start to end, or as a grid of little loops you can start whenever you like. And whatever you do, your original sounds stay safe.

deeper.title: live's screen
deeper.say: Press Tab to swap between session view and arrangement view. The music keeps playing while you switch, because both views show the same tracks underneath. Every track, whether it holds audio or midi, exists in both views with the same devices and mixer settings.

deeper.title: saving and moving a project
deeper.say: A Live project is saved as an .als file. That file points to your samples instead of holding them, so before you move a project to another computer use File > Collect All and Save, which copies the samples in with it.

say.mentor:
Here's your song, and here's your lead as a track. Every track in a DAW has a fader, a slider for how loud it is, and a pan knob, for where it sits between your left and right speakers.
Turn level down until your lead tucks behind the beat, then bring it back. Turn pan a little left or right and hear it move across. Leave it where your song sounds best.
say.straight: Your lead as a track. Level is its fader, how loud it is. Pan places it left or right. Set both by ear.
say.eli5: Your tune has its own lane. Level makes it louder or quieter. Pan moves it to the left speaker or the right one. Stop where you like it.

steps.q: What does DAW stand for?
steps.why: A digital audio workstation, a program for making, recording and mixing music.

whyWrong.1: Close, but the w is workstation, the whole program.
whyWrong.2: A DAW does far more than drums.
whyWrong.3: It's a whole program, not one window.

steps.q: Which of Live's views is a grid of clips you can start in any order?
steps.why: Session view is the grid. Arrangement view is the timeline that runs left to right.

whyWrong.1: Arrangement is the left to right timeline.
whyWrong.2: The mixer sets levels, it doesn't launch clips.
whyWrong.3: The browser is where you find sounds.

steps.q: You reverse a sample in Live. What happens to the original file on your computer?
steps.why: Live's edits are instructions it follows when it plays. The file itself is never changed.

whyWrong.1: Live leaves the file alone and plays it backwards.
whyWrong.3: The project points to the file, it doesn't copy it.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, find the same handful of things on our instrument and in Live.

lessons.title: around live

song.why: your song's tempo, set from the one place every DAW keeps it, the bar along the top

lessons.learn: The five things you reach for in any song, where you've already met them here, and where they live in Live's window.
youCan: name the five main parts of Live's window
say where tempo, notes and sound controls live in Live
set your song's tempo

say.mentor:
A kick and a clap. Simple, but to make even this you've already used five things: a speed for the song, a place to find sounds, a list of your parts, the notes one part plays, and knobs that shape how it sounds.
Every DAW has those same five things. Once you know where they live, any music program stops looking scary.
say.straight: Even a kick and clap need five things: tempo, sounds, parts, notes and knobs. Every DAW has all five.
say.eli5: To make this beat you need a speed, some sounds, a list of parts, the notes, and knobs. Every music program has these five things.

say.mentor:
In Live, the speed of the song sits in the control bar along the top, with play, stop, the metronome (the click that keeps time) and the tempo in bpm, beats per minute.
Sounds live in the browser down the left side. Your parts, the tracks, fill the middle, which Live calls the main view: either the session grid or the arrangement timeline.
Notes and knobs share the bottom panel, the detail view. Click a clip and it shows the notes. Click a track's instrument and it shows the knobs. That's the same split you've been using here: play the notes in, then shape the sound.
say.straight: Live's window: control bar on top (tempo, play, metronome), browser on the left (sounds), main view in the middle (your tracks), detail view at the bottom (notes or knobs, for whatever you clicked).
say.eli5: Speed goes at the top. Sounds are on the left. Your parts are in the middle. The notes and knobs for one part show up at the bottom when you click it.

deeper.title: the info view
deeper.say: There's a fifth panel in the bottom corner called the info view. Hover over any control in Live and it tells you what that control does. When you're lost, look there before you reach for the manual.

deeper.title: shortcuts worth knowing
deeper.say: Tab swaps the main view between session and arrangement. Every panel can be shown or hidden with the small triangles at its edge or from the View menu, which helps a lot on a small laptop screen.

say.mentor:
Here's your song, and here's the control bar's job: the tempo. Turn it and every part of your song speeds up or slows down together, because they all follow this one number.
Try slower and it lays back. Try faster and it pushes. House usually sits somewhere around 120 to 128. Leave it where your song feels right.
say.straight: Your song's tempo, the same number Live keeps in its control bar. Every part follows it. Set it by feel.
say.eli5: This makes your whole song go faster or slower. All the sounds follow it together. Stop where it feels good to dance to.

steps.q: Where does Live keep the tempo?
options: the control bar along the top
the detail view at the bottom
steps.why: Tempo, play, stop and the metronome all sit in the control bar along the top.

whyWrong.1: The browser holds sounds, samples and presets.
whyWrong.2: The detail view shows one clip's notes or one track's devices.
whyWrong.3: Every clip follows the one tempo in the control bar.

steps.q: You click a clip. What shows up in the detail view?
steps.why: Click a clip and the detail view shows what's inside it, the notes or the audio.

whyWrong.1: Tempo sits in the control bar.
whyWrong.3: Every track is the main view's job.

steps.q: What does the Tab key do in Live?
options: swaps between session and arrangement view
steps.why: Tab flips the main view between the session grid and the arrangement timeline.

whyWrong.1: That's the space bar.
whyWrong.2: The browser is shown or hidden on its own.
whyWrong.3: Recording has its own button.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, your drums as a rack of pads.

lessons.title: the drum rack in live

song.why: each drum is its own pad with its own controls, so you can reshape your kick without touching your clap

lessons.learn: How a drum kit becomes a rack of pads, one sound per pad, each with its own controls, and how Live's Drum Rack does the same.
youCan: say what a pad in a drum rack is
change one drum without touching the others
say what a choke group does

say.mentor:
A kick and a clap. On a drum machine each of those is its own pad: hit one pad, you get the kick, hit another, you get the clap. Your drums here work the same way. Every drum in your song sits on its own pad.
That's handy, because a pad isn't just a button. It's a whole little instrument with its own knobs.
say.straight: Kick and clap, each on its own pad. A pad is a small instrument with its own knobs.
say.eli5: The boom and the clap each have their own button, called a pad. Each pad has its own knobs too.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with the knobs for one pad: your kick. Tune moves its pitch up or down. Decay is how long it rings: short and tight, or long and boomy. Drive pushes it into a gentle distortion so it sounds harder and grittier.
Listen to your clap and hats while you turn. They don't change at all. That's the whole point of a rack: every pad is shaped on its own. Keep the kick you like best.
say.straight: One pad's knobs: your kick. Tune is pitch, decay is length, drive is grit. The other drums stay as they are. Keep the kick you like.
say.eli5: These knobs only change your boom. Tune makes it higher or lower, decay makes it shorter or longer, drive makes it crunchy. The clap doesn't change. Keep the boom you like.

say.mentor:
Live's version is called Drum Rack. It shows sixteen pads at a time in a four by four grid, and it can hold up to 128. Drag any sample onto a pad and that pad plays it. Each pad answers to one midi note, so a kick pattern is just that note repeated.
Like your kick here, each pad has its own volume, pan, mute and solo, and its own chain of devices. A device is anything that makes or changes sound, like an equaliser or a reverb. So you can put something on the kick alone and leave the snare clean.
say.straight: Live's Drum Rack: 16 pads visible, up to 128. Drop a sample on a pad, it plays from one midi note. Each pad has its own volume, pan, mute, solo and devices.
say.eli5: Live has a drum box called Drum Rack with sixteen pads you can see. Drop any sound on a pad and it plays. Each pad can have its own effects.

deeper.title: choke groups
deeper.say: Put two pads in the same choke group and one cuts the other off. The classic use is hats: an open hat rings on, and the closed hat silences it the moment it hits, just like a drummer closing the pedal.

deeper.title: what's inside a pad
deeper.say: Drag a sample onto a pad and Live builds a chain for it, usually holding a Simpler, Live's simple sampler, playing that one-shot. A pad can hold any instrument and any effects, even another Drum Rack. Drop an EQ Eight on the kick's chain and only the kick is equalised.

steps.q: In a drum rack, what does one pad usually hold?
steps.why: One sound per pad, so each drum can be played and shaped on its own.

whyWrong.1: The rack is the whole kit. A pad is one piece of it.
whyWrong.3: Tempo belongs to the whole song.

steps.q: You turn up drive on your kick pad. What happens to your clap?
options: nothing, it has its own pad
steps.why: Each pad has its own controls. Changing the kick leaves every other pad alone.

whyWrong.1: Drive on one pad only touches that pad.
whyWrong.2: Its level is set on its own pad.
whyWrong.3: Tune is a separate knob on each pad.

steps.q: Why put an open hat and a closed hat in the same choke group?
options: so the closed hat cuts the open one off
so they play at the same time
so the open hat rings longer
steps.why: A choke group lets one pad silence another, like a drummer closing the hi-hat.

whyWrong.1: Choking stops one, it doesn't stack them.
whyWrong.2: Each pad still has its own volume.
whyWrong.3: It makes the open hat stop sooner, not later.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, add your first synth sound.

lessons.title: live's instruments

song.why: the same drum notes played by a different instrument, synthesised or recorded, change the whole feel of your beat

lessons.learn: What an instrument is in a DAW, why the same notes can sound completely different, and the instruments that come with Live.
youCan: say what an instrument does with notes
swap the instrument playing your drums
name a few of Live's instruments and what they're good at

say.mentor:
A kick, a clap and hats. What you see in your song for each part is a list of notes: when to hit and how hard. The notes don't make a sound on their own. Something has to turn them into sound, and that something is called an instrument.
Change the instrument and the same notes come out sounding completely different.
say.straight: Your parts are notes. An instrument turns notes into sound. Same notes, new instrument, new sound.
say.eli5: Your song is a list of when to play each drum. An instrument is what makes the actual sound. Swap it and the same beat sounds new.

say.mentor:
Here's your song, with two instruments for your drums. Synth drums are made from scratch by the engine, out of waves and noise. Recorded drums play back real hits, recorded once and played on your pattern. An instrument that plays recordings like that is called a sampler.
Switch between them while it plays. The pattern doesn't change at all, only the sound. Keep the kit that suits your song.
say.straight: Two instruments, same drum pattern. Synth drums are generated; recorded drums are samples. Switch, then keep one.
say.eli5: Same beat, two drum kits. One is made by the computer, one is real drums that were recorded. Pick the one you like.

say.mentor:
In Live an instrument sits on a midi track, a track that holds notes. Drop one on, play some notes, and you hear it. Live comes with a whole set.
Drum Rack holds drum kits, one sound per pad. Simpler and Sampler play recordings. Wavetable, Analog and Drift are synths, and Operator is an fm synth, a different way of making sound you'll meet in a later lesson. Meld is one of the newer synths in Live 12.
You don't need all of them. Most producers learn two or three really well.
say.straight: In Live, instruments sit on midi tracks. Drum Rack for kits, Simpler and Sampler for recordings, Wavetable, Analog, Drift and Meld for synths, Operator for fm. Learn two or three well.
say.eli5: Live has lots of instruments: one for drums, some that play recordings, and lots of synths. You only need to learn a few.

deeper.title: finding them
deeper.say: Instruments live in the browser under Instruments. Drag one onto a midi track, or onto empty space to make a new midi track for it. Simpler plays one sample across the keys; Sampler can map many samples across the keyboard and by how hard you play, and you can turn one into the other with a right-click.

deeper.title: what each is good at
deeper.say: A rough guide: pads and evolving sounds from Wavetable or Meld, plucks, bells and tight basses from Operator, anything built on a recording from Simpler or Sampler, and kits from Drum Rack. A Drum Rack pad can hold any instrument, not only samples.

steps.q: What does an instrument do in a DAW?
steps.why: Notes say what to play and when. The instrument makes the sound.

whyWrong.1: Tempo lives in the control bar.
whyWrong.2: The browser is where samples are kept.
whyWrong.3: That's the mixer's job.

steps.q: You swapped your drum kit. What stayed the same?
steps.why: Same notes, different instrument. Only the sound changed.

whyWrong.1: The kick sound is exactly what changed.
whyWrong.2: The clap changed with the kit.
whyWrong.3: Your pattern stayed put.

steps.q: An instrument that plays back recordings is called?
steps.why: A sampler plays recorded sounds, like Simpler and Sampler in Live.

whyWrong.1: A synth builds its sound from waves.
whyWrong.3: A metronome is the click that keeps time.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, the oscillator, where every synth sound starts.

lessons.title: oscillators, the sound source

song.why: the wave your lead starts from sets its whole character, before any other knob gets a say

lessons.learn: The oscillator, the part of a synth that makes the raw sound, the classic wave shapes, and picking one for your lead.
youCan: say what an oscillator does
name the four classic wave shapes and how they sound
pick a wave for your lead by ear

say.mentor:
One note, three times: a soft wave, a saw and a square. Same pitch, same loudness, three different characters. The soft one is round, the saw is bright and buzzy, the square is hollow, a bit like a clarinet.
The part of a synth that makes these raw waves is called the oscillator. It's where every synth sound starts. Everything after it, filters and envelopes, only shapes what the oscillator gives it.
say.straight: Soft wave, saw, square. Same note, different shapes. The oscillator makes the raw wave; everything else shapes it.
say.eli5: Three sounds, same note, different shapes. The oscillator is the part of a synth that makes the wave. Round sounds soft, saw sounds buzzy, square sounds hollow.

say.mentor:
Nearly every synth offers the same four shapes. A sine is the smoothest, pure and plain. A triangle is a little brighter but still soft. A square is hollow. A saw, short for sawtooth, is the brightest and the most used, because it has the most going on for a filter to carve.
That's why most bass and lead sounds start from a saw, and clean subs, the deep bass you feel more than hear, start from a sine.
say.straight: Sine is pure, triangle soft, square hollow, saw bright. Most basses and leads start on a saw; subs on a sine.
say.eli5: Sine is smooth. Triangle is gentle. Square is hollow. Saw is buzzy and bright. Lots of synth sounds start with a saw.

deeper.title: oscillators in live
deeper.say: Live's synths all start here. Analog and Drift give each oscillator a shape to pick. Wavetable goes further and sweeps through a whole table of shapes, so the wave can morph while a note plays. A square wave often has a pulse width control too, which squeezes the wave thinner and gives that classic 70s sound.

say.mentor:
Here's your song, with one knob on your lead's oscillator. Wave slides from saw at one end to square at the other, with blends in between.
Turn it slowly while your melody plays. Saw is bright and forward. Square is hollower and a little more retro. Somewhere in between is a mix of both. Keep the one that suits your song.
say.straight: Your lead's oscillator. Wave goes from saw to square. Saw is bright, square is hollow. Keep one.
say.eli5: This knob changes the shape of your tune's wave, from buzzy saw to hollow square. Pick the one you like.

steps.q: What does an oscillator do?
options: makes the raw wave a synth starts from
steps.why: The oscillator makes the sound. The rest of the synth shapes it.

whyWrong.1: That's the envelope's job.
whyWrong.2: Echo is an effect added later.
whyWrong.3: Tempo belongs to the whole song.

steps.q: Which shape is the brightest and most used for leads and bass?
steps.why: The saw has the most going on, so it's bright and there's lots for a filter to shape.

whyWrong.1: A sine is the smoothest and plainest.
whyWrong.3: A square is hollow, less bright than a saw.

steps.q: You want a clean, deep sub bass. Which shape would you start from?
steps.why: A sine is pure, so it gives weight without anything else fighting in the mix.

whyWrong.1: A saw is too bright and busy for a clean sub.
whyWrong.2: A square adds hollow overtones on top.
whyWrong.3: Noise has no pitch at all.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, pitch and loudness, the two things every note has.

lessons.title: pitch vs amplitude

song.why: nudging pitch by a few cents and setting level are two separate moves, and your lead needs both

lessons.learn: How pitch and loudness are two separate things in every note, where a synth controls each, and tiny pitch changes measured in cents.
youCan: say what controls pitch and what controls loudness in a synth
say what a cent is
detune your lead and set its level separately

say.mentor:
Low, then high. Same loudness, different pitch. Pitch is how fast the wave wiggles: faster, higher. Loudness is something else entirely, how big each wiggle is, which is called amplitude.
They're independent. You can play a quiet high note or a loud low one. A synth controls them in different places too: the oscillator sets the pitch, and the amp, short for amplifier, sets how loud.
say.straight: Low and high: pitch is how fast the wave moves. Loudness, or amplitude, is how big it is. Separate things. Oscillator sets pitch, amp sets loudness.
say.eli5: Low note, high note. How high a note is and how loud it is are two different things. You can change one without the other.

say.mentor:
Pitch can move in big steps or tiny ones. The step from one piano key to the next is a semitone, and each semitone splits into 100 cents. A few cents is too small to hear as a new note. Instead the note sounds a touch sharp or flat.
Here's the cool part: stack two copies of the same note a few cents apart and they rub against each other, which makes the sound wider and thicker. That's called detuning.
say.straight: A semitone is 100 cents. A few cents won't change the note, it makes it slightly sharp or flat. Two copies a few cents apart sound wider. That's detune.
say.eli5: Notes can move a tiny, tiny bit, smaller than one key. Two copies of a note, one moved a tiny bit, make a big wide sound.

deeper.title: velocity
deeper.say: How hard you hit a key is called velocity. Synths usually send it to the amp, so harder hits come out louder at the same pitch, like a real instrument. In Live's piano roll each note has its own velocity bar, so you can make two notes the same pitch but different loudness.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with one knob for each idea. Your lead has three oscillators playing together. Detune pulls them apart by a few cents, up to 36. Turn it slowly: it thickens, then shimmers, and pushed too far it starts to sound out of tune.
Level is the other side, amplitude. Turn it and only the loudness changes, never the pitch. Set both until your lead sits right.
say.straight: Detune pulls your lead's three oscillators a few cents apart: wider, then out of tune if pushed. Level is loudness only. Set both.
say.eli5: Detune makes your tune wider and shinier. Too much sounds wobbly. Level makes it louder or quieter. Stop where you like it.

steps.q: Turning up a note's amplitude changes what?
steps.why: Amplitude is the size of the wave, which you hear as loudness. Pitch stays put.

whyWrong.1: Pitch is how fast the wave moves, not how big.
whyWrong.2: Length is set by the note and the envelope.
whyWrong.3: The wave shape is the oscillator's choice.

steps.q: How many cents are in one semitone?
steps.why: A semitone, one piano key to the next, splits into 100 cents.

whyWrong.1: Twelve semitones make an octave.
whyWrong.2: Far too few, cents are tiny.
whyWrong.3: Ten times too many.

steps.q: Why does detuning a few cents make your lead sound wider?
options: the copies rub against each other
steps.why: Copies a few cents apart drift in and out of step, and you hear that as width and movement.

whyWrong.1: Loudness is the level knob's job.
whyWrong.2: A few cents is too small to be a new note.
whyWrong.3: No echo is added, only slightly different pitches.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, hats on the grid.

lessons.title: the piano roll

song.why: hats sit on a grid of time, and snapping them to it is what keeps your groove tight

lessons.learn: What midi is, the piano roll grid where notes are drawn and edited, and snapping your hats to that grid.
youCan: say what midi stores about a note
read a piano roll, pitch up the side and time along the bottom
play hats onto the grid with snap on

say.mentor:
A kick on every beat, then hats on the beats, then the eighths, then the sixteenths. Each step splits the beat into smaller pieces. Those pieces make a grid, and every note in your song sits somewhere on it.
When you played your hats in, the app wasn't recording sound. It was writing down each hit: when it happened, which drum, and how hard. That written-down version is called midi.
say.straight: Beats split into eighths and sixteenths make a grid. Your hats are stored as midi: when, which drum, how hard. Not sound, instructions.
say.eli5: The beat can be cut into smaller and smaller pieces, like lines on paper. When you play your hats, the app writes down when you hit them. That writing is called midi.

say.mentor:
Midi stores a few things about each note: its pitch, when it starts, how long it lasts, and its velocity, how hard it was hit. Notice what's missing: the sound. Midi is like sheet music. The instrument reads it and plays.
A piano roll is where you see and edit those notes. Pitch runs up the side, like a keyboard turned on its edge. Time runs left to right across the grid. Each note is a little bar: move it to change when it plays, stretch it to make it longer, delete it and it's gone.
say.straight: Midi stores pitch, start, length and velocity, not sound. A piano roll shows it: pitch up the side, time across. Move, stretch or delete each note.
say.eli5: Midi is like a music list: which note, when, how long, how hard. The piano roll shows it as little bars on a grid. You can move them, make them longer, or delete them.

deeper.title: the piano roll in live
deeper.say: Double-click a midi clip and its notes open in the detail view at the bottom. Press B to switch to draw mode and click the grid to add notes. Drag a note's right edge to lengthen it. Each note's velocity is a bar along the bottom. Cmd or Ctrl plus 1 and 2 make the grid finer or coarser.

deeper.title: quantise
deeper.say: Select notes and press Cmd or Ctrl plus U to quantise them, which pulls each one onto the nearest grid line. Cmd or Ctrl plus Shift plus U opens the quantise settings, where you can pull them only part of the way for a looser feel.

say.mentor:
Your song, with snap switched on. Snap does what a piano roll's grid does: every hit you play lands on the nearest line. Play a few hats wherever you feel them. Then press play and watch them sit exactly in time.
Got one wrong? Tap undo and it's gone, the same as deleting a note in the grid.
say.straight: Snap is on: each hit lands on the nearest grid line. Play a few hats. Undo removes the last one.
say.eli5: Play some hats. The app moves each one onto the closest line, so they're perfectly in time. Made a mistake? Tap undo.

steps.q: What does midi store?
options: notes, when they play and how hard
steps.why: Midi is instructions, pitch, timing, length and velocity. An instrument turns them into sound.

whyWrong.1: Recorded sound is audio, not midi.
whyWrong.2: Reverb is an effect on the sound.
whyWrong.3: Midi is about notes, not files.

steps.q: In a piano roll, what runs up the side?
steps.why: Pitch goes up the side like a keyboard on its edge. Time runs left to right.

whyWrong.1: Time runs left to right.
whyWrong.2: Loudness is each note's velocity bar.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is set for the whole song.

steps.q: What does snapping or quantising a note do?
options: moves it to the nearest grid line
steps.why: It pulls the note onto the grid so it lands exactly in time.

whyWrong.1: Loudness is velocity.
whyWrong.3: The note stays, only its timing changes.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, a clap on two and four.

lessons.title: session view

song.why: switching parts on and off section by section is how a loop starts to become a song

lessons.learn: Your song as a grid of clips: which parts play together, switched on and off by section, and how Live's session view does it with clips and scenes.
youCan: say what a clip and a scene are in session view
switch parts of your song on and off by section
say why only one clip plays per track at a time

say.mentor:
One groove, then another, then both together. Same tempo, so they lock. Hear how each one is fine on its own, but the moment they play together it feels like a song.
That's the idea behind Live's session view: your music is a grid of short loops called clips, and you decide which ones play together, and when.
say.straight: Two grooves alone, then together. Session view is a grid of loops, clips, that you start and stop in any combination.
say.eli5: One beat, another beat, then both at once. Session view is a grid of little loops you can start and stop whenever you want.

say.mentor:
In session view, each track is a column. Each box in the column holds a clip, a loop of notes or sound. Press a clip's play button and it loops. Press a different clip on the same track and the first one stops: each track plays one clip at a time, the way one drummer can only play one pattern at a time.
Rows across the grid are called scenes. Press a scene's button and every clip in that row starts together. A scene for the intro, one for the drop, and you've got a song you can play live.
say.straight: Tracks are columns, clips sit in boxes. One clip plays per track at a time. A scene is a row: launch it and the whole row plays together.
say.eli5: Each sound gets a column of boxes. Each box is a loop. Press one and it plays. A row of boxes is a scene, and pressing it starts the whole row at once.

deeper.title: launching on the bar
deeper.say: Clips don't start the instant you click. Live waits for the next bar by default, set by global quantisation in the control bar, so everything lands in time. Set it to none and clips start immediately, which is easy to get wrong when playing live.

deeper.title: launch modes
deeper.say: Each clip has a launch mode. Trigger starts it on a click. Gate plays it only while you hold the button. Toggle turns it on and off with each click. Repeat keeps retriggering it while held. Scenes can also carry a tempo and time signature, so launching a scene can change the song's speed.

say.mentor:
Here's your song as a grid. Your parts run down the side, your sections run across. Each box is one part in one section, on or off. It's the same idea as session view turned on its side: in Live, tracks go across the top and scenes go down.
Make the first section drums only: switch your lead off there. Then let everything play in the next one. Press play and hear the song build.
say.straight: Parts down the side, sections across. Switch parts on and off. Try drums alone in the first section, then everything.
say.eli5: Each row is a sound, each column is a part of your song. Tap boxes to turn sounds on and off. Try just the drums first, then everything together.

steps.q: What does pressing a scene do?
options: starts every clip in that row
steps.why: A scene is a row of clips, and launching it starts them all together.

whyWrong.1: Stopping has its own buttons.
whyWrong.2: One clip is one box, not a scene.
whyWrong.3: Recording is a different button.

steps.q: You launch a second clip on the same track. What happens to the first?
steps.why: Each track plays one clip at a time, so the new one takes over.

whyWrong.1: Only one clip per track can play.
whyWrong.2: Its level doesn't change, it stops.
whyWrong.3: The clip stays in its box, ready to launch again.

steps.q: By default, when does a clip you click actually start?
options: at the start of the next bar
steps.why: Global quantisation waits for the next bar by default, so clips land in time.

whyWrong.1: Only if quantisation is set to none.
whyWrong.2: Clips start while the song plays.
whyWrong.3: Launching and recording are separate.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, what's inside a clip, notes or sound.

lessons.title: clips, midi vs audio

song.why: your parts are midi, so they follow any tempo you pick without a single note going out of time

lessons.learn: The two kinds of clip, midi and audio, what each holds, and why midi parts follow a tempo change for free.
youCan: say what a midi clip holds and what an audio clip holds
say why audio needs warping to change speed
change your song's tempo and hear your parts follow

say.mentor:
Kick, clap, hats. In a DAW each part lives in a clip, and a clip comes in two kinds. A midi clip holds notes, instructions for an instrument. An audio clip holds a recording, the sound itself, like a vocal or a drum loop someone recorded.
Your song so far is all midi. Every part is a list of notes that an instrument plays.
say.straight: Two kinds of clip. Midi holds notes for an instrument. Audio holds a recording. Your song so far is all midi.
say.eli5: A clip is a box for music. A midi box holds a list of notes. An audio box holds a real recording. Your song is made of note lists.

say.mentor:
Because a midi clip is just notes, you can change almost anything after you've played it. Swap the instrument, move a note, change the speed. The instrument simply plays the new instructions.
An audio clip is the sound itself, so changing its speed means stretching the recording. Live does this with warping, which squeezes or stretches audio to fit the tempo, a bit like stretching a photo. It works well, but push it far and you'll hear it.
say.straight: Midi is notes, so you can change instrument, notes or speed freely. Audio is sound, so changing speed means stretching it, called warping.
say.eli5: A note list is easy to change: new sound, new speed, no problem. A recording has to be stretched to change speed, and stretching too much sounds funny.

deeper.title: clips in live
deeper.say: Click a clip and the detail view at the bottom shows what's inside: a piano roll for midi, a waveform for audio. Audio clips have warp settings and a choice of warp mode. Midi clips have no warp mode, because notes don't need stretching. Drag a sample onto a track and Live warps it to the song's tempo automatically.

deeper.title: length and loop
deeper.say: A clip has a length and a loop brace, the section that repeats. A one bar clip can loop for 32 bars without being copied 32 times. Mixing up the clip's length and its loop length is a classic way to lose half your pattern.

say.mentor:
Here's your song. Turn the tempo right down, then right up. Every part follows, perfectly in time, and nothing sounds stretched. That's midi doing its thing: the notes just arrive sooner or later.
If your hats were a recording instead, the app would have to stretch the sound to keep up. Pick the tempo that feels best and keep it.
say.straight: Change the tempo. Your midi parts follow cleanly, nothing stretched. Pick a tempo and keep it.
say.eli5: Make your song faster and slower. All your notes keep up perfectly, because they're note lists, not recordings. Pick a speed you like.

steps.q: What does a midi clip hold?
options: notes for an instrument to play
steps.why: Midi is notes, when to play, which pitch, how hard. An instrument turns them into sound.

whyWrong.1: That's an audio clip.
whyWrong.2: Tempo is set for the whole song.
whyWrong.3: Reverb is an effect, not a clip.

steps.q: What's warping for?
options: stretching audio to fit the tempo
steps.why: Warping squeezes or stretches a recording so it plays at your song's speed.

whyWrong.1: Midi notes are added in the piano roll.
whyWrong.2: Midi clips have no warp mode.
whyWrong.3: Warping keeps the clip and reshapes its timing.

steps.q: You double the tempo. Which clip follows without being stretched?
steps.why: Midi is instructions, so the notes simply play faster. Audio has to be warped.

whyWrong.1: Audio is the sound itself, so it has to be stretched.
whyWrong.3: Only audio needs stretching.

steps.next: Back to your song: path 2 starts with your first bass line.

lessons.title: bass and poli

song.why: a thicker bass voice gives your low end weight and character without adding a single note

lessons.learn: What makes a bass sound thick: a sub underneath, the wave on top, and a little drift, and the two Live instruments built for bass and for chords.
youCan: say what a sub oscillator adds to a bass
make your bass thicker without changing its notes
say what Live's Bass and Poli are for

say.mentor:
A soft wave, a saw and a square. Your bass is built from these too. Under the hood it has two oscillators, one making a saw and one a square, plus a third one playing a sine wave an octave below your notes. That low one is called a sub oscillator, the sub for short.
The sub is the weight you feel in your chest. The saw and square on top are the character you hear.
say.straight: Your bass has a saw and a square on top and a sine sub an octave below. Sub is weight, the top is character.
say.eli5: Your bass is made of a few waves. A deep, smooth one underneath gives the rumble. Brighter ones on top give it its sound.

say.mentor:
Here's your song, with three knobs that thicken your bass without touching its notes. Sub turns up the sine an octave below: more weight, more rumble. Wave blends the top from saw to square, bright and buzzy to hollow and round.
Drift is the subtle one. It lets the pitch wander a few cents, slowly and at random, like an old analogue synth warming up. A little makes the bass feel alive instead of perfect. Keep the bass that fills your song best.
say.straight: Sub is weight, an octave down. Wave moves the top from saw to square. Drift lets the pitch wander a few cents, like analogue. Keep the thickest bass that still sounds clean.
say.eli5: Sub makes the rumble bigger. Wave changes the buzzy part. Drift makes it wobble a tiny bit, like an old synth. Keep the one you like.

say.mentor:
Live has two instruments named for exactly these jobs. Bass is made for single-note bass lines. Poli, short for polyphonic, plays many notes at once, so it suits chords, pads and keys.
Both are built to sound good fast: load a preset, play, turn a few knobs. When you want to go deeper, Wavetable and Operator give you every control.
say.straight: Live's Bass is for bass lines. Poli is polyphonic, for chords, pads and keys. Quick to get a sound; Wavetable and Operator go deeper.
say.eli5: Live has a synth called Bass for bass lines and one called Poli for chords. They're quick to use. Other synths let you go further.

deeper.title: mono and poly
deeper.say: A monophonic synth plays one note at a time. Play a new note and the old one stops, which suits a bass line and lets notes slide into each other. A polyphonic synth plays several at once, which chords need. Your bass here is monophonic, and its glide knob slides between notes when they overlap.

steps.q: What does a sub oscillator add to a bass?
options: weight, from a sine an octave below
steps.why: The sub plays a sine an octave under your notes, the deep weight you feel.

whyWrong.1: Brightness comes from the saw and square on top.
whyWrong.3: Sound knobs don't touch tempo.

steps.q: What does drift do to your bass?
options: lets the pitch wander a few cents, like analogue
steps.why: Drift is a slow, random pitch wobble of a few cents, the imperfection of an old analogue synth.

whyWrong.1: Loudness is level.
whyWrong.3: The low end stays, drift only moves pitch slightly.

steps.q: Why is Poli the better pick for chords?
options: it's polyphonic, so it plays many notes at once
it plays one note at a time
steps.why: Polyphonic means several notes at once, which a chord needs.

whyWrong.1: Loudness isn't the difference.
whyWrong.2: It plays across the whole range.
whyWrong.3: That's monophonic, like a bass synth.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, a second kind of synth for your lead.

lessons.title: operator

song.why: more than one oscillator on every note, set in a ratio to each other, is what gives a lead its edge

lessons.learn: How Live's Operator builds sound by letting oscillators shape each other, why the ratio between them matters, and stacking oscillators on your own lead.
youCan: say what fm synthesis is in one line
say what a carrier and a modulator are
stack and spread your lead's oscillators

say.mentor:
The note a at 220 hz, then the a above it at 440. Twice as fast, so the ratio between them is two to one. Your ear hears that as the same note, higher. Ratios like this are the secret of a synth called Operator.
Operator is an fm synth. Fm stands for frequency modulation: one oscillator wobbles another one's frequency so fast that you don't hear a wobble at all. You hear a brand new tone, brighter and richer than either wave alone.
say.straight: 220 hz then 440 hz, a two to one ratio, one octave. Operator is an fm synth: one oscillator bends another's frequency very fast, which makes a new, richer tone.
say.eli5: Low a, then high a, exactly twice as fast. Operator is a synth where one wave shakes another wave super fast, and that makes a whole new sound.

say.mentor:
In Operator each oscillator is called an operator, and there are four, named a, b, c and d. An operator you hear is a carrier. An operator that only bends another one is a modulator. The modulator doesn't change the note you hear. It changes the colour.
That's why Operator does bells, glassy keys and tight, punchy bass so well. Start from plain sine waves, let one bend another, and suddenly there's a whole stack of harmonics, the extra higher tones that give a sound its character.
say.straight: Four operators, a to d. Carriers are heard; modulators bend a carrier's frequency. That changes the colour, not the note. Great for bells, keys and bass.
say.eli5: Operator has four little wave makers. Some you hear. Others just shake the ones you hear, which changes the sound but not the note.

deeper.title: the ratio knob
deeper.say: Each operator has a coarse and fine frequency, set as a ratio to the note you play. A modulator at a whole-number ratio like 1 or 2 gives musical, harmonic tones. Odd ratios give metallic, bell-like ones. Change a modulator's ratio and the timbre changes dramatically while the pitch stays where it is. Turn up the modulator's level and the tone gets brighter and more metallic.

deeper.title: algorithms and feedback
deeper.say: An algorithm decides which operators modulate which, and which ones reach your speakers. Operator a also has a feedback control that bends it with itself: a little turns its sine towards a saw, and pushed high it turns to noise.

say.mentor:
Your lead isn't an fm synth, but it does share Operator's big idea: more than one oscillator on every note. It has three. Detune spreads them apart by a few cents, so they rub and widen into one bigger voice. Wave changes what each one is made of, saw at one end, square at the other.
Push detune up and listen to your lead go from a single line to a wide stack. Then try the wave with it. Keep the voice that cuts through your song best.
say.straight: Your lead has three oscillators per note. Detune spreads them a few cents for width. Wave goes from saw to square. Keep the voice that cuts through.
say.eli5: Your tune is made of three waves at once. Detune spreads them out so it sounds big. Wave changes their shape. Pick the one you like.

steps.q: What does fm stand for?
steps.why: Frequency modulation, one oscillator bending another's frequency.

whyWrong.1: It's about how sound is made, not melody.
whyWrong.3: Mono is about how many notes play at once.

steps.q: In Operator, what's a modulator?
options: an operator that bends another one
steps.why: A modulator shapes a carrier's tone. The carrier is the one you actually hear.

whyWrong.1: The one you hear is the carrier.
whyWrong.3: Echo is a separate effect.

steps.q: You change a modulator's ratio. What changes?
steps.why: The ratio changes which harmonics appear, so the colour changes while the pitch stays.

whyWrong.1: The carrier sets the note.
whyWrong.2: Tempo is the whole song's speed.
whyWrong.3: Ratio changes are some of the biggest tone changes in fm.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, make room for your kick and bass.

lessons.title: sidechain in live

song.why: a bass that dips on every kick and swells back gives your low end that pumping dance-floor movement

lessons.learn: How sidechain lets your kick turn your bass down, how deep the dip goes and how fast it recovers, and how to set it up in Live.
youCan: say what a sidechain is
set how deep and how long your bass ducks under the kick
set up sidechain compression in Live

say.mentor:
Kick on every beat. Picture your bass playing underneath. Every time the kick hits, they pile up in the low end. A sidechain fixes that: it lets one sound control what happens to another. Here, the kick reaches over and turns the bass down for a moment on every hit.
Do it hard and you get that pumping, breathing sound all over dance music. Do it gently and you just get a cleaner kick.
say.straight: Sidechain: one sound controls another. Here the kick turns the bass down on every hit. Hard, it pumps. Gentle, it's just cleaner.
say.eli5: Every time the boom hits, the bass gets quieter for a moment, then comes back. That's called a sidechain. It makes music go pump, pump, pump.

say.mentor:
Here's your song. Duck sets how much your bass dips under the kick, and it sets the release with it, the time the bass takes to come back up. A little duck is a quick, shallow dip. More duck is a deeper dip with a longer swell, so the bass pumps.
Decay shapes it from the other side: shorter bass notes leave gaps of their own around the kick. Find the pump that suits your song. Subtle is fine, so is obvious.
say.straight: Duck sets the depth of the dip and how long the bass takes to come back. More duck, deeper and longer pump. Decay shortens bass notes. Set the pump you want.
say.eli5: Turn up duck and the bass gets quieter on each boom and slowly comes back. More duck, more pumping. Decay makes bass notes shorter. Stop where it feels good.

say.mentor:
In Live, the duck is done by a compressor, a device that turns a sound down when it gets loud. Put Live's Compressor on your bass track and open its sidechain section. Switch it on and set audio from to your kick track.
Now the compressor ignores the bass and listens to the kick instead. Every kick hit pulls the bass down. Threshold and ratio set how deep the dip goes, and release sets how fast the bass comes back, the same two things your duck knob did at once.
say.straight: Live: Compressor on the bass, open sidechain, switch it on, audio from your kick. Threshold and ratio set depth, release sets recovery.
say.eli5: In Live you put a squeezing tool on the bass and tell it to listen to the kick. Then every kick pushes the bass down.

deeper.title: the sidechain eq
deeper.say: The sidechain section has its own eq, which filters what the compressor hears. Set it to a high pass around 100 hz and only the click of the kick triggers the duck, not its long low tail. Without it, a booming kick can keep the bass held down for most of the bar.

deeper.title: beyond kick and bass
deeper.say: The same trick works on pads and chords for a big pumping sound. You can also duck a reverb under a dry vocal so the words stay clear and the reverb blooms in the gaps. If the bass suddenly gets loud, check the kick track isn't muted, because no kick means no duck.

steps.q: What is a sidechain?
options: one sound controlling an effect on another
steps.why: The kick controls how much the bass is turned down. One sound steering another.

whyWrong.1: Reverb is space, not control.
whyWrong.2: It works on any sound, not just bass.
whyWrong.3: It's a routing trick, not a pattern.

steps.q: Your bass pumps too slowly and stays down too long. What do you shorten?
steps.why: Release is how fast the bass comes back up after each kick.

whyWrong.1: Threshold is about when it starts ducking, not how long.
whyWrong.3: The sub is part of the bass sound, not the duck.

steps.q: In Live's Compressor, why high-pass the sidechain eq around 100 hz?
options: so only the kick's click triggers the duck
steps.why: Filtering out the kick's low tail stops it holding the bass down for the whole bar.

whyWrong.1: It only changes what the compressor hears, not the bass.
whyWrong.3: Eq doesn't add reverb.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, the compressor itself, on your drums.

lessons.title: the compressor

song.why: squeezing the loudest part of your kick and bringing the level back up makes it hit denser and harder

lessons.learn: What a compressor does, threshold and ratio in plain words, and squeezing your kick by ear.
youCan: say what threshold and ratio do
say why a compressed sound needs makeup gain
squeeze your kick and set its level by ear

say.mentor:
A kick on every beat. Each hit has a loud front, the click, and a quieter body after it. A compressor is a device that turns down the loud parts of a sound automatically, so the gap between loud and quiet gets smaller. Think of it as a volume knob with reflexes.
Squeeze the loud front a little, bring the whole thing back up, and the kick sounds denser and hits harder. That's why nearly every dance track compresses its drums.
say.straight: A compressor turns down the loud parts automatically, shrinking the gap between loud and quiet. Squeeze, then turn back up, and drums hit harder.
say.eli5: A compressor is like a helper who turns the volume down whenever a sound gets too loud. It makes the loud and quiet bits closer together.

say.mentor:
Two controls decide most of it. Threshold is the line: anything louder than it gets turned down, anything quieter is left alone. Ratio is how hard it's turned down. At a ratio of 4 to 1, a sound that goes 4 dB over the line comes out only 1 dB over. A dB, or decibel, is the unit loudness is measured in.
Squeezing makes the sound quieter overall, so a compressor has a makeup control to add that level back. The result is the same peak, with the quieter body brought up around it. That's the punch.
say.straight: Threshold is where it starts. Ratio is how hard: at 4 to 1, 4 dB over becomes 1 dB over. Makeup adds the lost level back, so the sound ends up denser.
say.eli5: Threshold is how loud something has to be before it gets squeezed. Ratio is how much squeezing. Then you turn it back up so it's not too quiet.

deeper.title: live's compressor
deeper.say: Drop Compressor on a track and you'll find threshold, ratio, attack, release and makeup, with a gain reduction meter showing how many dB it's turning down. Attack is how fast it grabs. A slow attack, around 30 ms, lets the click of a kick slip through before it clamps the body, which adds punch instead of removing it. Release is how fast it lets go. A common drum starting point is a 4 to 1 ratio, 30 ms attack and a fast release.

deeper.title: too much
deeper.say: A threshold set very low with a high ratio squashes everything flat and lifeless. And forgetting makeup is the classic mistake: the sound comes out quieter, not better. In Live's Compressor the sidechain section lets a different track drive it, which is the kick-ducks-bass trick from the last lesson.

say.mentor:
Your kick doesn't have a compressor knob, but drive does a rougher version of the same job. It flattens the loudest moments of each hit, a bit like a compressor with a very fast grab and a very high ratio, so the body comes up next to the click and the kick gets denser and grittier.
Turn drive up until the kick feels thicker. Then use level the way you'd use makeup: set how loud the squeezed kick sits against your clap and hats. Keep it where it punches.
say.straight: Drive flattens the kick's loudest moments, like a very fast, hard compressor, so it sounds denser. Level works like makeup: set how loud it sits.
say.eli5: Drive squashes the loudest bit of your boom so it sounds fatter and crunchier. Then level sets how loud it is. Keep the boom that punches.

steps.q: What does a compressor do?
options: turns down the loud parts automatically
steps.why: It's an automatic volume knob that pulls the loud moments down.

whyWrong.1: Echo is a delay effect.
whyWrong.3: Tempo isn't touched.

steps.q: What does the threshold set?
options: how loud a sound must be before it's turned down
steps.why: Threshold is the line. Only what goes over it gets squeezed.

whyWrong.1: That's the ratio.
whyWrong.3: A compressor doesn't touch tempo.

steps.q: With a 4 to 1 ratio, a hit goes 8 dB over the threshold. How far over does it come out?
steps.why: Divide by the ratio. 8 dB over at 4 to 1 comes out 2 dB over.

whyWrong.1: That would be no compression at all.
whyWrong.2: That's halving it, a 2 to 1 ratio.
whyWrong.3: Compressors turn down, they don't multiply.

steps.q: Why does a compressor have a makeup control?
options: squeezing makes it quieter, so you add level back
steps.why: Turning the peaks down lowers the overall level. Makeup brings it back up so it sounds denser, not quieter.

whyWrong.1: Threshold has its own control.
whyWrong.3: Attack is its own control.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, shape your synth properly with resonance and envelopes.

lessons.title: filters, carving the sound

song.why: a filter decides which part of your lead's sound gets through, from dark and round to thin and bright

lessons.learn: What a filter does, the main filter types, low-pass, high-pass and band-pass, and resonance, all on your own lead.
youCan: say what low-pass, high-pass and band-pass filters keep
say what resonance does at the cutoff
carve your lead with a low-pass and a high-pass

say.mentor:
A soft wave, then a saw, then a square. The saw is the brightest because it's packed with high frequencies, the fizzy top part of the sound. A filter is a device that takes some of those frequencies away.
Starting bright and taking things away is called subtractive synthesis, and it's how most classic synth sounds are made. Almost every big sweep you've heard in a dance track is a filter moving.
say.straight: Bright waves are full of high frequencies. A filter removes some. Start bright, take away: subtractive synthesis.
say.eli5: Some sounds are very bright and fizzy. A filter is like a sieve that lets some of the sound through and holds the rest back.

say.mentor:
A low-pass filter lets the lows pass and cuts the highs above a point called the cutoff. Lower the cutoff and the sound goes darker and rounder. This is the one you'll use most.
A high-pass does the opposite: it keeps the highs and cuts the lows, so a sound gets thinner and lighter. A band-pass keeps only a slice in the middle, which sounds like a telephone or a small radio.
Resonance is a boost right at the cutoff. Turn it up and the filter starts to ring and whistle there. Sweep the cutoff with resonance up and you get the classic synth wah.
say.straight: Low-pass keeps lows, cuts highs above the cutoff. High-pass keeps highs, cuts lows. Band-pass keeps a middle slice. Resonance is a ringing peak at the cutoff.
say.eli5: Low-pass makes a sound darker. High-pass makes it thinner. Band-pass makes it sound like an old phone. Resonance makes it whistle.

deeper.title: filters in live
deeper.say: Live's synths each have a filter section where you pick the type, low-pass, high-pass, band-pass or notch, which cuts a narrow slice out. Auto Filter puts the same filters on any track as an effect. A filter's slope, often 12 or 24 dB per octave, sets how steeply it cuts: 24 is the more aggressive.

deeper.title: careful with resonance
deeper.say: High resonance with a low cutoff can make big, sudden peaks in the bass. Keep an eye on your meters. Pushed far enough, a filter's resonance can even ring on its own as a pure tone.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with all three filter types on your lead. Cutoff is the low-pass: turn it down and your lead goes dark. Cut is a high-pass on the lead's channel: turn it up and the lows fall away so it thins out. Bring cutoff down and cut up together and you've made a band-pass, just a slice in the middle.
Then add resonance and sweep the cutoff to hear it sing. Keep the shape that sits best in your song.
say.straight: Cutoff is low-pass, cut is high-pass. Both together make a band-pass. Res adds a peak at the cutoff. Carve your lead and keep it.
say.eli5: Cutoff makes your tune darker. Cut makes it thinner. Both together make it sound like a phone. Res makes it whistle. Pick the sound you like.

steps.q: What does a low-pass filter do?
options: keeps the lows, cuts the highs
keeps the highs, cuts the lows
steps.why: Low-pass lets the lows pass and cuts above the cutoff, so the sound goes darker.

whyWrong.1: That's a high-pass.
whyWrong.3: A filter removes sound, it doesn't add level.

steps.q: What does resonance do?
options: boosts a ringing peak at the cutoff
steps.why: Resonance boosts the frequencies right at the cutoff, so it rings and whistles.

whyWrong.1: Cutoff is its own control.
whyWrong.3: Note length is the envelope's job.

steps.q: You want your lead to sound like it's coming through a small radio. Which filter?
steps.why: Keeping only a middle slice, cutting both lows and highs, gives that small radio sound.

whyWrong.1: Low-pass alone keeps all the lows, so it's dark and full.
whyWrong.2: High-pass alone keeps all the highs, so it's thin and fizzy.
whyWrong.3: No filter leaves the full range.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, how loud each note is from start to finish.

lessons.title: amp envelope

song.why: how each note starts and stops turns the same melody into a pluck or a soft pad

lessons.learn: The amp envelope, attack, decay, sustain and release, and turning your lead into a pluck or a pad with attack and release.
youCan: say what each part of an adsr envelope does
make your lead a pluck or a pad
say the difference between decay and release

say.mentor:
One soft synth note, held for most of the bar. Listen to how it starts and how it ends. Does it pop in or fade in? Does it stop dead or ring on?
That journey from start to finish is set by an envelope, a shape that tells part of the synth what to do over the life of each note. The amp envelope controls loudness.
say.straight: A held note. How it starts and ends is set by an envelope. The amp envelope shapes loudness over time.
say.eli5: Listen to how the note starts and stops. An envelope decides that: does it pop in, or slowly fade in? Does it stop fast, or ring on?

say.mentor:
The classic envelope has four stages, written adsr. Attack is how long the note takes to rise from silence to full volume when it starts. Decay is how long it then takes to fall to the sustain level. Sustain is how loud it stays while the note is held. Release is how long it takes to fade to silence after the note ends.
A short attack, little sustain and a short release make a pluck. A long attack, high sustain and a long release make a pad, a soft sound that swells in and fades away.
say.straight: Attack is the rise. Decay falls to sustain. Sustain is the level while held. Release is the fade after. Short everything is a pluck; long attack and release is a pad.
say.eli5: Attack is how fast the note gets loud. Release is how long it takes to go quiet after. Fast is a pluck. Slow is a soft, dreamy pad.

deeper.title: envelopes in live
deeper.say: Every Live synth has an amp envelope with these stages, and the same four letters turn up on samplers and drum devices too. A 0 ms attack can click on some waves, so a few milliseconds is usually safer. Anything under about 10 ms still reads as a sharp start.

deeper.title: decay vs release
deeper.say: Decay happens while the note is still held. Release happens after it ends. If sustain is at zero the note has already died during decay, so release has nothing left to do.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with your lead's amp envelope. Attack first: at zero each note snaps in, turn it up and the notes swell in softly. Release next: short, and each note stops tight; long, and the notes ring into each other.
Try both short for a pluck, then both long for a pad. Same melody, two completely different songs. Keep the one you like.
say.straight: Attack is how fast each note comes in. Release is how long it rings after. Short and short is a pluck, long and long a pad. Keep one.
say.eli5: Attack makes notes start fast or slow. Release makes them stop fast or ring on. Try both short, then both long. Pick your favourite.

steps.q: Which part of the envelope is how fast a note fades in?
steps.why: Attack is the rise from silence to full volume.

whyWrong.1: Decay is the fall after the peak.
whyWrong.2: Sustain is the level while held.
whyWrong.3: Release is the fade after the note ends.

steps.q: For a soft pad that swells in, what attack do you want?
steps.why: A long attack makes each note swell in slowly.

whyWrong.1: Zero snaps in, like a pluck.
whyWrong.2: Attack is most of what makes a swell.
whyWrong.3: Decay is a separate stage.

steps.q: What's the difference between decay and release?
options: decay happens while held, release after the note ends
release is while held, decay after
decay is pitch, release is volume
steps.why: Decay falls to sustain while you hold the note. Release fades it once the note ends.

whyWrong.1: They're two separate stages.
whyWrong.3: Both are loudness on the amp envelope.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, an envelope on the filter instead of the volume.

lessons.title: filter envelope

song.why: brightness that opens on every note and closes again gives your lead movement and bite

lessons.learn: Pointing an envelope at the filter instead of the volume, the envelope amount, and setting the resting cutoff first.
youCan: say what a filter envelope does on each note
say what envelope amount controls
make your lead brighten and close on every note

say.mentor:
One soft held note. It stays the same colour the whole way through. Now imagine it starting bright and then darkening as it holds, like a plucked string. That movement is what makes synth sounds feel alive.
You already know an envelope can shape volume. Point the same kind of shape at the filter's cutoff and the brightness moves on every note instead. That's a filter envelope.
say.straight: This note's colour doesn't move. A filter envelope moves the cutoff on every note, so it opens bright and closes again.
say.eli5: This note sounds the same all the way through. A filter envelope makes each note start bright and then get darker, like plucking a guitar string.

say.mentor:
Two controls work together. The cutoff is where the filter rests, the base. The envelope amount is how far the envelope pushes the cutoff up on each note. Zero amount and the envelope does nothing at all.
Set the base first, quite dark, then add amount. Now every note jumps bright and closes back down to the base. A fast filter envelope with lots of amount is the classic plucky lead. Add resonance and the sweep whistles as it closes.
say.straight: Cutoff is the resting point. Envelope amount is how far each note pushes it up. Set the base dark first, then add amount. Resonance makes the sweep whistle.
say.eli5: First make your sound dark. Then turn up env, and each note will flash bright and go dark again. Res makes that flash whistle.

deeper.title: in live's synths
deeper.say: Most synths give the filter its own adsr envelope with an amount control. A short decay with little sustain gives a pluck. A long decay with more sustain gives a slower, brassy swell. Many let the amount go negative, so the cutoff dips on each note instead of rising. Sending velocity to the envelope amount means hard notes open brighter than soft ones.

deeper.title: a common mistake
deeper.say: Lots of envelope amount with the cutoff already wide open does almost nothing, because the filter has nowhere higher to go. Bring the base cutoff down and you'll hear the envelope straight away.

say.mentor:
Here's your song. Your lead's filter envelope jumps open at the start of each note and closes over about a third of a second. Turn cutoff down until your lead is dark. Then bring up env and listen to every note bite and close.
Add a touch of res and the sweep starts to sing. Too much and it squeals. Keep the bite that suits your melody.
say.straight: Cutoff down for a dark base. Env up and each note bites open and closes. Res adds a whistle. Keep what suits your melody.
say.eli5: Turn cutoff down so it's dark. Turn env up so each note flashes bright. Add a little res for a whistle. Keep the one you like.

steps.q: What does a filter envelope move on each note?
steps.why: It moves the cutoff, so the brightness opens and closes on each note.

whyWrong.1: Volume is the amp envelope.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is the whole song.

steps.q: The envelope amount is at zero. What does the filter envelope do?
options: opens the filter all the way
steps.why: Amount is how far the envelope moves the cutoff. Zero means it doesn't move.

whyWrong.1: Zero amount means no movement.
whyWrong.3: Length is the amp envelope too.

steps.q: Your filter envelope does nothing you can hear, even with lots of amount. What's the likely fix?
steps.why: With the cutoff wide open there's nowhere higher to go. A darker base gives the envelope room.

whyWrong.1: Opening it further leaves even less room.
whyWrong.2: Louder doesn't make the sweep audible.
whyWrong.3: Tempo doesn't affect the filter.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, both envelopes on one note.

lessons.title: two envelopes, one voice

song.why: when the volume and the brightness of each note move on different schedules, your lead gets its character

lessons.learn: How the amp envelope and the filter envelope run side by side on one note, and what happens when they don't line up.
youCan: say what each of the two envelopes controls
hear a note swell in while it darkens
say why mismatched envelopes change a sound's character

say.mentor:
The same note, quiet then loud. Loudness is one thing a note does over time. Brightness is another. A synth usually gives each its own envelope: the amp envelope for volume, the filter envelope for the cutoff.
They run at the same time, side by side, and they don't have to agree. That's where a lot of a sound's character comes from.
say.straight: Two envelopes per note: amp for volume, filter for brightness. They run together but don't have to match.
say.eli5: Each note has two shapes going on: how loud it is and how bright it is. They can do different things at the same time.

steps.title: in step or out of step

say.mentor:
Line them up and a note sounds natural and predictable. Pull them apart and you get something more interesting. A loud note that holds its volume while its brightness slowly closes sounds like it's fading dark. A long volume fade with a quick filter close gives a tail that hangs on, dull and quiet.
One rule to remember: once the amp envelope reaches silence, you can't hear anything the filter is still doing. The amp decides whether you hear the note at all. The filter only colours what's there.
say.straight: Matched envelopes sound natural. Mismatched ones give character, like a loud note that goes dark. Once the amp is silent, filter movement can't be heard.
say.eli5: If the loud shape and the bright shape match, the note sounds normal. If they don't, it sounds more unusual. When the note goes silent, the bright shape doesn't matter any more.

deeper.title: setting them apart in live
deeper.say: Live's synths let you give the filter an envelope of its own, separate from the amp's, each with its own attack, decay, sustain and release. Try amp sustain at full with filter sustain at zero: the note holds its volume while the cutoff closes. Or start the filter's attack a few milliseconds later than the amp's for a subtle bloom on every note.

deeper.title: an 808-style stab
deeper.say: For a stab that goes dull fast but rings on long, give the amp no attack, a long decay and no sustain, and give the filter no attack, a short decay and no sustain.

say.mentor:
Here's your song. On your lead the filter envelope has a fixed shape: it jumps open at the start of each note and closes over about a third of a second. The amp envelope is yours to set. So they're already out of step, and you get to choose how far.
Turn env up so you can hear the filter move. Now raise attack: the volume swells in slowly while the brightness has already started closing, so each note fades in getting darker. Then try release for how long the dark tail rings. Keep the shape you like.
say.straight: Your lead's filter envelope opens fast and closes in about a third of a second. Env sets how much. Attack and release shape the volume. Slow attack plus env: notes swell in as they darken.
say.eli5: Turn env up so each note flashes bright. Turn attack up so notes fade in slowly. Now they get louder while getting darker. Release makes the end ring on.

steps.q: Which envelope decides whether you hear the note at all?
steps.why: The amp envelope sets the volume. When it reaches silence, the note is gone.

whyWrong.1: The filter only colours a note you can already hear.
whyWrong.3: The amp envelope does.

steps.q: Amp sustain is full and filter sustain is zero. You hold a note. What do you hear?
options: it stays loud but gets darker
it fades out and stays bright
steps.why: Volume holds at full sustain while the filter envelope falls back to the base cutoff.

whyWrong.1: That's the other way round.
whyWrong.2: The cutoff is moving, so the colour changes.
whyWrong.3: Neither envelope changes pitch here.

steps.q: Your note fades out over two seconds, but the filter has finished closing after a tenth of a second. How does the tail sound?
steps.why: The filter closes fast, so the long volume fade carries a dark, dull tail.

whyWrong.1: The filter has already closed, so it can't be bright.
whyWrong.2: The amp is still fading, so you hear it.
whyWrong.3: Envelopes don't change tuning.

steps.next: Back to your song: next, timbre, the colour of your lead.

lessons.title: saturator and distortion

song.why: a little drive gives your kick harmonics, so it feels fuller and still comes through on small speakers

lessons.learn: What saturation and distortion add to a sound, and drive on your own kick, judged at the same loudness.
youCan: say what drive adds to a sound
hear the line between warmth and distortion
match loudness before deciding if drive helped

say.mentor:
Here's a kick on its own. It's clean: mostly one low, round tone. That's lovely on big speakers and nearly invisible on a phone, because tiny speakers can't play very low notes.
Saturation is the fix producers reach for first. It bends the shape of the wave a little, and that bending adds harmonics: new, higher notes stacked on top of the original that weren't there before. Those harmonics are what your ear catches on a small speaker.
say.straight: A clean kick. Saturation bends the wave, which adds harmonics, higher notes on top of the original. Harmonics help a kick come through on small speakers.
say.eli5: This is a plain kick. If you squash its wiggle a little, it grows extra little sounds on top. Those extra sounds help you hear the kick even on a phone.

say.mentor:
Drive is how hard you push the sound into that bending. A little drive sounds warm and thick, like a tube amp just starting to work. Push it further and the peaks of the wave get sliced off, and you hear real distortion: gritty, buzzy, aggressive.
There's a trap. More drive also makes the sound louder, and louder always seems better for a second. So turn the level down until it's as loud as before, then decide if the drive helped.
say.straight: Drive sets how hard the sound is pushed. Low drive is warmth, high drive is distortion. Drive also adds loudness, so match the level before you judge it.
say.eli5: A bit of drive makes the sound warm and fat. Lots of drive makes it crunchy. Drive also makes it louder, so turn it back down before you decide if you like it.

deeper.title: saturator in live
deeper.say: Live's Saturator has a Drive knob that pushes the signal into a curve, and an Output knob to bring the level back down. The curve type changes the flavour: Analog Clip and Soft Sine are gentle, Sinoid Fold folds the wave back on itself for a more synth-like grit, Digital Clip is hard. A Soft Clip switch tames the loudest peaks, and Dry/Wet lets you blend the saturated sound with the clean one, which often keeps more punch.

deeper.title: the other distortions
deeper.say: Live also has Overdrive, Pedal, Dynamic Tube and Roar. They push further than gentle saturation, and because they add harmonics high up, an EQ after them is useful to tame the top end.

say.mentor:
Your song is playing, with drive on your kick. Turn drive up slowly. First the kick thickens and gets a little edge, then it starts to crunch. Find the point where it feels bigger but still sounds like your kick.
Now the honest test: pull level down until the kick is about as loud as it was, and listen again. If it still sounds better, the drive is doing real work. Keep it.
say.straight: Raise drive on your kick until it thickens, before it crunches. Then lower level to match the old loudness and check it still sounds better.
say.eli5: Turn drive up and listen to your kick get fatter. Stop before it sounds broken. Then turn level down a bit so it's not just louder. Still better? Keep it.

steps.q: What does saturation add to a sound?
options: harmonics, new higher notes on top
steps.why: Bending the wave adds harmonics that weren't in the original.

whyWrong.1: Reverb is space, a different effect.
whyWrong.2: It's the same kick, with more harmonics.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is the speed of the song.

steps.q: You turn drive up and the kick sounds better. What do you check?
steps.why: Drive adds loudness, and louder always seems better. Match the level, then judge.

whyWrong.1: Tempo doesn't change with drive.
whyWrong.2: The hats don't affect the kick's drive.
whyWrong.3: That's exactly the trap to avoid.

steps.q: Why can saturation help a kick on a phone speaker?
options: phones can play the harmonics but not the deepest lows
steps.why: Tiny speakers miss the deepest notes, but the added harmonics sit higher where they can play them.

whyWrong.1: The harmonics are higher, not lower.
whyWrong.2: Phones play everything they can reach, clean or not.
whyWrong.3: The low end is still there; harmonics are added on top.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try roar for a bigger drive on your bass.

lessons.title: roar

song.why: a heavier drive on your bass gives it growl and edge that cuts through the rest of the song

lessons.learn: Roar, Live 12's big distortion with stages, bands and feedback, and a bigger drive on your own bass.
youCan: drive your bass hard and keep it musical
use tone to choose where the grit sits
say what bands and feedback do in Roar

say.mentor:
Listen to the same note three ways: a soft, round wave, then a buzzy saw, then a square. The buzzy ones are full of harmonics, extra higher notes riding on top. Heavy distortion does something similar to any sound you feed it: it piles on harmonics until a round sound starts to growl.
Roar is Live 12's distortion for when a little warmth isn't enough. You're about to put that kind of growl on your bass.
say.straight: Soft wave, saw, square. The buzzier ones carry more harmonics. Heavy distortion adds harmonics to any sound, turning round into growl. Roar is Live 12's big distortion.
say.eli5: A smooth sound, then two buzzy ones. Big distortion makes a smooth sound buzzy and growly. You're going to do that to your bass.

say.mentor:
Roar has up to three stages of distortion. You can run them one after another, side by side, or split your sound into frequency bands and treat each band differently. That last one is the clever part: you can roughen the mids of a bass, where the growl lives, and leave the deep lows cleaner so they still hit.
It also has a feedback path, which sends some of the output back into the input. A little adds richness. A lot makes it howl and ring on its own, which can be great or a mess.
say.straight: Roar has up to three distortion stages, run in a row, side by side, or split by frequency band. Bands let you grit up the mids and keep the lows cleaner. Feedback loops the output back in.
say.eli5: Roar can split a sound into low, middle and high parts and make each one crunchy in its own way. It can also feed the sound back into itself to make it howl.

deeper.title: roar in live
deeper.say: Roar arrived in Live 12. Each stage has its own drive, tone and mix, and the stages can be routed in series, in parallel, or as a multiband split with adjustable crossover points. It has built-in modulators, an lfo and an envelope follower, so the drive can move over time or react to how loud the input is. Watch the mix control: a fully wet Roar on a bass can swallow the low end.

deeper.title: feedback, carefully
deeper.say: Push feedback high and Roar can start to ring by itself. That's a sound design trick, but on a bass line you usually want it low, or the notes blur together.

say.mentor:
