Your song is playing, and these knobs sit on your bass. Push drive well past where you'd stop on a kick. Hear the bass start to growl and bark.
Now turn tone. One way the grit goes dark and heavy, the other way it gets bright and fizzy. On our instrument the drive works on the whole bass, so tone is how you steer where the growl sits. Then bring level back so the bass isn't just louder than before. Keep it if your bass sounds meaner in a good way.
say.straight: Drive your bass hard. Use tone to make the growl darker or brighter. Pull level back to match, then keep it if it's better.
say.eli5: Turn drive way up and your bass growls. Turn tone to make the growl darker or brighter. Turn level down a bit. Like it? Keep it.

steps.q: What does splitting a sound into bands let Roar do?
options: distort the mids hard and keep the lows cleaner
steps.why: Each band gets its own treatment, so the growl and the deep low end can be handled separately.

whyWrong.1: Distortion doesn't change the key.
whyWrong.2: It's the same bass, treated in parts.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is untouched.

steps.q: What does a feedback path do?
options: sends some of the output back into the input
steps.why: The sound loops back in, which adds richness and, pushed hard, can make it ring by itself.

whyWrong.1: Feedback tends to add energy, not take it away.
whyWrong.3: It adds harmonics rather than removing them.

steps.q: Your bass drive sounds great, but it's also much louder. What first?
options: turn level down to match, then listen again
steps.why: Louder always sounds better at first. Match it, then judge the drive itself.

whyWrong.1: That only adds to the loudness problem.
whyWrong.2: Reverb doesn't help you judge drive.
whyWrong.3: The kick isn't the issue here.

steps.next: Back to your song path: drums from recordings is next.

lessons.title: sampler and simpler

song.why: recorded hits on your pads give your beat the sound of real drums instead of generated ones

lessons.learn: What a sampler does, the difference between Simpler and Sampler in Live, and recorded hits on your own pattern.
youCan: say what a sampler does
say when you'd use Simpler and when Sampler
put recorded hits on your own beat

say.mentor:
Kick, clap, hats. Every one of these is made by the engine, built from waves and noise as it plays. There's another way to get a sound: record it once, then play the recording back whenever you hit a pad or a key.
That's a sampler. A sample is just a recording, and a sampler is an instrument that plays recordings. Any sound can become an instrument this way: a drum, a voice, a door slam.
say.straight: These drums are generated. A sampler plays a recording instead, every time you hit a pad or key. Any recording can become an instrument.
say.eli5: These drums are made by the computer. A sampler plays a recording instead. Record any sound and you can play it like a drum.

say.mentor:
A sampler can play its recording at any pitch. Play a higher key and it plays the sound higher, a lower key and it plays lower. One recorded bell becomes a whole melody.
For drums you usually want the opposite: the hit played once, whole, at its own pitch, every time you tap the pad. That's called one-shot: tap it and the whole sound plays out, however long you hold.
say.straight: A sampler plays its recording higher or lower by key. For drums you use one-shot: the full hit plays once per tap.
say.eli5: A sampler can play a sound high or low, like a keyboard. For drums it just plays the whole hit once each time you tap.

deeper.title: simpler and sampler in live
deeper.say: Simpler plays one sample and has three modes. Classic plays the sample across the keys with a loop, One-Shot fires the whole sound once (good for drum hits and vocal chops), and Slice chops a loop into pieces you can play. Sampler is the bigger instrument: many samples mapped across key and velocity ranges, which is how sampled pianos and orchestras are built.

deeper.title: the quick way in
deeper.say: Drag any audio file onto a MIDI track and Live creates a Simpler with that sample loaded. If you outgrow it, right-click the Simpler's header to turn it into a Sampler with the same sample.

say.mentor:
Here's your own beat. Switch from the synth kit to the recorded kit: same pattern, same timing, but now every hit is a recording of a real kick, clap, hat and snare, played back by a sampler on each pad.
Listen to the texture. The recordings carry a bit of room and grit. Pick the kit your song wants and keep it.
say.straight: Your beat on the synth kit, then the recorded kit. Same pattern, recordings on each pad. Pick one.
say.eli5: Same beat, two kits. The recorded one uses real drum sounds. Tap between them and keep the one you like.

steps.q: What does a sampler do?
options: plays a recording when you hit a pad or key
makes sound from a sine wave
steps.why: It plays back a recorded sound, at any pitch, on every hit.

whyWrong.1: That's a synth.
whyWrong.2: Reverb is an effect, not an instrument.
whyWrong.3: It can play back any recording.

steps.q: You want a drum hit to play in full every time, however short your tap. Which mode?
steps.why: One-shot plays the whole sound from start to end on each tap.

whyWrong.1: Classic follows how long you hold the note.
whyWrong.2: Slice is for chopping a loop into pieces.
whyWrong.3: A loop repeats; you want the hit once.

steps.q: In Live, which one is built for many samples across the keyboard?
steps.why: Sampler maps many samples across key and velocity ranges. Simpler plays one.

whyWrong.1: Simpler holds a single sample.
whyWrong.2: A Drum Rack holds pads, each with its own instrument.
whyWrong.3: Saturator is a distortion effect.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or go deeper with sampler, deep.

lessons.title: sampler, deep

song.why: setting the pitch and length of a hit is how a sample is made to fit your song

lessons.learn: How Live's Sampler maps many recordings across keys and velocities, and the pitch and length of a hit on your own kick.
youCan: say what key zones and velocity layers are
say why round-robin stops the machine-gun sound
set the pitch and length of a hit by ear

say.mentor:
One note low, then high. A sampler can do this with a recording: play it on a higher key and it plays faster and higher. That's fine for a few notes, but stretch one recording too far and it stops sounding real. A piano played an octave up from one sample sounds thin and toy-like.
So real sampled instruments use lots of recordings, each one covering a small range of keys.
say.straight: Low, then high. A sampler can play one recording at any pitch, but stretched too far it sounds fake. Real sampled instruments use many recordings, each covering a few keys.
say.eli5: Low note, high note. A sampler can play one sound high or low, but too far and it sounds silly. So good sampled pianos record lots of notes.

say.mentor:
A key zone is the range of keys one recording covers. A sampled piano might use a different recording every few keys, so every note stays close to its real sound.
A velocity layer is a recording chosen by how hard you play. Velocity means how hard you hit a key or pad. A soft hit plays a soft recording and a hard hit plays a hard one, and a real drum or piano really does change tone when you hit it harder, not just volume.
Round-robin is the third trick. Hit the same snare twice in a row and you'd hear the exact same recording twice, which sounds like a machine gun. Round-robin cycles through several recordings of the same hit, so repeats sound alive.
say.straight: Key zone: the keys one recording covers. Velocity layer: a recording picked by how hard you play. Round-robin: several recordings of the same hit, cycled, so repeats don't sound robotic.
say.eli5: A sampler can keep lots of recordings. Some for low keys, some for high keys, some for soft hits, some for hard hits. It can even swap between a few copies so the same drum never sounds exactly the same twice.

deeper.title: sampler in live
deeper.say: Sampler's zone editor maps samples by key range, velocity range and a selector range, which is how round-robin and random choice are set up. Each sample can have its own envelope, filter and lfo routing, and Sampler responds to MPE, per-note pitch, pressure and slide. Overlapping key zones play together, which is handy for layering.

deeper.title: start and loop
deeper.say: In Sampler and Simpler you can move a sample's start point, to skip a slow fade-in or cut into the punchiest part of a hit, and set a loop so a short recording sustains for as long as you hold the key. Velocity can even move the start point, so harder hits start later in the transient for more snap.

say.mentor:
Every sample on every pad gets two basic choices: what pitch it plays at, and how long it lasts. Here they are on your kick, with your song playing.
Turn tune and the kick sits lower and heavier or higher and tighter. Turn decay and it gets short and clipped or long and booming. Find the kick that sits with your bass, and keep it.
These knobs work on the synth kit. If your song is on the recorded kit, switch back to synth in drums from recordings to hear them.
say.straight: Tune sets your kick's pitch, decay sets how long it lasts. Set both so it sits with your bass, then keep it. These knobs act on the synth kit, not the recorded one.
say.eli5: Tune makes your kick higher or lower. Decay makes it shorter or longer. Turn them until your kick sounds right with your bass.

steps.q: What is a velocity layer?
options: a recording chosen by how hard you play
a recording for a range of keys
steps.why: Soft hits play one recording, hard hits another, so the tone changes like a real instrument.

whyWrong.1: That's a key zone.
whyWrong.2: Reverb has nothing to do with it.
whyWrong.3: Velocity is how hard, not how fast the song is.

steps.q: Why use round-robin on a snare?
options: so repeated hits don't sound identical
steps.why: Cycling through several recordings avoids the machine-gun sound of one sample repeated.

whyWrong.1: It's about variety, not level.
whyWrong.2: Key isn't the problem with repeated hits.
whyWrong.3: Reverse is a different setting.

steps.q: Why do sampled pianos use many recordings instead of one?
options: one recording stretched far from its pitch sounds fake
Live can only play one octave
so the piano is in stereo
steps.why: Each recording covers a few keys, so every note stays close to how it really sounds.

whyWrong.1: Live can play any range.
whyWrong.2: More recordings take more space, not less.
whyWrong.3: Stereo is a separate thing.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try drum sampler for a kit built from recordings.

lessons.title: drum sampler

song.why: a recorded kit on your pads gives your beat real hits with real texture

lessons.learn: What Live 12's Drum Sampler is for, why recorded kits sound alive, and your own beat on recorded hits.
youCan: say what Drum Sampler is for
say what velocity layers and round-robin do for drums
choose between a synth and a recorded kit by ear

say.mentor:
Kick on every beat, clap on two and four. Notice every kick is exactly the same. That's perfect for a lot of electronic music, but a real drummer never hits twice the same way. Each hit is a little softer or harder, and the drum sounds a little different each time.
A recorded kit brings some of that life in, and a sampler built for drums can bring in more.
say.straight: Every hit here is identical. Real drums vary from hit to hit. Recorded kits, and samplers built for drums, bring that variety back.
say.eli5: Every boom here sounds exactly the same, like a robot. A real drummer is never that exact. Recorded drums sound more like a real drummer.

say.mentor:
Live 12 has a sampler built just for drum pads, called Drum Sampler. It sits on a pad in a drum rack, the grid of pads where each pad holds its own sound.
What makes a sampled kit feel real is two tricks. Velocity layers play a different recording depending on how hard you hit, so a soft snare sounds light and a hard one cracks. Round-robin cycles through several recordings of the same hit, so a fast run of hats doesn't sound like a machine gun.
say.straight: Drum Sampler is Live 12's sampler for drum rack pads. Velocity layers pick a recording by how hard you hit. Round-robin cycles recordings so repeats vary.
say.eli5: Drum Sampler is a sampler just for drums. It can play a soft recording for soft taps and a loud one for hard taps, and swap between copies so it never sounds robotic.

deeper.title: drum sampler in live
deeper.say: Drum Sampler lives on a Drum Rack pad, where older kits used Simpler. It's made for one-shot hits and works with the rack's choke groups, which let one pad cut off another, like a closed hat stopping an open hat.

say.mentor:
Here's your beat on the pads. Switch to the recorded kit and every pad plays a recording: a real kick, clap, hat and snare, on exactly the pattern you made.
Go back and forth a few times. The synth kit is clean and easy to shape. The recorded kit has air and grit around each hit. Keep the one your song wants.
say.straight: Your beat on the synth kit and the recorded kit. Same pattern, recorded hits. Pick one and keep it.
say.eli5: Same beat, two kits. One is made by the computer, one is real drum recordings. Keep the one you like.

steps.q: Where does Drum Sampler sit in Live?
options: on a pad in a drum rack
steps.why: It's an instrument for one pad, so each pad can have its own.

whyWrong.1: The master is for the whole mix, not one drum.
whyWrong.2: You find it in the browser, but it plays on a pad.
whyWrong.3: It's an instrument, not part of an effect.

steps.q: A fast run of hats sounds like a machine gun. Which trick helps?
steps.why: Cycling through several recordings means repeats don't sound identical.

whyWrong.1: Reverb adds space; each hit is still identical.
whyWrong.2: Faster makes the problem more obvious.
whyWrong.3: Louder identical hits are still identical.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try slicing to chop a loop onto pads.

lessons.title: slicing to midi

song.why: pieces of sound played from pads in your own order become a new rhythm in your song

lessons.learn: What slicing does to a loop, how Live turns slices into pads, and a new rhythm played from pads into your song.
youCan: say what slicing a loop does
say how slices are triggered once they're on pads
play pieces from pads into a new rhythm

say.mentor:
Hats on the beats, then on the eighths, then on the sixteenths. Each step cuts the bar into smaller, even pieces. Slicing does the same thing to a recording: it chops a loop into pieces, often at each drum hit, sometimes on an even grid like this.
Once a loop is in pieces, each piece can go on its own pad. Then you can play the pieces in any order you like, and an old drum loop turns into a brand new beat.
say.straight: The bar cut into quarters, eighths, sixteenths. Slicing chops a recording the same way, puts each piece on a pad, and lets you replay the pieces in a new order.
say.eli5: Hear the bar get chopped into smaller and smaller bits? Slicing chops a drum recording into bits and puts each bit on a pad. Then you can play them in any order.

say.mentor:
Live does this in one move. It finds the hits in a loop, cuts it there, and puts every slice on its own pad in a drum rack. Each pad is played by a midi note, and midi is just the note data: which pad, when, and how hard, with no sound of its own.
So once the loop is sliced, the rhythm lives in notes you can move. Shift a note and that slice plays somewhere else. That's how producers remix breakbeats into something new.
say.straight: Live cuts the loop at its hits and puts each slice on a drum rack pad. Midi notes trigger the pads, so moving notes rearranges the loop.
say.eli5: The computer cuts the drum recording into pieces and puts each piece on a pad. Then you just play the pads in a new order.

deeper.title: slicing in live
deeper.say: Right-click an audio clip and choose Slice to New MIDI Track. Live asks how to slice: by transients (each detected hit), by a fixed grid such as sixteenths, or by the clip's warp markers. It builds a Drum Rack with one slice per pad and a MIDI clip that plays them in the original order, starting at C1. Edit that MIDI clip in the piano roll to rearrange the loop.

deeper.title: or inside simpler
deeper.say: Simpler's Slice mode chops a sample into slices inside the one device, each playable from its own note, without making a new track.

say.mentor:
Your pads are your slices. Each one holds a short piece of drum sound, the way a sliced loop would. Your beat keeps playing underneath.
Press rec, wait out the count-in, and play a new rhythm on pads your beat isn't using yet, like the toms, the rim or the percs. Snap is on, so every tap lands on the grid. Play at least four hits, then listen to how the new pieces change your groove.
say.straight: Treat the pads as slices. Record a new rhythm over your beat on unused pads: toms, rim, percs. Snap is on. Four hits or more.
say.eli5: Each pad is a little piece of drum sound. Press rec and tap a new pattern on the pads you haven't used yet. The snap helper keeps your taps in time.

steps.hint: Leave the kick pad alone, or your new taps replace your kick.

steps.q: What does Slice to New MIDI Track put on each pad?
steps.why: The loop is cut up and each slice gets its own pad.

whyWrong.1: The point is to split it up.
whyWrong.2: The pads hold pieces of your recording.
whyWrong.3: The pads hold sound, not effects.

steps.q: Once a loop is sliced, how do you rearrange it?
options: move the midi notes that trigger the pads
steps.why: Each note plays a slice, so moving notes moves slices.

whyWrong.1: No need, the pieces are already there.
whyWrong.3: Reverb changes space, not order.

steps.q: Which of these is a way Live can decide where to slice?
options: at each detected hit, the transients
steps.why: Transients are the sharp starts of hits. Live can also slice on a fixed grid or at warp markers.

whyWrong.1: Slicing follows the audio or a grid, not chance.
whyWrong.2: Colour has nothing to do with it.
whyWrong.3: The name doesn't tell Live where hits are.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try audio clips to edit a sample's start, end and gain.

lessons.title: audio clips

song.why: the pitch, length and gain of a sound decide how it sits in your song

lessons.learn: What an audio clip is, what you can change without touching the original file, and pitch, length and gain on your own kick.
youCan: say what an audio clip is
say what transpose and detune measure
set pitch, length and gain on a sound by ear

say.mentor:
A full beat: kick, clap, hats. In Live, a beat like this can live in two kinds of clip. A midi clip holds notes, instructions for an instrument. An audio clip holds a recording, the actual sound.
You can bend an audio clip a lot: play it higher, cut where it starts and ends, turn it up or down, flip it backwards. And the original file on your computer never changes. Live just remembers your edits.
say.straight: A midi clip holds notes. An audio clip holds a recording. You can change an audio clip's pitch, start, end and gain without changing the original file.
say.eli5: Some clips are notes, some are recordings. You can make a recording higher, shorter or quieter, and the real recording stays safe.

say.mentor:
Transpose moves a clip's pitch in semitones. A semitone is the smallest step on a piano, one key to the very next. Twelve of them make an octave.
Detune is the fine version, in cents. A cent is a hundredth of a semitone, so it's for tiny nudges, like tuning a sample so it sits right with your bass.
say.straight: Transpose is in semitones, one piano key each, twelve to an octave. Detune is in cents, a hundredth of a semitone, for fine tuning.
say.eli5: Transpose moves the sound up or down one piano key at a time. Detune moves it just a tiny bit, for when it's almost right.

deeper.title: the clip view in live
deeper.say: Click an audio clip to open it in the detail view at the bottom of the screen. There you'll find Gain, Transpose, Detune, the start and end markers, loop settings and the Warp switch. Reverse, Crop and Consolidate are in the clip's right-click menu. Transpose covers 48 semitones up or down.

deeper.title: warp, in one line
deeper.say: With Warp on, an audio clip follows your song's tempo. With it off, the clip plays at its original speed. The warping lesson goes into this.

say.mentor:
The same three moves you'd make on an audio clip, on your kick with your song playing. Tune is transpose: it moves the kick up or down in semitones. Decay is where the sound ends, like dragging a clip's end marker earlier or later. Level is gain, how loud the sound is before anything else touches it.
Try a kick a couple of semitones lower, a bit shorter, sitting just under the clap. Keep whatever sounds best with your bass.
say.straight: On your kick: tune is transpose, decay is where it ends, level is gain. Set them so the kick sits with your bass, then keep it. These act on the synth kit.
say.eli5: Tune makes your kick higher or lower. Decay makes it shorter or longer. Level makes it louder or quieter. Turn them until it sounds good.

steps.q: What's the difference between an audio clip and a midi clip?
options: audio holds a recording, midi holds notes
steps.why: An audio clip is sound itself. A midi clip is instructions that an instrument turns into sound.

whyWrong.1: Loudness depends on the sound, not the clip type.
whyWrong.2: Midi is very easy to edit.
whyWrong.3: They hold different things.

steps.q: You transpose a clip by 12 semitones. How far did it move?
steps.why: Twelve semitones make one octave.

whyWrong.1: One key is one semitone.
whyWrong.3: Half an octave is six semitones.

steps.q: You edit an audio clip's start, gain and pitch. What happens to the file on your computer?
options: nothing, Live keeps the edits separately
steps.why: Clip edits are non-destructive. The original recording stays untouched.

whyWrong.1: Live never overwrites the source for clip edits.
whyWrong.2: The file stays where it is.
whyWrong.3: Audio stays audio.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try recording audio to capture your own sounds.

lessons.title: recording audio

song.why: a recorded take puts your own playing, with its own feel, into your song

lessons.learn: How recording works in Live: input, arm, monitor, level, record. Then a take of your own recorded into your song.
youCan: say the steps to record a sound in Live
say what arming and monitoring do
say what a healthy recording level is

say.mentor:
A kick on every beat, steady as a clock. Everything you've added so far started as something you played or shaped here. Recording audio is the same idea with the outside world: a voice, a guitar, keys jangling, a hand slapping a table. Whatever reaches a microphone can become part of your song.
The steps are always the same: choose where the sound comes from, get the track ready, check the level, hit record.
say.straight: Recording audio captures any real sound into your song. The steps: pick the input, arm the track, check the level, record.
say.eli5: You can record any sound into your song: your voice, a clap, a pan banging. You pick the microphone, get ready, and press record.

say.mentor:
Arming a track means telling it to record. Only armed tracks capture sound when you press record, which stops you recording over the wrong thing.
Monitoring means hearing yourself through the computer while you play. Handy, but there's a small delay called latency, the time sound takes to go in and come back out. Too much and it's hard to play in time.
Level is how loud the sound arrives. Aim for the loudest moments peaking around minus 12 to minus 6 on the meter. Hit the top and the recording clips: the peaks are cut off and it crackles, and you can't undo that afterwards.
say.straight: Arm: the track will record. Monitor: you hear yourself, with a little delay called latency. Level: peaks around minus 12 to minus 6 on the meter, never at the top, or it clips.
say.eli5: Press the arm button so the track is ready. Make sure you can hear yourself. Keep the sound out of the red on the meter, or it crackles.

deeper.title: recording in live
deeper.say: On an audio track, set Audio From to your interface's input, then arm the track with its record button. Monitor has three settings. In always lets the input through. Auto lets it through while the track is armed and not playing back a recording. Off never does. Then press the main Record button. In Session View the take lands in the selected empty clip slot; in Arrangement View it goes on the timeline where playback is.

deeper.title: latency
deeper.say: Preferences, then Audio, shows your buffer size and latency. A smaller buffer means less delay. If your audio interface has direct monitoring, you can use that and set Live's monitor to Off so you hear yourself with no delay at all.

deeper.title: take lanes
deeper.say: When you record over a loop several times in Arrangement View, Live keeps each pass in take lanes, so you can pick the best bits afterwards.

say.mentor:
We can't reach your mic here, but recording a take works the same way. Your song is playing. Press rec, and the count-in is your moment to get ready, like arming a track. Then play the pads along with your song: a rim on the offbeats, a tom fill at the end of the bar, whatever feels good.
That take is your playing, with your timing. Listen back, and keep it if it adds something.
say.straight: Record a take over your song on the pads. Press rec, wait out the count-in, play at least four hits on spare pads. Keep it if it works.
say.eli5: Press rec, wait for the ticks, then tap some pads along with your song. That's a recording of you playing.

steps.hint: Use pads your beat doesn't use yet, so your kick and clap stay as they are.

steps.q: What does arming a track do?
steps.why: Only armed tracks capture sound when you hit record.

whyWrong.1: Mute is a different button.
whyWrong.3: Nothing is deleted.

steps.q: Where should your recording's loudest moments peak?
options: around minus 12 to minus 6 on the meter
steps.why: That leaves room above for loud surprises, so nothing clips.

whyWrong.1: At the top it clips, and clipping can't be undone.
whyWrong.2: Too quiet and you'll hear more noise when you turn it up.
whyWrong.3: Clipping ruins a take for good, so it matters.

steps.q: What is latency?
options: the delay as sound goes in and back out
steps.why: It's the time the sound takes to travel through the computer and back to your ears.

whyWrong.1: That's the level.
whyWrong.2: Tempo is the speed of the song.
whyWrong.3: Reverb is space, not delay through the computer.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try warping to fit a sample to your tempo.

lessons.title: warping

song.why: your song's tempo is the grid every sample has to fit, and warping is how a recording fits it

lessons.learn: What warping does to a recording, why a loop needs it to follow your tempo, and your song moved to a new tempo.
youCan: say what warping does
say what a warp marker is
set your song's tempo knowing your samples have to follow it

say.mentor:
Two grooves at the same tempo, then both together, locked. They only lock because they're at the same speed. Grab a drum loop recorded at 100 bpm, drop it into a song at 124, and it drifts out of time straight away.
Warping fixes that. It stretches or squeezes a recording in time so it follows your song's tempo, and it does it without changing the pitch. Your 100 bpm loop plays at 124, and it doesn't turn into a chipmunk.
say.straight: Two grooves lock because they share a tempo. Warping stretches a recording to your song's tempo without changing its pitch.
say.eli5: Two beats at the same speed fit together. If a recording is slower than your song, warping speeds it up to match, and it doesn't make it squeaky.

say.mentor:
To stretch a recording properly, Live needs to know where its beats are. A warp marker is a pin that says "this point in the sound belongs on this beat". Live places them on the hits, and you can drag one to fix a hit that's early or late.
Between the markers, Live stretches the audio to fit. How it stretches depends on the warp mode, which has a lesson of its own.
say.straight: A warp marker pins a point in the audio to a beat. Live stretches the audio between markers. Drag a marker to fix timing.
say.eli5: Warp markers are pins that hold each drum hit on the beat. Move a pin and the hit moves.

deeper.title: warping in live
deeper.say: Each audio clip has a Warp switch in the clip view. With Warp on, the clip follows the project tempo. With it off, it plays at its own speed. Double-click in the waveform to add a warp marker. Right-click a hit and choose Warp From Here (Straight) to lock a whole loop to the grid from that point.

deeper.title: six modes
deeper.say: Live has six warp modes: Beats, Tones, Texture, Re-Pitch, Complex and Complex Pro. Start with Beats for drums. Re-Pitch is the odd one out: like a tape machine, it changes pitch along with speed.

say.mentor:
Here's your song. Turn the tempo and every part follows, because your parts are notes and the engine plays each note on the beat it belongs to. Even the recorded kit follows: each hit is a short sample, fired on its step.
A long recorded loop wouldn't do that on its own. That's the job warping does in Live. Pick the tempo that feels right for your song, and know that any loop you bring in will be warped to it.
say.straight: Turn your song's tempo. Your parts are notes, so they follow. A recorded loop would need warping to do the same. Pick your tempo.
say.eli5: Turn the knob to make your song faster or slower. Everything you made keeps up. A recording would need warping to keep up too.

steps.q: What does warping do?
options: changes a recording's timing without changing its pitch
steps.why: It stretches or squeezes the audio in time to fit your tempo, keeping the pitch.

whyWrong.1: Pitch stays put; timing changes.
whyWrong.3: Level doesn't change.

steps.q: What is a warp marker?
options: a pin that holds a point in the audio to a beat
steps.why: Live stretches the audio between markers so each pinned point lands on its beat.

whyWrong.1: Reverb is space.
whyWrong.3: Colours are just labels.

steps.q: Which warp mode changes pitch along with speed, like a tape machine?
steps.why: Re-Pitch ties pitch to speed, so faster means higher.

whyWrong.1: Beats keeps the pitch and is made for drums.
whyWrong.2: Complex Pro keeps the pitch and is made for full mixes.
whyWrong.3: Texture keeps the pitch and is made for pads.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try warp modes for the same stretch done four ways.

lessons.title: warp modes

song.why: the further your song's tempo is from a sample's own tempo, the more the right warp mode matters

lessons.learn: What each of Live's warp modes is built for, and which one you'd pick for each part of your song.
youCan: match a warp mode to drums, a bass line, a pad and a full mix
say what Re-Pitch does differently
hear a big tempo change on your own song

say.mentor:
Kick, clap and fast hats, played straight, then swung. Every hit has a sharp start, a click of energy called a transient. Drums are mostly transients with little gaps between them.
That matters when you stretch a recording. Stretching drums is mostly about moving those sharp starts to the right place. Stretching a held note or a voice is a different job: keeping a smooth tone smooth. That's why Live has more than one way to warp, called warp modes.
say.straight: Drums are sharp starts, transients, with gaps between. A held note is a smooth tone. Each needs a different kind of stretching, so Live has several warp modes.
say.eli5: Drums go tick, tick, tick, with little gaps. A singer goes aaaah, all smooth. Stretching each one needs a different trick.

steps.title: a mode for each kind of sound

say.mentor:
Beats is for drums and other punchy loops. It cuts the audio at each transient and moves the pieces, so hits stay sharp. On a melody it can stutter.
Tones is for single melodic lines: a bass, a lead, a solo voice. Texture is for pads and noisy, washy sounds. Complex is for whole mixes with everything in them, and Complex Pro is the higher quality version of it, with a formants control that keeps voices from sounding like chipmunks when you move their pitch.
Re-Pitch is the odd one. It doesn't keep the pitch at all: speed and pitch move together, like slowing down a record. Half speed is an octave lower.
say.straight: Beats for drums. Tones for one melodic line. Texture for pads. Complex for full mixes, Complex Pro for the best quality, with formants for voices. Re-Pitch moves speed and pitch together, like vinyl.
say.eli5: Drums get Beats. A single tune gets Tones. Big soft sounds get Texture. A whole song gets Complex. And Re-Pitch is like a record player: slower is lower.

deeper.title: setting the mode in live
deeper.say: The warp mode is a menu under the Warp switch in the clip view. Beats has a Transient Loop Mode and a Transient Envelope to control how each slice fills the gap to the next. Complex Pro has a Formants control. Complex and Complex Pro use the most processing power.

deeper.title: common mistakes
deeper.say: Leaving everything on Complex Pro softens drum transients and costs processing. Beats on a melodic part stutters at every hit. And Re-Pitch on a vocal changes its key as soon as the tempo moves.

say.mentor:
Here's your song. Drag the tempo a long way, down to 90 and up to 140. Your parts are notes, so they follow without any stretching at all.
Now imagine each part were a recording instead. At 90 your drums would need Beats to stay crisp, your bass would want Tones, your chords would sit happily in Texture, and the whole song bounced to one file would need Complex. The bigger the move, the more that choice shows. Then set your song back to the tempo you love.
say.straight: Move your song far, 90 to 140. Notes follow cleanly. As recordings, your drums would want Beats, bass Tones, chords Texture, the full song Complex. Then set your tempo.
say.eli5: Make your song really slow, then really fast. Your notes keep up easily. Recordings would each need their own warp mode to keep up. Then pick the speed you like.

steps.q: Which warp mode would you pick for a drum loop?
steps.why: Beats keeps transients sharp by moving each hit as a slice.

whyWrong.1: Tones is made for single melodic lines.
whyWrong.2: Texture is made for pads and washy sounds.
whyWrong.3: Re-Pitch would change the drums' pitch with the tempo.

steps.q: Which mode suits a bass line?
steps.why: Tones is made for single melodic lines like a bass or a lead.

whyWrong.1: Beats can stutter on melodic parts.
whyWrong.3: Re-Pitch would move the bass out of key.

steps.q: You slow a record to half speed with Re-Pitch. What happens to the pitch?
steps.why: Re-Pitch ties pitch to speed. Half the speed is half the frequency, one octave down.

whyWrong.1: Keeping the pitch is what the other modes do.
whyWrong.3: Half speed is a much bigger drop than one semitone.

steps.q: What does the Formants control in Complex Pro help with?
options: keeping voices natural when their pitch moves
steps.why: Formants are the character of a voice. Keeping them stops the chipmunk sound.

whyWrong.1: For drums you'd pick Beats.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is set by your song.

steps.next: Back to your song path: width and movement is next.

lessons.title: detune and unison

song.why: a slightly detuned lead sounds wide and thick instead of thin and still

lessons.learn: Why two oscillators a few cents apart sound wide, what unison stacks on top, and width on your own lead.
youCan: say why detune makes a sound wider
say what unison does
set detune on your lead before it sounds out of tune

say.mentor:
One synth note, held. It's steady, almost too steady: one oscillator, one pitch, nothing moving. An oscillator is the part of a synth that makes the raw tone.
Add a second oscillator on the same note and pull it a few cents out of tune. A cent is a hundredth of a semitone, a tiny amount. The two tones drift in and out of line with each other, and the note starts to shimmer and spread.
say.straight: One oscillator, one steady note. A second one a few cents off makes the two drift in and out, and the note shimmers and widens. A cent is a hundredth of a semitone.
say.eli5: One plain note. Add a copy of it that's just a tiny bit out of tune, and the two wobble together and sound bigger.

say.mentor:
That shimmer has a name: beating. Two pitches very close together keep moving in and out of step, and you hear a pulse at the speed of the difference. Five hertz apart is five pulses a second, which you hear as a slow, lush wobble.
Unison takes the idea further. It stacks several copies of the whole voice, each detuned a little differently, often spread left and right. That's the classic huge supersaw lead.
There's an edge though. A few cents is wide. Too many cents and the note stops sounding wide and starts sounding out of tune.
say.straight: Close pitches pulse against each other, called beating. Unison stacks several detuned copies of a voice, often spread in stereo. Too much detune sounds out of tune.
say.eli5: Two nearly-same notes go wah-wah-wah together. Unison uses lots of copies for a giant sound. Too far apart and it just sounds wrong.

deeper.title: unison in live
deeper.say: Wavetable has unison built in. Turn it on and raise the voice count, and the sound thickens with every voice you add. Each voice costs a little more processing.

deeper.title: a starting point
deeper.say: Around 5 to 15 cents between oscillators is a common sweet spot for width that still sounds in tune. Past about 20 cents most ears hear it as out of tune.

say.mentor:
Your song is playing with your lead in it. Start detune at zero: clean and narrow. Bring it up slowly and listen for the moment the lead starts to shimmer and fill out. Keep going and it gets seasick. Find the edge and back off a touch.
Then try wave. A buzzier wave has more harmonics, and detune is easier to hear on buzzy sounds, so the two together go big fast. Keep the width that suits your song.
say.straight: Raise detune until your lead shimmers, back off before it sounds out of tune. A buzzier wave makes the width more obvious. Keep it.
say.eli5: Turn detune up until your tune sounds big and shimmery. Too far sounds wobbly, so turn it back a bit. Then try wave for a buzzier sound.

steps.q: Why does detuning two oscillators make a sound wider?
options: their pitches drift in and out of line and shimmer
steps.why: Close pitches beat against each other, and you hear that movement as width.

whyWrong.1: It's movement, not level.
whyWrong.3: Tempo doesn't change.

steps.q: What does unison do?
options: stacks several detuned copies of the voice
steps.why: Several slightly different copies, often spread left and right, make one huge voice.

whyWrong.1: Unison copies the voice, not the whole keyboard.
whyWrong.2: It adds detune, it doesn't remove it.
whyWrong.3: Reverb is an effect.

steps.q: Your lead sounds wide but also a bit sour. What do you change?
steps.why: Too much detune tips from wide into out of tune. Back off.

whyWrong.1: That makes it more sour.
whyWrong.3: More notes won't fix the tuning.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try the lfo for movement that runs by itself.

lessons.title: the lfo

song.why: a filter that sweeps open and closed in time makes your lead move instead of sitting still

lessons.learn: What an lfo is, what rate and depth do, and a slow sweep on your lead's filter, done by hand the way an lfo would do it.
youCan: say what an lfo is
say what rate and depth control
say what an lfo on pitch, filter or volume sounds like

say.mentor:
A low note, then a high one. Pitch is how fast a wave wiggles: hundreds of times a second for these notes. Slow a wave right down, below about 20 times a second, and you can't hear it as a note anymore.
But a wave that slow is still useful. Hook it up to a knob and it turns that knob up and down for you, over and over. That's an lfo, a low frequency oscillator: a wave too slow to hear, used to move things.
say.straight: Notes are fast waves. A wave slower than about 20 a second isn't heard as a note. An lfo, low frequency oscillator, is a slow wave used to move a knob up and down by itself.
say.eli5: A really, really slow wiggle is too slow to hear. But it can turn a knob up and down for you, again and again. That's an lfo.

say.mentor:
Rate is how fast the lfo goes round. Depth is how far it moves the knob. And the destination is which knob it moves.
Each destination has its own sound. An lfo on pitch is vibrato, the wobble a singer puts on a long note. On the filter it's a wah, the brightness opening and closing. On volume it's tremolo, a pulsing up and down.
Most lfos can sync to the tempo, so the movement locks to your beat: once a bar, once a beat, and so on.
say.straight: Rate is speed, depth is how far, destination is which knob. Lfo on pitch is vibrato, on the filter a wah, on volume tremolo. Tempo sync locks it to your beat.
say.eli5: You choose how fast it wobbles and how much. Wobble the pitch and it goes wee-oo-wee. Wobble the brightness and it goes wah-wah.

deeper.title: the lfo shape
deeper.say: The lfo's wave shape sets the feel. A sine moves smoothly. A square jumps between two values. Sample and hold jumps to a random value each step, which gives that bubbling, computer-ish movement.

deeper.title: lfos in live
deeper.say: Wavetable has two lfos. You connect them in its modulation matrix, at the bottom of the device, by picking a source and a destination and setting an amount.

say.mentor:
Our lead doesn't have its own lfo yet, so you're going to be the lfo. Your song is playing. Set res a little higher so the filter has some bite.
Now turn cutoff slowly up over one bar and back down over the next, again and again, in time with the kick. Hear that sweep? That's exactly what an lfo on the filter does, only it never gets tired. The speed you're turning is the rate. How far you turn is the depth. Leave cutoff where your lead sounds best when you stop.
say.straight: You're the lfo. Raise res a bit, then sweep cutoff up for a bar and down for a bar, in time. Your speed is the rate, your range is the depth. Leave cutoff where it sounds best.
say.eli5: Pretend you're a robot hand. Turn cutoff up slowly, then down slowly, again and again with the beat. That's what an lfo does by itself.

steps.q: What does lfo stand for?
steps.why: An oscillator so slow you don't hear it as a note, used to move other knobs.

whyWrong.1: Not a filter or an output.
whyWrong.3: Not a fade.

steps.q: An lfo moves your lead's pitch up and down. What do you hear?
steps.why: Pitch wobbling up and down is vibrato.

whyWrong.1: Tremolo is volume moving.
whyWrong.2: A wah is the filter moving.
whyWrong.3: Reverb is space.

steps.q: What does the lfo's rate set?
steps.why: Rate is speed. Depth is how far.

whyWrong.1: That's depth.
whyWrong.3: Level is separate.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try modulation routing to send movement somewhere else.

lessons.title: modulation routing

song.why: movement in brightness or in pitch gives your lead two very different kinds of life

lessons.learn: Sources, destinations and amounts, the way every modern synth wires up movement, and movement on your lead's brightness or its pitch.
youCan: say what a modulation source and destination are
say what a modulation matrix does
choose between brightness movement and pitch movement on your lead

say.mentor:
Three wave shapes on the same note. Each one is a still picture: the sound starts, holds, and stops without changing. Real instruments are never that still. A trumpet gets brighter as it's blown harder, a singer's pitch bends into a note.
Synths get that life from modulation: one thing moving another. And the cleanest way to think about it is as wiring, from a source to a destination.
say.straight: Three still sounds. Modulation adds movement by letting one thing move another, wired from a source to a destination.
say.eli5: These sounds don't move. Modulation makes one part of a synth push another part around, so the sound changes as it plays.

say.mentor:
A source is something that moves: an lfo, an envelope, how hard you play (velocity), the mod wheel on a keyboard. A destination is the knob it moves: filter cutoff, pitch, volume, pan.
The amount says how much. It can be negative too, so the source pushes the knob the other way.
A modulation matrix is a grid of all of these, so any source can go to any destination. Two sources can even move the same knob at once, and their movements add up.
say.straight: Source: what moves (lfo, envelope, velocity, mod wheel). Destination: the knob it moves. Amount: how much, positive or negative. A matrix lets any source reach any destination.
say.eli5: Pick something that wiggles, pick a knob for it to wiggle, and say how much. That's modulation.

deeper.title: a classic route
deeper.say: Velocity to filter cutoff makes a sound brighter when you play harder, the way real instruments behave. It's one of the first routes to try on any patch.

deeper.title: the matrix in wavetable
deeper.say: Wavetable's modulation matrix sits at the bottom of the device. Pick a source row, a destination column, and set the amount, positive or negative. Stacking Envelope 2 and an lfo on filter cutoff gives a sweep on every note with a slow wobble on top.

say.mentor:
Your lead has two routes already wired, and each knob is the amount. Env sends an envelope to the filter: each note starts bright and settles darker. Glide sends movement to pitch: each note slides up or down into the next instead of jumping.
Same melody, two destinations. Try env alone, then glide alone, then both, with your song playing. Keep the one that makes your lead feel right, or keep both.
say.straight: Env is an envelope routed to the filter: each note opens bright. Glide moves pitch: notes slide into each other. Try each, keep one or both.
say.eli5: Env makes each note start bright and get darker. Glide makes notes slide like a trombone. Try both and keep your favourite.

steps.q: In modulation, what is the destination?
steps.why: The source moves, the destination is what it moves.

whyWrong.1: That's the source.
whyWrong.3: It's all within one sound.

steps.q: You route velocity to filter cutoff. What happens?
options: harder notes sound darker no matter what
steps.why: Play harder and the filter opens further, like a real instrument.

whyWrong.1: Only with a negative amount.
whyWrong.3: Nothing reverses.

steps.q: Two sources move the same knob. What happens?
steps.why: Stacked modulation combines, which is how complex movement is built.

whyWrong.1: They only cancel if set to exactly opposite amounts.
whyWrong.3: Stacking is normal.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try fm basics for a whole new kind of tone.

lessons.title: fm basics

song.why: a bass with a bright, bitey start and a rounder tail is the sound fm is famous for

lessons.learn: How fm makes rich tones from simple waves, what the ratio and the modulator level do, and a bitey start on your own bass.
youCan: say what a carrier and a modulator are
say what whole-number and in-between ratios sound like
give your bass a bright start that settles

say.mentor:
A soft wave, a saw, a square. The saw and square sound rich because they come with lots of harmonics built in. Subtractive synths start from waves like these and filter harmonics away.
Fm, frequency modulation, does the opposite. It starts with plain, soft waves and builds harmonics up. One wave wobbles the pitch of another so fast that you don't hear a wobble at all. You hear a brand new, richer tone.
say.straight: Saws and squares come with harmonics built in. Fm starts with plain waves and creates harmonics by letting one wave wobble another's pitch very fast.
say.eli5: Some waves are already buzzy. Fm takes two smooth waves and has one shake the other super fast, and that makes a buzzy, shiny sound.

say.mentor:
The wave you hear is the carrier. The wave doing the wobbling is the modulator. Turn the modulator up and new frequencies appear around the note, called sidebands, and the tone gets brighter and more complex.
The ratio is the modulator's pitch compared to the carrier's. Whole numbers, like 1 to 1 or 2 to 1, give musical tones that sit in key. In-between numbers, like 1 to 1.41, give clangy, metallic sounds: bells, gongs, struck metal.
The famous fm bass trick is to make the modulator loud at the start of each note and fade it quickly. The note starts bright and bitey, then settles round.
say.straight: Carrier: the wave you hear. Modulator: the wave wobbling it. More modulator, more harmonics. Whole-number ratios sound musical, in-between ratios sound like bells and metal.
say.eli5: One wave is the singer, one is the shaker. More shaking, brighter sound. Shake in step and it sounds musical. Shake out of step and it sounds like a bell.

deeper.title: fm in live
deeper.say: Operator is Live's fm synth, with four oscillators that can modulate each other. Each oscillator has its own envelope, so a modulator with a short envelope gives the bright-start bass. Wavetable can do fm between its oscillators too.

say.mentor:
Our bass is a filter synth, not an fm one, so it can't do ratios. But it can do the famous fm bass shape, the bright start that settles, and that's what your ears will recognise. Your song is playing.
Turn wave toward the buzzier end so there are more harmonics to work with. Then raise env: each bass note now starts brighter and rounds off, just like a modulator fading out. Keep it if your bass bites better.
say.straight: Our bass can't set an fm ratio, but it can copy the fm bass shape. Buzzier wave, then raise env so each note starts bright and rounds off. Keep it.
say.eli5: Make the bass buzzier with wave. Then turn env up so every note starts with a bite and then goes soft.

steps.q: In fm, which wave do you actually hear?
steps.why: The modulator shapes the carrier's tone. The carrier is what reaches your ears.

whyWrong.1: The modulator changes the carrier, you don't hear it on its own.
whyWrong.3: An lfo is a slow wave for movement, a different thing.

steps.q: A ratio of 1 to 1.41 will sound like?
steps.why: In-between ratios make sidebands that don't line up with the note's harmonics, which sounds metallic.

whyWrong.1: A clean sine has no modulation at all.
whyWrong.2: Pads usually come from whole-number ratios or other synths.
whyWrong.3: That's a drum sound, not a ratio.

steps.q: What happens when you turn the modulator up?
options: more sidebands, a brighter, richer tone
steps.why: More modulation creates more new frequencies around the note.

whyWrong.1: Level isn't what the modulator mainly changes.
whyWrong.2: The note stays the same pitch.
whyWrong.3: It changes the tone a lot.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try wavetable to scan through shapes on your lead.

lessons.title: wavetable

song.why: scanning through wave shapes changes your lead's whole colour without touching the melody

lessons.learn: What a wavetable is, what scanning it does, and a scanned wave shape on your own lead.
youCan: say what a wavetable is
say what the position knob does
pick a wave colour for your lead by scanning

say.mentor:
Soft, saw, square. Three shapes, three colours of the same note. The shape of one single wiggle of the wave decides that colour, called timbre.
Now imagine not three shapes but dozens, lined up in a row, each a little different from the next. That row is a wavetable. Sweep along it and the sound morphs smoothly from one colour to the next, while the note stays the same.
say.straight: Each wave shape gives a different timbre. A wavetable is a row of many shapes, and sweeping along it morphs the sound smoothly.
say.eli5: Three shapes, three sounds. A wavetable is a long line of shapes, and you can slide along it to change the sound bit by bit.

say.mentor: The knob that moves you along the row is called position. Turn it and you scan through the table. The fun part is moving it while notes play: put an lfo or an envelope on position and the sound keeps morphing, which is how those evolving pads and talking basses are made.
say.straight: Position moves you along the wavetable. Modulate position with an lfo or envelope and the sound morphs while it plays.
say.eli5: Position is where you are along the line of shapes. Make it move by itself and the sound keeps changing.

deeper.title: wavetable in live
deeper.say: Live's Wavetable synth has two wavetable oscillators, each with its own position knob, plus a sub oscillator. It has two filters, envelopes and lfos, a modulation matrix at the bottom of the device, and unison for thick, stacked voices.

say.mentor:
Your lead's wave knob is a small wavetable: it morphs from a soft wave through a saw to a square. Your song is playing. Sweep wave slowly from one end to the other and watch the shape change on the screen as you hear the colour change.
Then use cutoff to tidy it: a buzzy shape with a lower cutoff can sound warm and full. Stop where your lead has the colour your song needs, and keep it.
say.straight: Wave scans your lead from soft to saw to square. Sweep it, pick a colour, then set cutoff. Keep it.
say.eli5: Turn wave slowly and hear your tune change from soft to buzzy. Stop on the sound you like.

steps.q: What is a wavetable?
options: a row of wave shapes you can sweep through
steps.why: Many single-cycle shapes in order, so moving through them morphs the sound.

whyWrong.1: Drum hits live in a sampler or drum rack.
whyWrong.2: Tempo has nothing to do with it.
whyWrong.3: Reverb is space.

steps.q: You put an lfo on position. What happens?
options: the sound keeps morphing between shapes
steps.why: The lfo sweeps position for you, so the timbre keeps changing.

whyWrong.1: The notes stay the same; the colour changes.
whyWrong.3: It keeps playing.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try meld for a voice made of two engines.

lessons.title: meld

song.why: a lead built from two blended layers sounds richer than one oscillator on its own

lessons.learn: Meld, Live 12's synth with two engines blended into one voice, its focus on per-note expression, and a two-layer voice on your own lead.
youCan: say what Meld's two engines do
say what MPE adds to playing
blend two layers into one lead voice

say.mentor:
Soft wave, saw, square. Each has its own character: the soft one is round and calm, the saw is bright and edgy. Pick one and you lose the others.
Meld's answer is to not pick. It has two separate engines, each making its own sound, and blends them into one voice. Round and edgy at once, or one morphing into the other as you play.
say.straight: Each shape has its own character. Meld runs two engines at once and blends them into one voice.
say.eli5: Instead of picking one sound, Meld plays two at once and mixes them together.

steps.title: two engines, every note its own

say.mentor:
Meld arrived in Live 12. Its two engines are called A and B, and each can use a different kind of oscillator, so one might be a classic synth wave and the other something stranger. You set how they blend, or let the way you play move the blend.
That last part is what Meld is built around: MPE, which stands for midi polyphonic expression. On an MPE controller every note you hold sends its own pitch bend, pressure and slide, so one finger can bend its note while the others stay put. Pressing harder on a note could morph it from engine A toward engine B.
say.straight: Meld (Live 12) has engines A and B, each with its own oscillator type, blended into one voice. It's built for MPE: every held note gets its own pitch bend, pressure and slide.
say.eli5: Meld has two sound makers, A and B, mixed together. With a special keyboard, pressing harder on one note can change just that note.

deeper.title: meld in live
deeper.say: Meld is great without an MPE controller too: its macros and engine blend are a fast way to explore sounds from a preset. With Push 3 or another MPE controller, pressure, slide and per-note bend can be routed to the blend, filters and more.

say.mentor:
Your lead has two oscillators too, which is a small version of Meld's idea. Your song is playing. Wave picks the shape both layers share. Detune pulls the second layer away from the first, so you hear them as two voices blended rather than one.
Then try env: each note starts brighter and settles, which makes the blend feel like it's moving. Keep the lead that sounds richest without getting muddy.
say.straight: Two layers on your lead: wave sets their shape, detune separates them, env adds movement to each note. Keep the richest version.
say.eli5: Your tune has two sounds inside. Detune pulls them apart so you hear both. Env makes each note shine at the start. Keep it if you like it.

steps.q: What is special about Meld's design?
options: two engines blended into one voice
it's an effect, not an instrument
steps.why: Engines A and B each make a sound, and Meld blends them.

whyWrong.1: It's a synth for any part.
whyWrong.3: Each engine has its own oscillator.

steps.q: What does MPE let you do?
options: bend and shape each held note on its own
steps.why: Every note gets its own pitch bend, pressure and slide.

whyWrong.1: Speed isn't what MPE is about.
whyWrong.3: The key stays the same.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try drift for an analog-style voice on your chords.

lessons.title: drift

song.why: a little wander in pitch makes your chords feel warm and played, like an old analog synth

lessons.learn: Live's Drift synth, why old analog synths sound warm, and analog-style wander on your own chords.
youCan: say what the drift control adds
say what subtractive synthesis is
add warmth to your chords without making them sound out of tune

say.mentor:
One synth note, perfectly steady. A computer can hold a pitch forever without moving a hair. Old analog synths couldn't. Their circuits warmed up and wandered, so every note was a tiny bit different in pitch and timing.
That wander turned out to be a big part of why people love them. It sounds alive, a little imperfect, warm. Drift is the name for it, and it's also the name of a synth in Live.
say.straight: A digital note holds perfectly still. Analog synths wander slightly in pitch and timing. That wander, drift, is a big part of their warm sound.
say.eli5: Computers play notes perfectly still. Old synths wobbled a tiny bit, and that wobble sounds warm and friendly.

say.mentor:
Drift is a subtractive synth. Subtractive means you start with a bright, buzzy wave full of harmonics and a filter takes some away, the way a sculptor carves. Most classic synths work like this.
Drift keeps it small: two oscillators, a filter, envelopes and a few ways to add movement, all on one screen, so you can make a sound fast by ear. And it has a drift control that adds that random analog wander to pitch and timing.
say.straight: Drift is subtractive: a bright wave, then a filter removes harmonics. Two oscillators, a filter, envelopes, all on one screen, plus a drift control for analog wander.
say.eli5: Drift starts with a buzzy sound and a filter makes it softer. It also has a knob that adds the old synth wobble.

deeper.title: drift in live
deeper.say: Drift has two filter types to switch between: a 12 dB state-variable filter that sounds open and musical, and a 24 dB ladder filter that's tighter and more classic. Set Drift to zero for a clean, digital sound, and raise it for more instability.

say.mentor:
Your song is playing with your chords in it. Start with drift low: tidy and a little stiff. Turn it up and the chord notes start to wander against each other, and the chords loosen up and warm up. Too much and they sound seasick, so find the warm spot.
Then shape the colour the subtractive way: cutoff to carve brightness away, res to give the edge of the filter some bite. Keep your warmer chords.
say.straight: Raise drift on your chords until they warm up, before they sound out of tune. Then carve with cutoff and res. Keep it.
say.eli5: Turn drift up so your chords wobble a little and sound warm. Not too much! Then make them brighter or darker with cutoff.

steps.q: What does a drift control add?
options: small random wander in pitch and timing
steps.why: It copies the slight instability of analog circuits.

whyWrong.1: The notes stay the same; they just wander.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is set by your song.

steps.q: What does subtractive synthesis mean?
options: start bright and filter harmonics away
add sine waves one by one
steps.why: A rich wave goes through a filter that removes some of its harmonics.

whyWrong.1: Building from sine waves is additive.
whyWrong.3: That's slicing.

steps.q: Your chords sound a bit sour after turning drift up. What do you do?
options: turn drift all the way up
steps.why: Past the warm spot, the wander starts to sound out of tune.

whyWrong.1: That makes it sourer.
whyWrong.3: Tempo isn't the cause.

steps.next: Back to your song path: fx, risers and sweeps is next.

lessons.title: noise

song.why: your hats are shaped noise, and their length and colour set how busy and bright your groove feels

lessons.learn: What noise is, why it's the raw stuff of hats, snares and risers, and the noise in your own hats shaped by hand.
youCan: say what white and pink noise are
say how an envelope and a filter turn noise into a drum
shape the noise in your hats

say.mentor:
Open hats between the kicks. Listen closely to the hat itself: there's no note in it. It's a hiss, a burst of noise that starts and dies away.
Noise is sound with every frequency in it at once, all jumbled, so no single pitch stands out. On its own it's just static. Shaped, it becomes hats, snares, breath, wind, and the whoosh of a riser.
say.straight: A hat has no note. It's a short burst of noise. Noise has every frequency at once. Shaped, it becomes hats, snares, wind and risers.
say.eli5: Hear the tss? That's noise, a hiss with no note in it. Make it short and it's a hat. Make it long and rising and it's a whoosh.

say.mentor:
White noise has equal energy at every frequency. That sounds very bright and hissy to us. Pink noise has equal energy in every octave, which puts more weight in the lows, and to our ears it sounds more even and natural, like rain or a waterfall.
To make noise into something, a synth uses two tools you already know. An envelope sets its shape in time: a fast attack and a short decay gives a click or a hat, a slow rise gives a riser. A filter sets its colour: high-passed noise is airy and thin, low-passed noise is dark and rumbly.
say.straight: White noise: equal energy at all frequencies, bright. Pink: equal per octave, more natural. An envelope shapes it in time, a filter shapes its colour.
say.eli5: White noise sounds like loud hiss. Pink noise sounds softer, like rain. Make noise short and it's a drum. Make it brighter or darker with a filter.

deeper.title: noise in live's synths
deeper.say: Most of Live's synths have a noise source you can mix in next to the oscillators. A touch of noise under a pad adds air, and noise with a short envelope layered on a snare adds snap.

deeper.title: risers
deeper.say: The riser in your song is noise too: a long envelope that builds, with a filter opening as it goes. The fx, risers and sweeps lesson puts one before your drop.

say.mentor:
Your hats are noise with an envelope and a filter on them, playing in your song right now. Turn decay down and each burst gets short and tight, a closed, ticking hat. Turn it up and the noise rings out longer, splashy and open.
Tune moves the colour of the noise higher or lower. Higher feels crisp and light, lower feels dusty and dark. Set the hats so they sit above your kick without hissing over everything, and keep them.
say.straight: Your hats are shaped noise. Decay sets how long each burst lasts, tune sets its colour. Set them to sit above your kick, then keep it.
say.eli5: Make your hats short or long with decay. Make them brighter or darker with tune. Keep the ones you like.

steps.q: What is noise?
options: every frequency at once, with no single pitch
steps.why: All frequencies jumbled together, so no note stands out.

whyWrong.1: A low note has a pitch; noise doesn't.
whyWrong.2: A sine is one pure frequency, the opposite.
whyWrong.3: A crowd is a recording, not noise in the synth sense.

steps.q: How do you turn noise into a hat?
options: a fast attack and a short decay
a slow attack and long release
steps.why: A quick, short burst of noise is a hat.

whyWrong.1: That would make a slow swell, like a riser or a pad.
whyWrong.3: Reverb adds space, not the hit itself.

steps.q: Which sounds more even and natural to our ears?
steps.why: Pink has equal energy per octave, which matches how we hear.

whyWrong.1: White sounds bright and hissy to us.
whyWrong.3: Both are sounds.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try synth effects to put an echo on your lead.

lessons.title: synth effects

song.why: an echo on your lead fills the gaps between notes and makes the melody feel bigger

lessons.learn: The effects that finish a synth sound, why their order matters, and an echo on your own lead.
youCan: say what echo, reverb, chorus and saturation each add
say why effect order changes the sound
set an echo on your lead that fills the gaps without clutter

say.mentor:
One synth note, dry. Dry means no effects at all, just the raw voice. It's honest, but it can sound a little bare, like someone singing in a cupboard.
Effects are the last part of building a synth sound. They don't change which notes play. They change the space around them, the width, the edge. A lot of the sounds you love in records are a plain synth with great effects after it.
say.straight: A dry synth note, no effects. Effects finish a sound: space, width, edge. They don't change the notes.
say.eli5: This note has nothing added. Effects are like putting the sound in a big room, or giving it an echo, or making it fuzzy.

say.mentor:
Echo, also called delay, plays your sound back again a moment later, often in time with the beat, so a short melody fills the bar. Reverb adds the sound of a room. Chorus doubles the sound with tiny shifts in pitch and timing for width and warmth. Saturation adds harmonics and edge.
Order matters. Distortion before reverb is a crunchy synth in a room. Reverb before distortion distorts the room too, and it turns to mush. The usual order is the synth itself, then drive, then echo, then reverb.
say.straight: Echo repeats the sound in time. Reverb adds a room. Chorus adds width. Saturation adds edge. Order changes the result: drive before reverb stays clear, reverb before drive gets muddy.
say.eli5: Echo says it again, again, again. Reverb puts it in a big room. Chorus makes it wider. Drive makes it fuzzy. And the order you add them changes the sound.

deeper.title: in live
deeper.say: Echo is Live's delay with character, including a mode that copies the warmth of tape delay. Reverb and Hybrid Reverb add space, Chorus-Ensemble adds width, Saturator adds edge. Devices run left to right on a track, so the order you see is the order the sound goes through them.

deeper.title: sends
deeper.say: Reverb usually lives on a return track. Each part sends some of itself there, so every part shares the same room and the mix holds together.

say.mentor:
Your song is playing. Turn echo up on your lead and listen to each note come back a moment later, filling the space before the next one. A little is lush. Too much and the repeats crowd the melody.
Send pushes some of your lead into the reverb room. Drive adds edge before the echo. Try them in small amounts. Keep the version where your lead sounds finished and still clear.
say.straight: Echo repeats your lead in the gaps. Send adds reverb. Drive adds edge. Small amounts. Keep the clearest, fullest version.
say.eli5: Turn echo up and hear your tune repeat. Add a bit of send for a big room. Stop before it gets messy.

steps.q: What does an echo, or delay, do?
options: plays the sound back again a moment later
adds the sound of a room
steps.why: Repeats, often in time with the beat.

whyWrong.1: That's reverb.
whyWrong.3: Effects don't change which notes play.

steps.q: Why does effect order matter?
options: each effect works on what came before it
only the last effect is heard
the first effect is always muted
steps.why: Reverb then distortion distorts the reverb too. Distortion then reverb keeps it clearer.

whyWrong.1: Swap two effects and you'll hear the difference.
whyWrong.2: Every effect in the chain is heard.
whyWrong.3: Nothing is muted.

steps.q: Which effect adds width with tiny shifts in pitch and timing?
steps.why: Chorus doubles the sound with small shifts, so it spreads wider.

whyWrong.1: Echo repeats the sound later.
whyWrong.3: An eq changes tone, not width.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try granulator iii to turn sound into a cloud.

lessons.title: the mixer in live

song.why: how loud your chords are and where they sit left to right is a mixer decision

lessons.learn: What a mixer is, the fader and pan on every part, and your chords placed on the stage by ear.
youCan: say what a fader, pan, solo and mute do
place your chords with level and pan
find the mixer in Live

say.mentor:
Every part of your song runs through a mixer on its way to your ears. Picture the desk at the back of a club: one channel strip per musician, each with a fader for how loud and a pan knob for where it sits, from left to right. All the strips add up into one master, and that's what comes out of the speakers.
Producers call that left to right picture the stage. Kick and bass stand in the middle, other parts step a little to the sides.
say.straight: A mixer has one strip per part. The fader sets how loud, pan sets left or right. Every strip adds up into the master.
say.eli5: A mixer is a big desk with a slider for every sound. Slide it up and that sound gets louder. Turn the pan knob and the sound moves left or right.

say.mentor:
Two buttons sit on every strip. Mute silences that part. Solo does the opposite: it plays that part alone and silences everything else, so you can hear exactly what one part is doing.
Solo is great for checking, but don't set levels with it. A part always sounds different on its own than it does inside the whole song.
say.straight: Mute silences one part. Solo plays one part alone. Check with solo, set levels with everything playing.
say.eli5: Mute makes one sound go quiet. Solo makes all the other sounds go quiet, so you only hear one.

deeper.title: the mixer in live
deeper.say: In Session view, each track's mixer sits at the bottom of its column: volume, pan, sends, mute, solo and a level meter. Every track ends up in the Master track, the sum of everything. Volume runs from minus infinity up to +6 dB, and pan from 50 left to 50 right.

deeper.title: cue
deeper.say: Cue lets you pre-listen to a track on headphones before anyone else hears it. For it to work, the Cue Out has to be set to a different output from the Master Out.

deeper.title: headroom
deeper.say: Pushing every fader up leaves no room at the top. Many engineers leave 3 to 6 dB of headroom on the master, turning tracks down rather than up.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with a channel strip on your chords. Bring the level down until the chords nearly vanish, then up until they fill the space behind your lead. Then pan them a little to one side and listen to the middle open up for your kick and bass.
There's no right spot. Leave them where your song feels balanced.
say.straight: Chords level: down until they nearly vanish, up until they fill the space. Pan a little off centre. Stop where it feels balanced.
say.eli5: Make your chords quieter, then louder, until they sound just right. Then turn pan to move them a little to one side.

steps.q: What does solo do?
steps.why: Solo silences everything else so you hear one part on its own.

whyWrong.1: That's mute.
whyWrong.2: Getting ready to record is the arm button.
whyWrong.3: Loudness is the fader.

steps.q: Why not set levels while a part is soloed?
options: a part sounds different alone than in the whole song
steps.why: Levels are about parts against each other, so set them with everything playing.

whyWrong.1: Solo doesn't change the part's volume.
whyWrong.3: Pan stays where it is.

steps.q: Where do all the strips end up?
steps.why: The master is the sum of every strip, the sound that leaves the speakers.

whyWrong.1: The first track is just one part.
whyWrong.2: Only what you send goes to the reverb.
whyWrong.3: Cue is a separate pre-listen output.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, eq, a place for everything.

lessons.title: mixing basics

song.why: levels, then tone, then space, in that order, is how a pile of parts turns into a mix

lessons.learn: The order most mixes follow, levels then eq then dynamics then space, worked through on your hats.
youCan: say the usual order of a mix
set a part's level before touching its tone
check a mix on more than one speaker

say.mentor:
Mixing means taking every part of your song and making them sit together as one record that sounds good anywhere: a phone, a car, a club. It sounds like a huge job, but most mixes follow the same order. Levels first, then eq, then dynamics, then space.
The order matters because each step builds on the one before. Eq fixes clashes between parts, but you can only hear a clash once the levels are roughly right.
say.straight: Mixing follows an order: levels, eq, dynamics, space. Each step builds on the last.
say.eli5: Mixing is making all your sounds fit together. You do it in steps: how loud first, then the tone, then the echoes.

say.mentor:
Levels: with faders only, get a rough balance. Most of a good mix is already here.
Eq: cut the clashes, like a lead fighting the bass down low. Dynamics: how much a part jumps between loud and quiet. A compressor evens that out. Space: reverb and echo give the mix depth, some parts close, some further back.
say.straight: Levels with faders. Eq to cut clashes. Dynamics, how much a part jumps between loud and quiet, with a compressor. Then reverb and echo for depth.
say.eli5: First make each sound the right loudness. Then fix sounds that bump into each other. Then add a little echo so some sounds feel far away.

deeper.title: reference tracks
deeper.say: Compare your mix with a released track you love. Match their loudness first: the louder of two mixes nearly always sounds better, even when it isn't.

deeper.title: more than one speaker
deeper.say: A good mix translates, meaning it sounds balanced on any system. Check on at least three: speakers, headphones and a phone. Mixes made only on headphones often come out wider than they should.

deeper.title: the mono check
deeper.say: Now and then, switch the master to mono. Anything that vanishes has a phase problem, and it will vanish on mono systems too.

deeper.title: breaks
deeper.say: Take a break every 45 to 60 minutes. Tired ears make bad decisions.

say.mentor:
Here's your song. Do the whole order on one part, your hats. Level first: down until they nearly vanish, then up until they just tick along on top. Then high, the eq: a small cut if they sting, a small boost if they sound dull. Last, send: a touch of reverb pushes them back behind the kick.
Keep each move small, and listen to the whole song, not just the hats.
say.straight: Level first, until the hats just sit on top. Then high: cut if they sting, boost if dull. Then a little send for space.
say.eli5: Make your hats the right loudness first. Then make them a bit brighter or darker. Then add a tiny bit of echo.

steps.q: What usually comes first in a mix?
steps.why: Get the balance roughly right with faders, then everything else is easier to hear.

whyWrong.1: Space comes last, once the parts sit together.
whyWrong.2: Dynamics come after levels and eq.
whyWrong.3: You can only judge tone once levels are set.

steps.q: In mixing, what does dynamics mean?
options: how much a part jumps between loud and quiet
where a part sits left or right
how much reverb a part has
steps.why: Dynamics is the range between loud and quiet. A compressor evens it out.

whyWrong.1: That's tempo.
whyWrong.3: That's space.

steps.q: Why match loudness before comparing your mix with a released track?
options: the louder one nearly always sounds better
it makes your mix louder for good
steps.why: Louder fools the ear. Match it and you hear the real differences.

whyWrong.1: You can compare anything once levels match.
whyWrong.3: Released tracks are usually loud.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, eq, a place for everything.

lessons.title: the signal chain

song.why: the order your lead's sound passes through things changes how it comes out

lessons.learn: What a signal chain is, why the order of effects matters, and your lead's chain from voice to reverb.
youCan: say what a signal chain is
say why the order of effects matters
shape your lead one stage at a time

say.mentor: A sound in a music program travels like water through pipes. It starts at the voice, the synth making the note, then flows through each effect in turn: a filter, some drive, a reverb. That path is called the signal chain, and every stage works on whatever the stage before it handed over.
say.straight: The signal chain is the path a sound takes: the voice, then each effect in order. Each stage changes what the last one made.
say.eli5: Your sound goes on a little trip through one machine, then the next. Each machine changes it a bit.

say.mentor:
Swap two stages and you get a different sound. An eq after a distortion shapes the gritty new sound the distortion made. Put it before, and the distortion roughs up whatever the eq left.
Reverb usually goes near the end. Put a compressor after a reverb and it squeezes the reverb tail too, so the whole thing pumps.
say.straight: Order changes the sound. Eq after distortion shapes the grit; before, it shapes what gets distorted. A compressor after a reverb makes the tail pump.
say.eli5: If you change which machine comes first, the sound comes out different. Echo usually goes last.

deeper.title: chains in live
deeper.say: Every track has a device chain. Sound flows through the devices from left to right, so the device on the left works first. Drag a device to a new spot and you change the order.

deeper.title: a common order
deeper.say: A common starting order is: an eq to cut problems, then dynamics like compression, then an eq to boost, then saturation, then modulation, then time effects like delay and reverb. It's a habit, not a rule.

deeper.title: bypass
deeper.say: Switch each device off and on to check it's earning its place. If you can't hear a difference, you may not need it.

say.mentor:
Here's your lead's chain, in order. Wave is the voice itself. Cutoff is the filter right after it. Drive roughs it up. Send passes a copy to the reverb at the end.
Move them one at a time, from the first to the last, and listen to each stage change what came before it. Keep the chain that makes your lead sound most like yours.
say.straight: Your lead's chain: wave (voice), cutoff (filter), drive, send (reverb). Set them in order, one at a time.
say.eli5: These four knobs are your lead's trip. Turn them one at a time, left to right, and hear each one change the sound.

steps.q: What is a signal chain?
options: the path a sound takes through each stage in order
