a list of your song's parts
steps.why: Voice first, then each effect in turn, each working on what the last handed over.

whyWrong.1: Parts are tracks. The chain is inside one track.
whyWrong.3: Reverb is one stage in a chain.

steps.q: Why does the order of effects matter?
options: each stage works on what the last one handed it
effects only work first in line
the last effect is always loudest
steps.why: Change the order and each stage gets a different sound to work on.

whyWrong.1: Every stage in the chain works.
whyWrong.3: It matters on any part.

steps.q: In Live, which way does sound flow through a track's devices?
steps.why: The device on the left works first.

whyWrong.1: It's the other way round.
whyWrong.2: The device chain runs across, not up.
whyWrong.3: Each device works in turn.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, eq, a place for everything.

lessons.title: groups and routing

song.why: shaping your whole drum kit at once makes the drums sound like one instrument

lessons.learn: What a group is, where a part's sound goes next, and your drum kit shaped as one.
youCan: say what a group and a bus are
shape several parts at once
group tracks in Live

say.mentor:
Your kick and clap are separate sounds, but they live together in your drum kit and come out through one channel. That's a group: several parts added together into one strip, so one fader or one eq moves them all at once.
Producers group drums, synths and vocals, so a mix with forty parts can be handled as five or six.
say.straight: A group adds several parts into one strip. One fader or eq then moves them all together.
say.eli5: A group is like a box with lots of sounds inside. Turn the box's knob and every sound inside changes together.

say.mentor:
Routing is where each part's sound goes next. By default every part flows straight to the master. Point a few parts into a group instead and the group becomes a little mix of its own, called a bus: one channel carrying several parts, before everything reaches the master.
That's why you can compress your whole kit together, so every hit squeezes as one.
say.straight: Routing decides where a sound goes next. Send parts to a group and it becomes a bus, a channel carrying several parts mixed together.
say.eli5: Every sound goes somewhere next, like a road. You can send lots of sounds down the same road, then change them all at once.

deeper.title: groups in live
deeper.say: Select tracks and press Cmd+G on a Mac or Ctrl+G on Windows to group them. The group track is a real audio bus with its own devices, mixer strip, sends and automation. Groups can sit inside other groups.

deeper.title: audio to and audio from
deeper.say: Each track has Audio To and Audio From menus. A track's output can go to the master, a group or another track's input. Resampling, in Audio From, records Live's master output onto an audio track.

deeper.title: glue on the group
deeper.say: A common move is a Glue Compressor on the drum group, so every drum is compressed together.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with an eq on your whole drum kit, not just one drum. Turn low and the kick and clap both get fuller. Turn high and both get brighter. They move together, like one instrument.
Set it so your kit sounds like one drummer playing one kit.
say.straight: One eq on the whole kit. Kick and clap change together. Set it so they sound like one instrument.
say.eli5: These knobs change all your drums at the same time. Turn them until your drums sound like one big drum kit.

steps.q: What is a group?
options: several parts added together into one strip
steps.why: One strip for several parts, so they can be shaped together.

whyWrong.1: Groups hold parts inside one song.
whyWrong.2: Reverb is an effect. A group can hold effects.
whyWrong.3: The parts inside stay different.

steps.q: What is a bus?
options: a channel carrying several parts mixed together
steps.why: A group is a bus. So is the master.

whyWrong.1: A bus carries sound, it doesn't make it.
whyWrong.2: Tempo is the speed of the song.
whyWrong.3: Patterns are notes. A bus is where sound flows.

steps.q: Why group your drums?
options: to shape them all at once, like one instrument
steps.why: One move on the group changes every drum inside it.

whyWrong.1: Grouping doesn't touch timing.
whyWrong.2: Every part in the group stays.
whyWrong.3: Grouping doesn't change stereo.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, eq, a place for everything.

lessons.title: eq eight

song.why: three bands of eq decide how deep, how solid and how clear your bass sounds

lessons.learn: Lows, mids and highs, what lives where, and three bands of eq on your bass.
youCan: say roughly where lows, mids and highs sit
clean up a muddy sound with a small cut
shape your bass with three bands

say.mentor:
An eq splits a sound into ranges of frequency and lets you turn each one up or down. Roughly: the lows, from about 20 to 200 hz, are weight and boom. The mids, from about 200 hz to 3 khz, are the body of a sound. The highs, above about 3 khz, are bite, clarity and air.
Your bass lives mostly in the lows, but its mids and highs are what let you hear it on small speakers.
say.straight: Lows, about 20 to 200 hz: weight. Mids, 200 hz to 3 khz: body. Highs, above 3 khz: bite and air.
say.eli5: Every sound has a deep part, a middle part and a high part. An eq lets you turn each part up or down.

say.mentor:
A lot of muddy mixes have too much going on between about 200 and 500 hz, where many parts overlap. A small cut there often cleans a sound up more than any boost would.
Cutting first is a good habit: take away what's in the way before you add anything.
say.straight: Mud usually lives around 200 to 500 hz. A small cut there cleans things up. Cut before you boost.
say.eli5: When sounds get muddy, take a little bit away from the middle. Taking away often works better than adding.

deeper.title: eq eight in live
deeper.say: EQ Eight has eight bands. Each band has a shape: low cut and high cut remove everything past a frequency, shelves tilt a wide region up or down, a bell boosts or cuts around one point, and a notch removes one narrow frequency.

deeper.title: frequency, gain and q
deeper.say: Each band has three controls. Frequency is where it works, gain is how much it boosts or cuts, and Q is how wide or narrow the band is. A narrow Q is surgical, for hunting one ringing note. A wide Q is musical, for shaping tone.

deeper.title: mid and side
deeper.say: In M/S mode, EQ Eight works on the middle of the stereo picture and on the sides separately. Cutting the lows on the sides keeps the low end mono and tight.

say.mentor:
Your bass with three bands. Low is the weight: a little up for more boom, down if it's swamping your kick. Mid is the body, and where a bass turns muddy, so try a small cut. High is the edge that lets a bass come through on a phone speaker.
Keep the moves small and keep listening to the whole song.
say.straight: Low: weight, down if it swamps the kick. Mid: try a small cut for less mud. High: edge for small speakers.
say.eli5: Turn low for more or less boom. Turn mid down a little if it sounds muddy. Turn high for a bit of edge.

steps.q: Roughly where do the lows sit?
steps.why: About 20 to 200 hz is weight and boom.

whyWrong.1: That's the highs.
whyWrong.3: Each range has its own place.

steps.q: A sound is muddy. Where might you try a small cut?
steps.why: That's where lots of parts overlap and build up.

whyWrong.1: That's air, not mud.
whyWrong.2: That's below what most of us hear.
whyWrong.3: Boosting usually adds more mud.

steps.q: In EQ Eight, what does Q set?
options: how wide or narrow a band is
steps.why: Narrow for surgery, wide for tone.

whyWrong.1: That's the frequency control.
whyWrong.3: There are always eight.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, space, reverb and echo.

lessons.title: effects overview

song.why: one effect from each family on your lead shows you what each family is for

lessons.learn: The main families of effects, the problem each one solves, and one of each on your lead.
youCan: name the main families of effects
pick a family for a problem
try eq, drive, echo and reverb on your lead

say.mentor:
There are thousands of effects, but almost all of them belong to a handful of families. Learn the families and you can reach for the right tool fast, instead of guessing.
This plain synth note is a blank page. Every family would change it in its own way.
say.straight: Thousands of effects, a handful of families. Know the families and you know which tool to reach for.
say.eli5: There are lots of effects, but they come in a few families, like a family of cats and a family of dogs.

say.mentor:
Eq shapes tone by frequency. Dynamics, like compressors and limiters, control loud and quiet. Time effects, reverb and echo, put a sound in a space. Saturation, or drive, adds grit and warmth by roughing up the wave. Modulation, like chorus and phaser, makes a sound move by wobbling it with a slow wave called an lfo. Utility tools do plain jobs like gain and stereo width.
Each family fixes a different problem. Too dull is an eq job. Jumping between loud and quiet is a dynamics job.
say.straight: Eq: tone. Dynamics: loud and quiet. Time: reverb and echo. Saturation: grit. Modulation: movement. Utility: gain and width. Match the family to the problem.
say.eli5: Eq changes the tone. Dynamics change loud and quiet. Reverb and echo add space. Drive adds crunch. Pick the one that fixes your problem.

deeper.title: the families in live
deeper.say: Live's own devices cover every family: EQ Eight for eq, Compressor, Glue Compressor and Limiter for dynamics, Reverb, Hybrid Reverb and Delay for time, Saturator for drive, and Utility for gain and width.

deeper.title: fewer is better
deeper.say: Learn one effect in each family well before collecting more. The effects that come with your music program are often plenty. Switch each one off and on, and if you can't hear it helping, take it out.

deeper.title: insert or send
deeper.say: Reverb and delay usually go on a send that many parts share. It uses less processing power and puts everything in the same space.

say.mentor:
One effect from each family on your lead. High is eq: a little brighter or darker. Drive is saturation: grit. Echo and send are time: repeats, and a room.
Try each one on its own first, then together. Keep only the ones that make your lead better, and set the rest back to where they were.
say.straight: High is eq, drive is saturation, echo and send are time effects. Try each alone, then together. Keep what helps.
say.eli5: Try each knob on your tune, one at a time. Keep the ones that make it sound better.

steps.q: Which family is reverb in?
steps.why: Reverb and echo put a sound in a space.

whyWrong.1: Eq shapes tone by frequency.
whyWrong.3: Saturation adds grit.

steps.q: A part jumps between loud and quiet too much. Which family helps?
steps.why: A compressor evens out loud and quiet.

whyWrong.1: Reverb and echo add space, not control.
whyWrong.3: Eq is about tone, not loudness over time.

steps.q: What does drive do?
options: adds grit and warmth by roughing up the wave
puts the sound in a room
steps.why: Drive is saturation, the grit family.

whyWrong.1: That's reverb.
whyWrong.3: That's echo.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, space, reverb and echo.

lessons.title: sends and returns

song.why: sending your chords into a shared reverb puts them in the same room as your other parts

lessons.learn: What a send and a return are, why one shared reverb glues a mix, and how much of your chords to send.
youCan: say what a send and a return are
set how much of a part goes to the reverb
make a return track in Live

say.mentor: Picture a band playing in one hall. Everyone shares the same room, and that shared space is a big part of why they sound like one band. Mixes copy this with one reverb that every part can feed into, a little or a lot.
say.straight: One shared reverb puts every part in the same room, which helps them sound like one record.
say.eli5: If all your sounds play in the same big room, they sound like they belong together.

say.mentor:
A return is a channel that holds an effect, usually a reverb or a delay, and nothing else. A send is a knob on each part that decides how much of that part gets copied over to the return. The dry part keeps playing as it was, and the return adds the room underneath.
So with one reverb you can give the lead a lot, the chords some and the kick none. By default a send comes after the fader, so turning a part down turns its reverb down too.
say.straight: A return holds a shared effect. Each part's send sets how much goes to it. The dry part stays. Sends follow the fader by default.
say.eli5: There's one echo room. Each sound has a knob that says how much of it goes into the room.

deeper.title: returns in live
deeper.say: Cmd+Alt+T on a Mac or Ctrl+Alt+T on Windows makes a return track. Put a Reverb on it, and every track gets a send knob for it.

deeper.title: pre and post
deeper.say: Sends are post-fader by default, so the send follows the track's fader. Switch one to pre-fader and it ignores the fader, handy when you want the reverb to keep going while the dry track is turned down.

deeper.title: why share
deeper.say: One reverb on a return uses far less processing power than a reverb on every track, and it puts every part in the same room. Returns can even send to other returns.

say.mentor:
Here's your song. Send feeds your chords into the reverb, the same way a send feeds a return in Live. Turn it up and the chords move back into the room, behind your lead. Turn it down and they come close and dry.
Chords and pads often get more reverb than drums. Find the amount where they sit behind your lead without going blurry.
say.straight: Send sets how much of your chords goes to the reverb. Up moves them back, down brings them close. Stop before they blur.
say.eli5: Turn send up and your chords sound further away, in a big room. Stop before they get blurry.

steps.q: What does a send do?
options: copies some of a part to a return
steps.why: The dry part stays. A copy goes to the shared effect.

whyWrong.1: The dry sound keeps playing.
whyWrong.3: The part still plays.

steps.q: Why share one reverb across parts?
options: it puts every part in one room and uses less power
you can only have one effect
steps.why: One room glues the mix, and one reverb is lighter than many.

whyWrong.1: Tempo doesn't change.
whyWrong.2: You can have lots of effects.
whyWrong.3: It's about space, not level.

steps.q: By default, you turn a part's fader down. What happens to its reverb?
steps.why: Sends come after the fader by default, so they follow it.

whyWrong.1: Less part, less reverb.
whyWrong.3: It follows the fader down, it doesn't stop.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, glue, compression and loudness.

lessons.title: the browser

song.why: a different starting sound gives your lead a different character before you touch a single note

lessons.learn: What the browser in Live is for, how it's organised, and finding a new starting sound for your lead the way you'd flip through presets.
youCan: say what lives in Live's browser
audition sounds on your own part before you commit
pick a starting sound for your lead by ear

say.mentor:
Same note, three different sounds: a soft wave, a buzzy saw, a hollow square. Nothing about the melody changed, only the sound playing it. That's what browsing is really about. Most of the time you're not looking for notes, you're looking for the right voice to play them.
In Live, the place you go looking is called the browser.
say.straight: Same note, three sounds. Picking the sound that plays your part is most of what the browser in Live is for.
say.eli5: One note, three different voices singing it. Finding the right voice for your tune is a big part of making music.

say.mentor:
The browser is the panel down the left side of Live. It holds everything you can drag into a song: instrument sounds, drum kits, audio and midi effects, samples, plug-ins and packs, which are Ableton's own sound libraries.
You find something, click it to hear a preview, and drag it onto a track. That's it. Drag works in both views, so it doesn't matter whether you're in session or arrangement.
Live 12 added categories too, tags like bass or pads, so you can search by what a sound is instead of what someone named the file.
say.straight: The browser is Live's left panel: sounds, drums, effects, samples, plug-ins and packs. Preview a sound, drag it onto a track. Live 12 added tag categories for searching by type.
say.eli5: The browser is a big list of sounds on the left side of Live. Click one to hear it, then drag it onto a track to use it.

deeper.title: what each section holds
deeper.say: Sounds are instrument presets. Drums are kits and single hits. Instruments, audio effects and midi effects are Live's devices. Plug-ins are third party ones you've installed. Samples are audio files, including your own. Packs are Ableton's libraries, and you can add your own folders as places too.

deeper.title: similar sounds
deeper.say: Live 12 can also find samples that sound like the one you've picked, by listening to the audio rather than reading the name. There's a whole deeper lesson on it further down this path.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with your own lead playing. Turn wave and listen to your melody change voice, soft to buzzy to hollow. That's what clicking through presets in the browser feels like: same notes, new sound, until one makes you sit up.
Then use cutoff to darken or brighten whichever one you land on. Keep the one that suits your song.
say.straight: Your lead in your song. Wave flips its basic sound, like clicking through presets. Cutoff darkens or brightens it. Keep the one that fits.
say.eli5: Turn wave to give your tune a new voice. Turn cutoff to make it darker or brighter. Stop when you like how it sounds.

steps.q: What do you mostly use Live's browser for?
options: finding sounds and dragging them onto tracks
steps.why: It's your library. Find a sound, preview it, drag it onto a track.

whyWrong.1: Tempo is in the control bar at the top.
whyWrong.3: Export is in the file menu.

steps.q: Can you drag from the browser into both session and arrangement view?
options: yes, either view takes a drop
neither, you have to use a menu
steps.why: Both views accept sounds dragged from the browser.

whyWrong.1: Arrangement takes drops too.
whyWrong.3: Dragging is the main way in.

steps.q: Which Live version added categories to the browser?
steps.why: Categories arrived in Live 12, so you can search by what a sound is.

whyWrong.1: Too early.
whyWrong.3: One version too early.

steps.next: Your lead has its sound. Back to your song path, or carry on to preferences.

lessons.title: preferences

song.why: the tempo and key you settle on become your song's defaults, the place everything else starts from

lessons.learn: The settings you set once in Live and leave alone, and the two your song starts from every time: its tempo and its key.
youCan: open Live's preferences and say what the main tabs are for
explain the buffer size trade-off
set your song's default tempo and key by ear

say.mentor:
Before a single sound like this comes out of Live, a few quiet decisions have already been made: which sound card it talks to, how fast it has to answer you, where your plug-ins live. You set those once in preferences and forget about them.
Your song has defaults too, the tempo and key it always starts from. You'll set those here.
say.straight: Live's preferences hold the settings you set once: audio, midi, plug-ins. Your song has its own defaults, tempo and key. You'll set both kinds.
say.eli5: Before music plays, the computer needs a few settings, like where the sound comes out. You set those once. Your song also has a speed and a key it always starts with.

say.mentor:
Open preferences with cmd or ctrl and the comma key, the same shortcut most apps use for settings.
The audio tab is the important one. It picks your audio driver, the sample rate, and the buffer size. The buffer is a small chunk of sound the computer prepares before you hear it. Smaller means less latency, the delay between pressing a key and hearing it, but the computer has to work harder. Too small and you get clicks and glitches. 256 samples is a safe place to start.
say.straight: Cmd or ctrl and comma opens preferences. The audio tab sets driver, sample rate and buffer size. Lower buffer means less delay but more work for the computer. 256 samples is a safe default.
say.eli5: Press cmd and comma (or ctrl and comma) to open the settings. The most important bit is the buffer. Small buffer, quick sound, but the computer works hard. Big buffer, a bit of delay, but no crackles.

deeper.title: the other tabs
deeper.say: Link, tempo and midi is where you switch on controllers and Ableton Link. The plug-ins settings tell Live which folders to scan, and if a plug-in goes missing, rescanning there is the first thing to try. The library tab sets where packs install.

deeper.title: recording versus mixing
deeper.say: When you're recording, a small buffer keeps what you play feeling instant. When you're mixing a big song, nothing needs to be instant, so a larger buffer gives the computer room and stops the clicks.

say.mentor:
Preferences are the settings for Live. Tempo belongs to your song, so in Live it sits in the control bar at the top of each set instead. Think of this knob as your song's default: the speed it opens at every time you come back to it.
Play it at a few speeds and pick the one that feels most like home.
say.straight: Tempo lives in the control bar, not preferences, because it belongs to the song. Set your song's default tempo.
say.eli5: Pick the speed your song always starts at. Try a few and choose the one you like most.

steps.hint: Most house sits between 120 and 128.

say.mentor: The key is the other default. It's the set of notes your bass, chords and lead all draw from. Minor tends to feel darker, major brighter. Flip between them and listen to your own parts move to the new notes, then keep the one that fits the mood.
say.straight: Your song's key, minor or major. Every melodic part follows it. Pick the mood you want.
say.eli5: Minor sounds a bit moody, major sounds sunny. Try both and keep the one you like.

steps.q: Which shortcut opens Live's preferences?
steps.why: Comma is the usual settings shortcut, and Live follows it.

whyWrong.1: That's usually print.
whyWrong.2: Tab switches between session and arrangement.
whyWrong.3: Not a Live shortcut for this.

steps.q: What happens when you make the buffer size smaller?
options: less delay, but the computer works harder
steps.why: A small buffer answers faster, but the computer has less time per chunk.

whyWrong.1: That's what a bigger buffer does.
whyWrong.3: Too small and you'll hear clicks.

steps.q: Why is tempo in the control bar and not in preferences?
options: it belongs to each song, not to Live
steps.why: Preferences are for Live itself. Each song keeps its own tempo.

whyWrong.1: Preferences hold plenty of numbers, like buffer size.
whyWrong.2: You can change it any time.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is part of every set.

steps.next: Your song has its defaults. Back to your song path, or on to controllers.

lessons.title: push and controllers

song.why: drums played in with your fingers carry the small pushes and pulls that make a beat feel played

lessons.learn: What a controller is, what Push does that other controllers don't, and finger drumming a bar into your song on pads.
youCan: say what a controller does for Live
name Push's two main pad layouts
finger drum a bar of your beat on pads

say.mentor:
A beat like this can be clicked in with a mouse, one note at a time. Or you can play it, with your fingers on pads, the way a drummer would. Playing it is faster, and it sounds more alive because your hits are never perfectly even.
A controller is the box that lets you do that: pads, knobs and faders that play Live.
say.straight: You can click a beat in, or play it on pads. A controller is a box of pads, knobs and faders that plays Live.
say.eli5: You can draw a beat with the mouse, or you can tap it on squares with your fingers like a little drum kit. The box with the squares is called a controller.

say.mentor:
Push is Ableton's own controller. It has 64 pads that know how hard you hit them, called velocity sensitive, plus knobs and a screen. Plug it in and Live finds it straight away.
The clever part is that the pads change with what you're doing. On a drum track they become drum pads, 16 for the sounds and the rest a step sequencer for whichever pad you picked. On a synth track they're laid out in your song's scale, so every pad is a note in key and wrong notes simply aren't there.
say.straight: Push has 64 velocity sensitive pads, knobs and a screen. Drum mode gives 16 drum pads plus a step sequencer. Melodic mode lays the pads out in your scale, so no wrong notes.
say.eli5: Push is Ableton's controller with 64 squares to tap. Hit harder and it plays louder. On drums the squares are your drum sounds. On a synth every square plays a note that fits your song.

deeper.title: other controllers
deeper.say: Push isn't the only option. Controllers like Akai's APC and Novation's Launchpad also work closely with Live, and any midi controller can be set up under preferences, in the link, tempo and midi tab, as a control surface.

deeper.title: push 3 on its own
deeper.say: Push 3 Standalone has a computer inside, so it can run Live with no laptop at all. That has its own deeper lesson further down this path.

say.mentor: These are your song's drum pads. Press rec, wait out the count-in, and finger drum eight hits. Kick on the beats, clap or hats between them, whatever feels good. Use two or three fingers, like you would on Push. Hit some harder than others and listen to the difference.
say.straight: Your drum pads. Press rec, wait for the count-in, then play eight hits with a few fingers. Vary how hard you hit.
say.eli5: Press rec, wait for four ticks, then tap the drum squares eight times. Try using more than one finger.

steps.q: What does a controller do?
options: lets you play and control Live with pads, knobs and faders
steps.why: It's hands-on control of Live, instead of the mouse.

whyWrong.1: It doesn't change how fast the computer runs.
whyWrong.3: You still need speakers or headphones.

steps.q: What does velocity sensitive mean on a pad?
steps.why: The pad measures how hard you hit it and turns that into loudness.

whyWrong.1: Lights are separate from velocity.
whyWrong.2: Velocity is about force, not speed of the song.
whyWrong.3: Colour is just a display thing.

steps.q: In Push's melodic mode, why can't you play a wrong note?
options: the pads only hold notes in your scale
Push corrects mistakes after you play
steps.why: Out-of-scale notes just aren't on the grid.

whyWrong.1: Nothing is corrected later. The notes aren't there to begin with.
whyWrong.2: Nothing is muted. They're left off the layout.
whyWrong.3: You can play any note in the scale, and chords too.

steps.next: Those hits are in your song now. Back to your song path, or on to midi mapping.

lessons.title: midi mapping

song.why: a filter you can sweep by hand turns a static lead into one that rises and falls with the track

lessons.learn: Tying a knob on a controller to any control in Live, and finding the one on your lead you'd most want under your hand.
youCan: map a hardware knob to a control in Live
limit a mapping to a useful range
sweep your lead's filter by ear

say.mentor:
A held synth note on its own. Now imagine reaching out and slowly opening it up from dark and muffled to bright and buzzy, in time with the music. That move is half of dance music, and it's much more fun with a real knob than a mouse.
Midi mapping is how you tie a knob on a controller to any control in Live.
say.straight: One synth note. Sweeping its brightness by hand is a classic move. Midi mapping ties a hardware knob to a control in Live.
say.eli5: Listen to this note. What if you could turn a real knob and make it go from muffled to bright? Midi mapping lets you do that.

say.mentor:
Press cmd or ctrl and m and Live goes into midi map mode. Every control you can map gets highlighted. Click the one you want, wiggle a knob on your controller, and they're joined. Press cmd or ctrl and m again to get out and play.
The mapping is saved with your set, so the knob still does the same job next time you open the song.
say.straight: Cmd or ctrl and m enters midi map mode. Click a control, move a hardware knob, done. Press it again to exit. Mappings save with the set.
say.eli5: Press cmd and m. Click the thing you want to control, then wiggle a real knob. Now that knob controls it. Press cmd and m again when you're done.

deeper.title: min and max
deeper.say: Each mapping has a min and a max. Set them and the full turn of your knob only covers part of the control's range, so you get fine control over the bit that sounds good. Set min higher than max and the knob works backwards.

deeper.title: when the knob and the screen disagree
deeper.say: If your knob is at one place and the control on screen is somewhere else, the takeover mode decides what happens. None jumps straight to the knob. Pickup waits until the knob passes the current value, so nothing jumps. Value scaling eases the two together.

deeper.title: key map mode
deeper.say: Cmd or ctrl and k does the same thing with your computer keyboard: click a control, press a key, and that key now controls it. Handy on a laptop with no controller.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with your lead playing. Cutoff is the knob you'd map: the filter that decides how much brightness gets through. Sweep it slowly from closed to open while the song plays and feel the lift.
Res, short for resonance, adds a ring right at the cutoff point, which makes a sweep sound even more obvious. Leave both where your lead sounds best.
say.straight: Your lead in your song. Cutoff is the one you'd map. Sweep it closed to open. Res adds a ring at the cutoff. Leave both where they sound best.
say.eli5: Turn cutoff slowly and your tune goes from muffled to bright. Res makes it sing a bit more. Stop where you like it.

steps.q: Which shortcut turns on midi map mode?
steps.why: M for midi map.

whyWrong.1: That's key map mode, for the computer keyboard.
whyWrong.3: Tab switches views.

steps.q: How do you map a knob once you're in map mode?
options: click the control, then move the knob
move the knob, then save the song
drag the knob onto the track
steps.why: Click what you want, wiggle the hardware, and they're joined.

whyWrong.1: Saving keeps it, but you still have to click the control first.
whyWrong.3: You click, not type.

steps.q: Why set a mapping's min and max?
options: so the knob only covers the useful part of the range
to map two knobs at once
steps.why: A smaller range means finer control over the bit that sounds good.

whyWrong.1: It changes the range, not the volume.
whyWrong.2: Mappings still save with the set.
whyWrong.3: Min and max are for one mapping.

steps.next: Your lead's filter is set. Back to your song path, or on to Push 3.

lessons.title: push 3 workflow

song.why: a melody played in on in-key pads keeps your hands moving and your eyes off the screen

lessons.learn: How Push 3 lets you make a whole track without the mouse, and playing your lead in on pads that only hold notes in your song's key.
youCan: say how Push's pads change with the track you pick
name the drum and melodic step sequencer layouts
play a lead line in on in-key pads

say.mentor:
Low note, high note. On a piano keyboard there are black and white keys between them, and plenty of those would sound wrong in your song. Push lays its pads out differently: only the notes in your key, in a grid, so every pad you touch fits.
That idea is a big part of why people make whole tracks on Push without touching the mouse.
say.straight: Push's melodic pads only hold notes in your key, so every pad fits. It's built so you can make a whole track without the mouse.
say.eli5: A low note and a high note. Push has a grid of squares where every square plays a note that fits your song, so you can't hit a wrong one.

steps.title: the whole track from one box

say.mentor:
Push 3 follows whatever you've selected in Live. Pick a drum track and the pads become drum pads. Pick a synth and they become notes in your scale. The knobs, called encoders, always control the device you've got selected, and the screen shows what they're doing.
From there you can add tracks, browse for sounds, play, record into clips and launch scenes, all from the hardware.
say.straight: Push 3 mirrors your selection in Live. Drum track, drum pads. Synth, in-scale notes. Encoders control the selected device. You can add, browse, play and record from Push.
say.eli5: Push copies what you pick on the computer. Drums, and the squares become drums. A synth, and they become notes. The knobs change the sound you picked.

deeper.title: step sequencing on push
deeper.say: In drum mode, 16 pads are your drum sounds and the other 48 become a step sequencer for whichever pad you've picked. There's also a 64 pad mode where the whole grid is a step sequencer for a melody.

deeper.title: per-finger expression
deeper.say: Push 3's pads support mpe, which means each finger can bend, slide and press its own note. There's a deeper lesson on mpe further down this path.

say.mentor: These keys are your lead, and like Push's melodic mode they only hold notes in your song's key. The first and last are the home note. Press rec, wait out the count-in, and play eight notes. Don't think too hard. Start on the home note, wander, and come back to it. Every key fits, so nothing can go badly wrong.
say.straight: In-key notes for your lead, like Push's melodic mode. Press rec, wait for the count-in, play eight notes. Start and end on the home note, first or last.
say.eli5: Every key here fits your song. Press rec, wait for four ticks, then tap eight keys. Try starting on the first one.

steps.q: On a synth track, what are Push's pads laid out in?
steps.why: Melodic mode shows only the notes in your key.

whyWrong.1: A piano has every note. Push's melodic mode leaves the out-of-key ones off.
whyWrong.2: That's what you get on a drum track.
whyWrong.3: The layout is fixed to your scale.

steps.q: What do Push's encoders control?
steps.why: They follow your selection, so they're always on the device in front of you.

whyWrong.1: They follow whatever's selected.
whyWrong.3: Push sets them up for you.

steps.q: You select a drum track in Live. What happens on Push?
options: the pads stay as notes in your scale
steps.why: Push follows your selection, so a drum track gets drum pads.

whyWrong.1: It changes straight away.
whyWrong.3: That's what you get on a synth track.

steps.next: Your lead line is in. Back to your song path, or on to Push 3 standalone.

lessons.title: push 3 standalone

song.why: a song laid out as sections you can bring in and out is a song you can perform, with or without a laptop

lessons.learn: What it means for Push 3 to run Live with no laptop, and laying your song out as sections you could launch one after another on stage.
youCan: say what Push 3 Standalone does that a normal controller doesn't
say how projects move between Push and a computer
lay your song out as sections to perform

say.mentor: A groove like this, played out of a club system. Usually there's a laptop behind it, running Live, with a controller plugged in. Push 3 Standalone takes the laptop away. The computer is inside the box.
say.straight: Normally a laptop runs Live and a controller plays it. Push 3 Standalone has the computer built in.
say.eli5: Usually you need a laptop to play music like this. Push 3 Standalone has a little computer inside, so you don't.

say.mentor:
Push 3 Standalone runs Live's audio engine on the hardware itself, with a built-in audio interface for sound in and out. You can start a song, add instruments, record and play a whole set on it. Max for Live devices run on it too.
Projects are saved on Push and open in Live on your computer just as they are, the same set format, no converting. Start on the couch, finish at the desk, play it out on Push.
say.straight: Push 3 Standalone runs Live's engine inside, with its own audio interface. Projects open on your computer as they are, same format.
say.eli5: Push 3 Standalone is a whole music studio in one box. You can make a song on it, then open the same song on your computer later.

deeper.title: before a gig
deeper.say: Samples have to be on Push's own drive, so copy them over before you go. Push's processor is good but not endless, so test a heavy set before the show and freeze the hungriest tracks, the same as you would on a laptop.

deeper.title: in controller mode
deeper.say: Plug Push 3 into a computer and it can work as a normal Push controller instead, playing the Live on your laptop.

say.mentor:
To play a song out, you need it in pieces you can bring in one after another. On Push those pieces are scenes, rows of clips you launch together. Here they're your sections.
Rows are your parts, columns are sections. Tap a cell to switch that part off or on there. Make an intro that's thin, a drop where everything plays, a break that takes something away. Play it through and shape it until it works as a set.
say.straight: Performing means launching sections one after another, scenes on Push. Rows are parts, columns are sections. Tap cells to switch parts off or on, then play it through.
say.eli5: Tap the squares to turn sounds on and off in each part of your song. Press play and listen to it go from quiet to big and back.

steps.q: What does Push 3 Standalone not need?
steps.why: Live runs on the hardware itself.

whyWrong.1: It still needs power.
whyWrong.2: The pads are how you play it.
whyWrong.3: You still need sounds to play.

steps.q: How does a project get from Push 3 to Live on your computer?
options: it opens as it is, same set format
you export an mp3 and import it
it has to be rebuilt by hand
steps.why: Same format on both, so no converting.

whyWrong.1: That would lose all your parts and devices.
whyWrong.3: Moving between them is the point.

steps.q: On Push, what do you call a row of clips you launch together?
steps.why: Scenes are how a song becomes sections you can play one after another.

whyWrong.1: A preset is a saved sound.
whyWrong.2: A mapping ties a knob to a control.
whyWrong.3: The buffer is an audio setting.

steps.next: Your song is in sections you could perform. Back to your song path, or on to tempo following.

lessons.title: tempo following

song.why: when your song follows a live drummer, it speeds up and settles with the room instead of fighting it

lessons.learn: How Live can listen to a drummer and follow their tempo, and hearing your own song move with a player who drifts.
youCan: say what Tempo Follower listens to
say what kind of sound it follows best
hear your song at the speeds a live drummer might push it to

say.mentor:
A kick, perfectly steady. A machine never drifts. A human drummer does, a little faster when the room gets excited, a little slower in a breakdown. That's part of why a band feels alive.
Normally the band has to follow Live's click. Live can also do it the other way round, and follow the drummer.
say.straight: Machines keep perfect time, drummers drift. Usually the band follows Live. Live can also follow the drummer.
say.eli5: A computer keeps a perfectly even beat. A real drummer speeds up and slows down a tiny bit. Live can listen to the drummer and follow along.

say.mentor:
Tempo Follower arrived in Live 11. It listens to an audio input, usually a mic on the kick drum, works out the tempo from the hits, and keeps changing Live's tempo to match. Every loop, every synced effect, every clip in your set rides along with the person playing.
It follows clear, punchy hits best. A kick or a click works well. Soft pads or long sustained sounds give it nothing to lock onto, and sparse or busy syncopated playing can make it wander.
say.straight: Tempo Follower (Live 11) listens to an audio input, works out the tempo and moves Live's tempo to match. Clear hits like a kick work best. Pads and sparse playing make it wander.
say.eli5: Tempo Follower listens to a real drum and makes your song go the same speed as the drummer. It works best with a loud, clear kick.

deeper.title: switching it on
deeper.say: Pick the input it listens to in preferences, in the link, tempo and midi tab. Then turn it on in the control bar at the top of Live. Turn it off again when you go back to programmed parts, or your tempo will keep following whatever comes in.

deeper.title: sudden changes
deeper.say: A big jump in tempo takes a few bars to settle while it catches up. Feed it a clean kick mic rather than the whole band and it tracks more steadily.

say.mentor:
Here's your song. Imagine a drummer playing along with it. They start at your tempo, then the crowd gets going and they push. Turn the knob up a few bpm and listen to your whole song follow, just as it would with Tempo Follower on. Then bring it back down for the breakdown.
When you're done, leave it at the tempo your song feels best at.
say.straight: Your song, following an imaginary drummer. Push the tempo up a few bpm, bring it back, then leave it where it feels best.
say.eli5: Pretend a drummer is speeding up. Turn the knob up a little and your song follows. Then turn it back and pick the speed you like best.

steps.hint: Small moves, two or three bpm, are what a real drummer drifts by.

steps.q: What does Tempo Follower listen to?
options: an audio input, like a kick drum mic
steps.why: It hears the hits and works out the tempo from them.

whyWrong.1: It listens to audio, not midi notes.
whyWrong.2: It needs a rhythm, not a level.
whyWrong.3: It's listening to a performer.

steps.q: Which sound would Tempo Follower follow best?
steps.why: Sharp hits give it something clear to measure.

whyWrong.1: A pad has no clear hits.
whyWrong.2: Held notes don't mark the beat.
whyWrong.3: There's nothing to hear.

steps.q: Which Live version added Tempo Follower?
steps.why: It arrived in Live 11.

whyWrong.1: Too early.
whyWrong.3: It was already there by Live 12.

steps.next: Your song's tempo is set. Back to your song path, or on to Ableton Link.

lessons.title: ableton link in practice

song.why: a tempo you share with another app or a friend's setup lets your song lock in with theirs, no cables

lessons.learn: Getting Live in time with another app or device over wifi, the bits that trip people up, and choosing the tempo your song brings to a jam.
youCan: turn on Link and join another device on the same network
say what start stop sync adds
spot the network problems that stop Link working

say.mentor:
Two grooves at the same tempo, first one, then the other, then both together. When they line up like that they sound like one track. When they don't, it falls apart into a mess of flams.
Getting two setups lined up used to mean midi cables and one machine in charge. Ableton Link does it over wifi.
say.straight: Two grooves, same tempo, then together in time. Ableton Link keeps separate apps and devices in time over wifi.
say.eli5: Two beats playing at the same speed, then together. They fit like one song. Link helps two computers or apps play together like that, without cables.

say.mentor:
Click the link button in Live's control bar. Open another app that supports Link on the same wifi network, another laptop running Live, an iPad app, a drum machine, and switch Link on there too. They find each other on their own, and Live shows how many others have joined.
Now change the tempo on either one and the other follows. Nobody's in charge. Every device is equal, so anyone can move the tempo and anyone can leave without stopping the rest.
say.straight: Click link in the control bar, switch Link on in another app on the same wifi. They find each other. Any device can change the tempo and the rest follow.
say.eli5: Press the link button, then turn on link in another app on the same wifi. Now they play at the same speed. Change the speed on one and the other changes too.

deeper.title: start stop sync
deeper.say: Link shares tempo and the beat by default, but not play and stop. Turn on start stop sync and pressing play on one device starts the others too. Leave it off if each player wants to drop in on their own.

deeper.title: when they can't find each other
deeper.say: Everyone has to be on the same network. Guest wifi that keeps devices apart, firewalls and vpns can all hide peers from each other. For shows, a phone hotspot or your own router is steadier than public wifi.

say.mentor:
Here's your song. Imagine a friend's laptop has just joined over Link at 124 and they nudge it to 128. Your song goes with them. Try a few speeds and hear how your song feels at each one.
Then pick the tempo you'd bring to the jam, the one you'd set before anyone else joins.
say.straight: Your song at the tempos a Link jam might move through. Try a few, then pick the one you'd start at.
say.eli5: Pretend a friend is changing the speed from their computer. Try a few speeds, then pick the one you like best.

steps.q: What does Link use to keep devices in time?
options: the local wifi or wired network
steps.why: Devices on the same network find each other. No cables.

whyWrong.1: No cables needed.
whyWrong.3: It shares tempo over the network, not through sound.

steps.q: Who's in charge of the tempo in a Link session?
options: nobody, any device can change it
steps.why: Every peer is equal, and the others follow any change.

whyWrong.1: There's no leader.
whyWrong.2: Other apps can move it too.
whyWrong.3: Speed of the computer doesn't matter.

steps.q: Two laptops have Link on but can't see each other. What's a likely cause?
options: they're not on the same network
the songs are in different keys
steps.why: Guest wifi, firewalls and vpns can keep peers apart.

whyWrong.1: Tempo doesn't stop them finding each other.
whyWrong.2: The sounds don't matter to Link.
whyWrong.3: Link doesn't deal with keys.

steps.next: Your song's tempo is set. Back to your song path, or on to how Link works.

lessons.title: ableton link

song.why: matching tempo is only half of being in time; your song's downbeat has to land with everyone else's too

lessons.learn: What Ableton Link actually shares, why the same tempo isn't enough on its own, and how joining mid-song still lands you on the beat.
youCan: say the two things Link keeps the same across devices
explain why tempo alone isn't enough
say who can use Link

say.mentor:
Two grooves at the same tempo. Notice they only sound like one track once their beats land at the same moment. If the second one came in half a beat late, same tempo, it would sound wrong the whole way through.
So being in time takes two things: the same speed, and the same place in the beat.
say.straight: Same tempo isn't enough. The beats also have to land together. Being in time means same speed and same position.
say.eli5: Two beats at the same speed. They only fit when the booms happen together. Same speed and same moment.

say.mentor:
Link shares both. The tempo, and the beat phase, which is where everyone is in the bar right now. That means every device hits beat one at the same moment, not just at the same speed.
It's also why you can join a session that's already playing. Switch Link on halfway through and your app lines itself up with the group's beat straight away. Nobody has to stop and count in again.
say.straight: Link shares tempo and beat phase, where you are in the bar. Everyone hits beat one together. Join mid-play and you lock to the group's beat straight away.
say.eli5: Link makes everyone go the same speed and hit the big first beat at the same time. You can even join in the middle and it lines you up.

deeper.title: free and open
deeper.say: Link is free and open, so any developer can build it into their app. That's why it works with so many things: other laptops running Live, Push, plenty of iPad and phone music apps, DJ software and some hardware.

deeper.title: where to find it
deeper.say: The link button is in Live's control bar, and the settings are in preferences, in the link, tempo and midi tab. Tempo changes from another device ease in rather than jumping.

say.mentor:
Here's your song, looping. Watch the beat lights: one, two, three, four. That position in the bar is the phase Link shares. Change the tempo and the lights speed up or slow down, but beat one still comes round at the top of every bar. On Link, every device would hit it with you.
Leave your song at the tempo you like.
say.straight: Your song looping. The beat lights are the phase. Change tempo, and beat one still lands at the top of each bar. Leave it where you like.
say.eli5: Watch the lights count one to four. Turn the knob and they go faster or slower. Pick the speed you like best.

steps.q: What two things does Link keep the same across devices?
steps.why: Same speed and same place in the bar.

whyWrong.1: Volume stays with each device.
whyWrong.3: Each device keeps its own sounds.

steps.q: Why isn't the same tempo enough on its own?
options: the beats also have to land at the same moment
steps.why: Same speed but half a beat apart still sounds wrong.

whyWrong.1: Tempo itself holds steady.
whyWrong.2: Level has nothing to do with timing.
whyWrong.3: Every device plays together.

steps.q: You switch Link on while a jam is already playing. What happens?
options: you lock straight onto the group's beat
everyone has to stop and restart
your app starts a new tempo
steps.why: Link lines you up with the group as soon as you join.

whyWrong.1: Nobody stops.
whyWrong.3: Nothing gets muted.

steps.next: That's Link. Back to your song path, or on to cv tools.

lessons.title: cv tools

song.why: a bass whose filter opens on every note is the sound a modular synth makes when Live is playing it

lessons.learn: What control voltage is, how Live's CV Tools let your song play a modular synth, and the classic modular move on your own bass: an envelope opening the filter on every note.
youCan: say what cv is and what pitch and gate do
name the main CV Tools devices
shape your bass the way a modular voice would

say.mentor: One synth note, starting and stopping. In a modular synth, a rack of separate boxes joined with patch cables, that start and stop is a voltage. One wire says how high the note is, another says when it's on. It's called control voltage, cv for short, and it's the language modular gear speaks.
say.straight: A note on and off. Modular synths control that with voltages on cables, called cv: one for pitch, one for on and off.
say.eli5: In some synths made of lots of little boxes, electricity on a wire tells the sound what note to play and when to start and stop.

say.mentor:
CV Tools is a free pack of Max for Live devices that lets Live talk to a modular. CV Instrument turns the notes on a midi track into two signals: pitch, usually one volt for every octave, and a gate, which is on while the note is held and off when it ends. The gate is what starts the modular's envelopes.
The signals go out of your audio interface like sound. That only works with an interface whose outputs are dc coupled, which means they can hold a steady voltage. Most normal ones block it.
say.straight: CV Tools is a free Max for Live pack. CV Instrument turns midi notes into pitch (usually one volt per octave) and gate (on while held). It needs a dc coupled audio interface.
say.eli5: CV Tools lets Live send notes to a modular synth as electricity. One signal says which note, another says when it starts and stops.

deeper.title: the other devices
deeper.say: CV LFO and the other cv modulators send movement out to the modular. CV Triggers sends clock and reset pulses to hardware sequencers. CV In works the other way, reading a voltage from the modular so it can move controls inside Live.

deeper.title: calibrate first
deeper.say: Run the calibration on CV Instrument against your oscillator. Skip it and notes drift out of tune as you go up the keyboard. A few vintage synths use a different pitch standard, hertz per volt, so check before you patch.

say.mentor:
Here's your song, with your bass. On a modular, the gate from Live would fire an envelope, and that envelope would open the filter on every note. That's what env does here: it sets how far each note opens the filter before it closes again.
Pull cutoff down so the bass starts dark, then bring env up and hear every note bark open. Res sharpens the edge. That squelch is the sound of so many modular basslines.
say.straight: Your bass. Env is how far each note opens the filter, the job a gate and envelope do on a modular. Cutoff down, env up, res for bite.
say.eli5: Turn cutoff down so the bass sounds dark. Turn env up and every note opens up bright for a moment. Res makes it squelchy.

steps.q: What is cv?
options: control voltage, how modular synths send values on cables
steps.why: A voltage on a wire carries pitch, gate or movement.

whyWrong.1: It's a signal, not a file.
whyWrong.2: It's what a modular understands, not a controller.
whyWrong.3: It's not an effect.

steps.q: What does a gate signal do?
options: stays on while a note is held and starts envelopes
sets how high the note is
steps.why: Gate is on and off. Pitch is the other signal.

whyWrong.1: That's the pitch signal.
whyWrong.2: Gate is per note, not tempo.
whyWrong.3: Nothing to do with reverb.

steps.q: Why does CV Tools need a dc coupled audio interface?
options: it can hold a steady voltage, which most interfaces block
steps.why: Cv needs steady voltages to get out of the interface.

whyWrong.1: Volume isn't the issue.
whyWrong.3: Quality isn't the issue either.

steps.next: Your bass opens on every note. Back to your song path, or on to external instruments.

lessons.title: external instrument

song.why: a lead with a bit of grit and drift has the character people go looking for in hardware synths

lessons.learn: How Live's External Instrument puts a hardware synth on a track like any software one, and giving your lead some of that hardware character.
youCan: say what External Instrument sends and receives
say why hardware latency needs setting
give your lead a rougher, wider, more hardware-like sound

say.mentor: A soft wave, a saw, a square. Every hardware synth starts from shapes like these, but each one adds its own colour: slightly uneven tuning, a circuit that grits up when you push it. People love that character, and they want to use it inside Live without a separate rig.
say.straight: Three basic shapes. Hardware synths start from these and add their own colour. External Instrument brings that into Live.
say.eli5: Three sounds. Real synth boxes make sounds like these, each with its own flavour. Live can play them too.

say.mentor:
External Instrument is a device you put on a midi track. It sends the track's notes out to your hardware synth through your interface, and brings the synth's audio back in, all on that one track. To Live it looks like any other instrument. You can record it, automate it and run it through Live's effects.
The trip out to the synth and back takes a moment. The hardware latency setting on the device makes up for it, so the hardware lands in time with everything else.
say.straight: External Instrument goes on a midi track. Notes out to the hardware, audio back in, one track. Set hardware latency so it lands in time.
say.eli5: External Instrument sends your notes to a real synth box and brings its sound back into Live, so it works like any other instrument.

deeper.title: setting it up
deeper.say: Pick the midi port and channel the synth listens on, and the audio input it comes back on. Set the synth to one midi channel rather than all of them, so it doesn't play notes meant for something else. The return needs its own input, not one you're already using.

deeper.title: committing
deeper.say: When you're happy with a part, record the hardware's audio onto an audio track. Then the synth is free to play something else.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with your lead. Give it some hardware character. Pick a wave, then bring in detune, which pulls its oscillators slightly apart so it sounds wider and less perfect. Then add drive, which pushes it until it grits up, like a circuit being leaned on.
Go too far and it gets messy. Find the point where it sounds like it came out of a box with knobs.
say.straight: Your lead. Wave picks the shape, detune pulls it slightly out of line for width, drive adds grit. Stop before it gets messy.
say.eli5: Pick a sound with wave. Turn detune up a bit to make it wobbly and wide. Turn drive up for a rough edge.

steps.q: What does External Instrument do?
options: sends notes to hardware and brings its audio back on one track
makes a software copy of the synth
steps.why: Notes out, audio back in, one track.

whyWrong.1: It sends midi out and gets audio back.
whyWrong.3: The real hardware still makes the sound.

steps.q: What kind of track does External Instrument go on?
steps.why: It plays notes, so it lives where notes live.

whyWrong.1: It needs notes to send.
whyWrong.3: Returns are for effects.

steps.q: Why set the hardware latency?
options: so the hardware's sound lands in time with everything else
steps.why: The round trip takes time, and the setting makes up for it.

whyWrong.1: It's about timing, not volume.
whyWrong.3: It's about timing.

steps.next: Your lead has some grit. Back to your song path, or on to linked-track editing.

lessons.title: linked-track editing

song.why: taking two parts out of the same section together keeps them locked as one move instead of two

lessons.learn: Why some tracks need every edit made to all of them at once, how Live's linked-track editing does that, and making one cut across two of your parts.
youCan: say what linked-track editing does
say when you'd link tracks and when you wouldn't
take two of your parts out of a section together

say.mentor:
A drum kit recorded for real often has a mic on every drum: one on the kick, one on the snare, two overhead. Each mic catches the same performance from a different spot, so they all end up as separate tracks that have to stay perfectly lined up.
Cut bar 17 on the kick track but not the overheads, and the kit falls apart. Every edit has to happen to every track at once.
say.straight: Multi-mic drums are several tracks of one performance. Every edit has to hit all of them at once, or they fall out of line.
say.eli5: Sometimes one drummer is recorded with lots of microphones, and each one becomes its own track. If you cut one, you have to cut them all the same way.

say.mentor:
In Live's arrangement view, select the tracks and choose link tracks. From then on, a split, a trim, a move or a fade on one of them happens on all of them, in the same place. It's made for multi-mic drums, stems, and any parts that have to stay aligned.
You can unlink them any time. Don't link parts that are meant to move on their own, like a delay throw you've nudged off the grid, or you'll drag them along by accident.
say.straight: In arrangement view, select tracks and link them. Splits, trims, moves and fades then hit all of them. Unlink any time. Don't link parts that should move on their own.
say.eli5: Live can glue tracks together so when you cut one, the others get cut in the same place too. You can unglue them whenever you like.

deeper.title: arrangement only
deeper.say: Linking is for arrangement view, where your song runs left to right. Clips in session view are separate from each other and aren't linked.

deeper.title: what gets shared
deeper.say: Structural edits are shared: splits, trims, moving clips and nudges. Check whether tracks are linked before a creative edit, so you don't cut something you meant to leave alone.

say.mentor:
Here's your song as sections. Rows are your parts, columns are sections. Treat two of them as linked, say your kick and your bass, and make the same edit to both: switch them both off in the same section, so they drop out together and come back together.
Play it through. Hear how the two moving as one makes the gap feel deliberate.
say.straight: Your song as sections. Pick two parts, like kick and bass, and switch both off in the same section. Play it and listen to them leave and return together.
say.eli5: Pick two sounds, like the boom and the bass. Turn both off in the same part of the song. Press play and hear them go away and come back together.

steps.q: What does linked-track editing do?
options: applies the same edit to every linked track at once
copies one track's sound onto another
steps.why: One cut, every linked track.

whyWrong.1: The tracks stay separate.
whyWrong.2: Each track keeps its own sound.
whyWrong.3: It's about edits, not level.

steps.q: Which is the best fit for linking?
options: a drum kit recorded with several mics
a lead and a pad that move separately
a delay throw nudged off the grid
steps.why: Several mics on one performance have to stay aligned.

whyWrong.1: They're meant to move on their own.
whyWrong.2: One track has nothing to link with.
whyWrong.3: Linking would drag it back with everything else.

steps.q: Which view is linked-track editing for?
steps.why: It's for edits along the timeline in arrangement.

whyWrong.1: Session clips stay separate.
whyWrong.3: Preferences are settings for Live.

steps.next: Two parts now move as one. Back to your song path, or on to sound similarity search.

lessons.title: sound similarity search

song.why: swapping your drums for ones with a different texture changes the whole feel without touching the pattern

lessons.learn: How Live 12 finds sounds by what they sound like instead of what they're called, and trying your own beat on a different kit.
youCan: say what sound similarity search compares
say what makes its results better or worse
choose your song's kit by ear

say.mentor:
A kick, a clap, some hats. Now imagine hunting for a kick a bit like that one in a library of thousands, named things like kick_final_v2. The names tell you almost nothing. You'd have to listen to every one.
Live 12 can do the listening for you.
say.straight: Finding a sound like this one by file name is slow, because names say little about the sound. Live 12 can search by sound instead.
say.eli5: Imagine looking for a boom like this one in a giant box of thousands of sounds. The names don't help. Live 12 can listen for you.

say.mentor:
Sound similarity search is new in Live 12. Pick a sample in the browser, ask for similar ones, and Live compares the audio itself, how bright it is, how punchy, its character, and lists the samples in your library that sound closest.
It's a score, not a perfect match, so preview what comes back. And it can only find what's in your own library, so the more you have, the more it can find.
say.straight: Live 12 compares the audio, not the name, and lists the closest samples in your library. Results are a score, so preview them.
say.eli5: Pick a sound, and Live finds others that sound a bit like it, by listening, not by reading the name.

deeper.title: what helps and what doesn't
deeper.say: Very short samples give it less to listen to, so results get looser. A sample drowned in reverb confuses it, because the tail takes over. Heavily distorted or pitched sounds can come back with surprises.

deeper.title: narrowing it down
deeper.say: Combine it with the browser's filters and categories to keep only, say, kicks, and surf outward from one sound you love to ones you'd never have found by name.

say.mentor:
Here's your own drum pattern on two kits. Switch between them and listen: the synth kit is clean and smooth, the recorded one carries the grit and room of real hits. Same pattern, same idea, two different textures, which is exactly the kind of swap similarity search is for.
Keep the one that feels right for your song.
say.straight: Your pattern on the synth kit and the recorded kit. Same notes, different texture. Keep the one that fits.
say.eli5: Same beat, two drum kits. Tap synth, then recorded. Which one do you like?

steps.q: What does sound similarity search compare?
steps.why: It listens to the sound, not the label.

whyWrong.1: Names are what it gets you away from.
whyWrong.2: Size says nothing about the sound.
whyWrong.3: Dates say nothing about the sound.

steps.q: Where does it look for similar sounds?
steps.why: It can only find what's in your library.

whyWrong.1: It searches your library, not the web.
whyWrong.3: Any sample in your library, not just kits.

steps.q: Why preview what it finds?
options: similar is a score, not a perfect match
steps.why: Close isn't the same as right for your song.

whyWrong.1: Often they're great. Just not guaranteed.
whyWrong.3: It gives you a list.

steps.next: Your kit is chosen. Back to your song path, or on to mpe and tuning.

lessons.title: mpe and tuning systems

song.why: notes that slide into each other and pitches that sit slightly off the grid make a lead sound sung instead of typed

lessons.learn: How mpe gives each note its own bend and pressure, how Live 12's tuning systems step outside the usual 12 notes, and a taste of both on your lead.
youCan: say what mpe adds to normal midi
say what a tuning system and a Scala file are
give your lead slides and in-between pitches

say.mentor: A low note, then a high one, jumping straight there. That's how a keyboard thinks: one note, then the next, each fixed to a set pitch. A singer or a violinist doesn't work like that. They slide between notes, bend them, lean on them, and land between the keys when it feels right.
say.straight: Low note, high note, a straight jump. Voices and violins slide, bend and land between notes. Keyboards don't, by default.
say.eli5: One note, then another, jumping. A singer can slide from one to the other like going down a slide.

say.mentor:
With normal midi there's one pitch bend for the whole keyboard. Bend one note in a chord and every note bends. Mpe, short for midi polyphonic expression, gives each note its own bend, its own slide and its own pressure. Press harder on one note and only that note changes.
You need a controller that can sense it, like Push 3's pads, a Roli Seaboard or a LinnStrument.
Live 12 also added tuning systems. The usual 12 equal notes in an octave is only one way to tune. Load a Scala file, a tuning file that ends in .scl, and your whole set plays in a different tuning: just intonation, 24 notes to the octave, an old historical tuning, or one of your own.
say.straight:
Normal midi has one bend for all notes. Mpe gives each note its own bend, slide and pressure. You need an mpe controller, like Push 3.
Live 12's tuning systems let the whole set leave the usual 12 notes. Load a Scala (.scl) file for just intonation, 24 notes to the octave, or older tunings.
say.eli5:
Usually if you bend one note, they all bend. With mpe, each finger can wiggle its own note.
Live 12 can also use notes that sit between the usual ones, if you load a special tuning file.

deeper.title: switching it on
deeper.say: Mpe has to be switched on in each device that supports it, and most start with it off. On a synth that doesn't support it, bends still move every note together.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with your lead. Glide makes each note slide up or down into the next instead of jumping, the way a voice would. Turn it up and listen to your melody start to sing.
Detune pulls your lead's three oscillators slightly away from each other, by fractions of a note, so the pitch sits a little off the grid. A touch sounds warm and alive. A lot sounds seasick. Keep what suits your song.
say.straight: Your lead. Glide slides between notes. Detune pulls its oscillators fractions of a note apart, off the usual pitches. Keep what suits your song.
say.eli5: Turn glide and your notes slide into each other. Turn detune and the sound gets wobbly and wide. Stop where you like it.

steps.q: What does mpe stand for?
steps.why: Polyphonic expression, expression on many notes at once.

whyWrong.1: Not a patch editor.
whyWrong.3: Not an edition.

steps.q: With normal midi, you bend one note in a chord. What happens?
steps.why: Normal midi has one bend for the whole keyboard. Mpe fixes that.

whyWrong.1: That's what mpe gives you.
whyWrong.2: Bend still works, just on everything.
whyWrong.3: Bend changes pitch, not volume.

steps.q: What's a Scala file for in Live 12?
steps.why: A .scl file describes a tuning, and the whole set follows it.

whyWrong.1: Kits come from the browser.
whyWrong.3: Mapping happens in map mode.

steps.q: What does glide do to your lead?
options: slides each note into the next
steps.why: Notes slide instead of jumping, like a voice.

whyWrong.1: Glide is pitch, not level.
whyWrong.3: Tempo stays the same.

lessons.title: midi effects tour

song.why: stacking extra notes on top of your chords makes them fuller without you playing a single new note

lessons.learn: What midi effects do before a note reaches the synth, a quick tour of Live's main ones, and stacking extra notes onto your chords the way the Chord effect does.
youCan: say where midi effects sit and what they change
name what Arpeggiator, Chord, Scale and Note Echo do
make your chords fuller by stacking notes

say.mentor: One note, held. Before a note like this ever reaches a synth, it's just an instruction: this pitch, this hard, this long. Midi effects work on that instruction. They can add notes, move them, repeat them or spread them out in time, and the synth plays whatever comes out the other side.
say.straight: Before a note reaches the synth it's just data: pitch, how hard, how long. Midi effects change that data first.
say.eli5: Before a note makes a sound, it's a little message saying which note and how long. Midi effects change the message before the synth hears it.

say.mentor:
Midi effects sit before the instrument on a midi track, so they only touch notes, never sound.
Arpeggiator takes a chord you hold and plays its notes one after another as a pattern. Chord adds up to six extra notes on top of every note you play, so one finger becomes a full chord. Scale moves every note into a key, so nothing clashes. Note Echo repeats notes like a delay, but each echo is a fresh note that goes through the synth again.
They stack, too. Scale, then Chord, then Arpeggiator turns one held key into a moving pattern that always fits.
say.straight: Midi effects go before the instrument and only change notes. Arpeggiator plays held chords as patterns. Chord adds up to six notes per note. Scale keeps notes in key. Note Echo repeats notes. They stack.
say.eli5: Arpeggiator plays your chord one note at a time. Chord adds more notes to each note. Scale keeps every note in tune with your song. Note Echo plays notes again and again, quieter.

deeper.title: a few more
deeper.say: Random adds surprise notes, with a chance setting for how often. Velocity changes how hard notes are played. Pitch moves everything up or down. Arpeggiator's hold mode keeps playing after you let go.

deeper.title: order matters
deeper.say: A midi effect after the instrument does nothing, because by then it's sound, not notes. And midi effects don't work on audio tracks at all.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with your chords. Voicing stacks extra notes onto every note your chords play: first a low octave underneath, then the octave above and the fifth, like pulling out organ stops. It's the same idea as Live's Chord effect, extra notes added on top of what's already there.
Spread pulls the voices slightly apart for a wider, shimmering sound. Turn both until your chords fill the space without crowding your lead.
say.straight: Your chords. Voicing stacks an octave below, then the octave above and the fifth, like the Chord effect. Spread widens it. Fill the space without crowding your lead.
say.eli5: Turn voicing and your chords get more notes, deeper and higher. Turn spread and they get wider. Stop when they sound full.

lessons.title: max for live

song.why: a filter that moves on its own every note gives your lead motion without you touching anything

lessons.learn: What Max for Live is, the devices you'll actually use from it, and giving your lead the kind of automatic movement those devices are famous for.
youCan: say what Max for Live is and which edition of Live has it
name a few Max for Live devices and what they do
give your lead filter movement that plays itself

say.mentor: A note that just sits there. Now picture its filter opening and closing on its own, in time, while you do something else. Live can't always do every move you can imagine out of the box, so it lets you build new devices for it. That's Max for Live.
say.straight: A static note. Max for Live lets you add devices that do things Live doesn't, like moving a filter on its own.
say.eli5: This note stays the same. Max for Live lets people build new gadgets for Live, like one that makes the sound move by itself.

say.mentor:
Max for Live comes with Live Suite. It's a visual programming tool from Cycling '74: instead of typing code, you connect small boxes, called objects, with patch cables. A device made this way sits in Live like any other, with its own knobs you can automate and map.
Most people never build one. They use the ones that ship with Live, like LFO, which wobbles any control you point it at, and Envelope Follower, which turns how loud a sound is into movement. Open a device in edit mode and you see the patch inside.
say.straight: Max for Live comes with Suite. You build devices by wiring objects with patch cables. Most people use ready-made ones: LFO wobbles any control, Envelope Follower turns loudness into movement.
say.eli5: Max for Live lets you build new sound gadgets by joining boxes with lines. Most people just use the ones that come with Live, like LFO, which wiggles a knob for you.

deeper.title: mapping an lfo
deeper.say: Drop LFO on a track, press its map button, and click the control you want it to move, like a filter's cutoff. The filter now sweeps on its own. Envelope Follower mapped to a delay's feedback makes the echoes swell when the sound gets louder.

deeper.title: careful with cpu
deeper.say: A badly built device can eat your computer's power, so watch the cpu meter when you load lots of them. Hundreds more are shared free online as .amxd files, and they load like presets.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with your lead. An LFO would sweep the filter on its own over time. The closest move here is env: it makes the filter open on every note and close again, so your lead moves by itself without you touching a thing.
Set cutoff low so there's room to open, then raise env until each note has a little wah to it. Keep it where your lead feels alive but not busy.
say.straight: Your lead. Env opens the filter on every note by itself, the kind of automatic movement Max for Live's LFO gives you. Cutoff low, env up, stop before it's busy.
say.eli5: Turn cutoff down, then turn env up. Now every note goes wah on its own. Stop where you like it.

lessons.title: accessibility in live

song.why: setting your lead's level and tone by keyboard alone shows your song never needs a mouse

lessons.learn: What Live 12 added so more people can make music in it, and shaping your own lead using only the keyboard.
youCan: name the accessibility features Live 12 added
say what key map mode does
shape a part of your song without a mouse

say.mentor:
A kick, steady as a heartbeat. You don't need to see it to feel it. Music has always been something you do by ear and by hand, but software has often assumed you can see a screen perfectly and steer a mouse precisely.
Live 12 changed a lot of that.
say.straight: Music is ears and hands. Software often assumes perfect sight and a mouse. Live 12 changed a lot of that.
say.eli5: You can feel this beat without looking at anything. Live 12 makes it easier to make music even if you can't see the screen well or use a mouse.

say.mentor:
Live 12 added support for screen readers, the software that reads what's on screen out loud, so the names and values of controls can be spoken. It added high contrast themes that make controls easier to tell apart, and much more of Live can now be moved around and changed from the keyboard.
These help everyone. High contrast is easier in a bright room, and keyboard control is often faster and more precise than dragging.
say.straight: Live 12 added screen reader support, high contrast themes and wider keyboard navigation. They help everyone, not only people who need them.
say.eli5: Live 12 can read controls out loud, can make the screen easier to see, and can be used with just the keyboard. That helps lots of people.

deeper.title: key map mode
deeper.say: Cmd or ctrl and k turns on key map mode. Click a control, press a key, and that key now works it. Map your clips, scenes and on or off switches to keys and you can run a whole set from the keyboard.

deeper.title: this app too
deeper.say: Here, enter moves you on to the next step, and when there's a question, the number keys pick an answer. Tab gets you to any knob.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with your lead. Try it without the mouse. Press tab until a knob is selected, then use the arrow keys: up or right turns it up, down or left turns it down. Hold shift for bigger steps. Home and end jump to the bottom and the top.
Set your lead's level so it sits where you want it against the beat, then use cutoff to brighten or darken it. All by keyboard.
say.straight: Your lead, by keyboard. Tab to a knob, arrows to turn it, shift for bigger steps, home and end for the ends. Set level, then cutoff.
say.eli5: Press tab to pick a knob. Press the arrow keys to turn it up and down. Set how loud your tune is, then how bright.

steps.why: Keyboard control and high contrast speed things up for lots of people.

whyWrong.1: They're vital for some and handy for everyone.
whyWrong.3: They work without any controller.

steps.why: Shift makes each press move further.

whyWrong.1: Home and end jump to the ends. Nothing resets.
whyWrong.2: It changes the knob, not mute.
whyWrong.3: The arrow sets the direction.
